At least three soldiers have died, and four others have been wounded in an attack involving explosives dropped from drones, followed by a clash inside a military compound in northeastern Colombia.

Local authorities blamed the attack late Friday, which targeted a military unit in the municipality of Ocaña, in the Norte de Santander department, which borders Venezuela, on the rebel National Liberation Army (ELN).

Two soldiers died at the scene and a third after receiving medical attention, Colombia's military said on X on Saturday.

President Abelardo de la Espriella condemned the attack.

"For every police officer or soldier murdered, we will bring the full weight and legitimate force of the State down upon the criminals,” Espriella said.

Much of ELN, an armed group active since 1964, is based in the Catatumbo region, which includes parts of the Norte de Santander and Cesar departments. ELN also harbors dissident factions of the now-defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) that did not join the peace agreement a decade ago.

Both groups are vying for control of the strategic region, which connects to the porous border with Venezuela and is one of Colombia’s primary coca-producing areas.

In August, an explosion outside a police station in Cucuta injured 11 police officers and killed a police dog. Officials also blamed that attack on the ELN. Earlier this week, at least one civilian was killed and 11 other people were injured after a car bomb exploded outside a police station in northeastern Colombia.

News.title: Newcastle’s limitations exposed by Bournemouth before hosts fightback for draw
News.content:
A reality check is not necessarily a bad thing. There has been a lot of hype and excitement on Tyneside and a self-congratulating tone to their own end of summer appraisals.

But this was a reminder of the team’s limitations and the fact that only three of their eight summer signings started the game, with two more coming off the bench, underlined they are a work in progress.

In truth, that is fine. It is the start of September and the Premier League campaign is only three games old. They have a new manager and a new-look team. There has been a significant amount of change in a very short period of time.

It was not the easiest summer, and despite the insistence from senior figures at the club that they had always remained calm and methodical during their summer reset, there was a whiff of crisis only a few weeks ago.

When Eddie Howe quit as manager and Bruno Guimarães, the captain, forced his move to Arsenal at the start of August, Newcastle looked in disarray. So, to have started the season unbeaten from three games against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth is encouraging.

It is also worth highlighting just how good the visitors were. In the first half Bournemouth were superb, rushing Newcastle, forcing mistakes and pouring forward in numbers. In Alex Scott, just as he was in their victory here last season, Bournemouth had the best player on the pitch.

That opens up another conversation. Newcastle played like this a lot at home in Howe’s final season in charge, especially in the second-half of the campaign, but tended to lose not draw the game.

On this occasion, they secured a decent point with a late equaliser thanks to substitute Ramsey, who looked good when he replaced the off-colour Lewis Miley.

Bournemouth will feel they should have held on. They had taken a deserved lead through Marcus Tavernier, who took advantage of a static and ball-watching Amar Dedić to bundle home from close range.

News.title: ‘It’s just a useless gimmick’: Telegraph readers react to Dyson’s latest gadget
News.content:
Would you spend over £400 on a toothbrush? Telegraph readers aren’t convinced.

The new Dyson CameraJet has just launched, retailing for £419.99, which brushes, flosses and mouth-washes in one, with the help of a camera.

After Rebecca Astill gave her verdict on the gadget, we asked Telegraph readers for their views and whether Dyson can convince them to trade in their old faithfuls.

They share the toothbrushes they swear by, from manual to electric models, and whether they see any reason to upgrade. Here’s what they had to say.

Why readers are unconvinced

The majority of readers seem unconvinced by the CameraJet, with John arguing that a toothbrush and a smartphone “sounds like two accidents waiting to happen. Squirted in the eye with mouthwash as you drop the phone down the toilet”.

“It’s just a useless gimmick,” argues reader Donald Mckie, a retired NHS dentist. “The average patient wouldn’t have a clue what they would be looking at in their mouth on a phone screen,” he adds.

“Dyson as a brand is an aspiration for many but I don’t know how this appliance would improve anyone’s oral health.”

In his view, “the tank for the mouthwash at 12.5ml is far too small, the industry average will be somewhere near 250-300ml” to last long enough and successfully dislodge sticky plaque.

He also questions the picture quality of the camera with water spray, saliva, lips, facial hair and toothpaste in the way. “People nowadays will expect pin sharp detail, which I doubt this will deliver.”

News.title: DiCaprio’s Amazonian warrior queen
News.content:
It was while she was in hiding after recovering from the sixth attempt on her life, that the activist Juma Xipaia got a call asking if she would agree to be the subject of a documentary. The first female chief of the Middle Xingu region of the Brazilian Amazon, Xipaia was well known in Brazil for her passionate attempts to protect her indigenous community from the effects of deforestation, illegal gold-mining and – in particular – the catastrophic environmental consequences of the $11 billion Belo Monte hydroelectric dam project, a wildly ambitious and destructive endeavour that has affected livelihoods, fish stocks, ecosystems and biodiversity, with legal challenges still ongoing today.

Thirty-four-year-old Xipaia’s outspoken resistance and exposure of corruption relating to the dam’s construction led to the threats on her life. The last attempt was by poisoning, via a food delivery company, which resulted in her being on a ventilator with 70 per cent organ failure. She was on the verge of death, when, she says, she had a dream that she was given a choice – to take the easy path of dying, or the difficult path of coming back, and because she’s a fighter, that’s the one she chose. And a week later she walked out of the hospital.

Leonardo DiCaprio described the activist as one of the most incredible people he’d ever met Credit : Lalo de Almeida/Folhapress, FSP

Like many activists representing indigenous communities she walked a tightrope between protecting the interests and traditions of her people, and not being perceived as standing in the way of progress in terms of the economic development that benefits Brazil as a whole, a paradox that was defined when President Lula da Silva regained power in 2023, and brought Xipaia into government.

Richard Ladkani, a film director who has made vibrant environmental documentaries such as The Ivory Game (about poaching) and Sea of Shadows (marine activists), was the man who called her. It was 2019, when Brazil was still under the brutal rule of Jair Bolsonaro and destruction of the Amazon was at its peak – an area of rainforest the size of Belgium was burned during his presidency, and thousands of illegal goldmines flourished, contaminating the forest, polluting the river with mercury (mercury is used to bind gold) and bringing crime and disruption to previously pristine areas.

Film-maker Richard Ladkani in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

“All summer long we had seen these dramatic apocalyptic images,” says Ladkani. “And I was posing for photos at the premiere of Sea of Shadows, with [executive producers] Leo DiCaprio and Jane Goodall, when Leo leaned over and whispered, ‘So Richard, what’s next?’

“And I said, 'We've got to do something about the Amazon.’”

DiCaprio came onboard as producer, and Goodall as an ambassador. Ladkani knew he had to find a powerful central figure to provide human and emotional context, someone who would be the voice of the Amazon. He drew up a list of possible candidates, until the Brazilian journalist Eliane Brum told him “do not make a decision until you have spoken to Juma Xipaia – when she speaks, the world listens. She can silence a whole room with her energy.”

‘For a long time I had been seen as a soldier, an army of one’

Right now, in a small restaurant in New York, Xipaia is not really in the mood to talk. It is February, and it’s snowing, and Ladkani, Xipaia and her husband, Hugo Loss, are here to publicise the resulting documentary, Yanuni – which took six years to make – at a screening attended by UN representatives and Brazilian diplomats. The recent news about Trump’s exploits in Venezuela has shaken them all and, more specifically, Juma has had a bad experience with American food which doesn’t really agree with her. She is a little reticent at first, but soon opens up with the help of an interpreter, and explains to me what it meant to be a cacique (chief), and how she was selected.

Indigenous leader Juma Xipaia and her husband Hugo Loss in the city of Aracaju, Brazil Credit : Lalo de Almeida/Folhapress, FSP

“I never chose to be a cacique,” she says, “but I couldn’t stay quiet in the face of exploitation of my people – there was violence, and women being harassed and raped.” She is referring to the collateral damage that importing thousands of workers to build a dam inevitably brings. “Usually the role of cacique is given to the oldest male in the community – my dad and my uncles and my brother were all caciques, but the elders knew that they could trust me never to negotiate our rights with corporations or politicians, never to compromise. For a long time I had been seen as a soldier, an army of one. I accepted the position for two years, with the goal of strengthening on our territories and bringing sovereignty to our people.”

Xipaia was born in 1991 and had an idyllic childhood, she says, growing up in Tucumã, a small indigenous community along the Iriri River, about 250 miles west of the city of Altamira. They lived in wooden houses and ate fruit and nuts from the forest and fish from the river, and in 2006 she moved to Altamira for her education. But threats were encroaching her community, with land opened up for mining and farming, and in 2011, a licence was granted to construct the Belo Monte Dam, to stop up parts of the Xingu River, one of the most species-rich areas of the Amazon.

Aged just 21, Xipaia spoke out against the dam at a public hearing, but despite lawsuits, protest from indigenous people and large sections of society, construction went ahead. Xipaia attended law school in Altamira and studied plans put forward by Norte Energia, the company that built Belo Monte, helping to expose corruption that was going on within. In 2015, at the age of 24, she became a cacique, the first female leader of her people. Other communities had been bought off by Norte Energia with gifts of stoves, fridges, TVs.

In November 2019, she led a protest of angry Brazilian landowners and farmers to disrupt the Amazon: Center of the World international conference in Altamira. But by now she had become a target, and by the time Ladkani called her she had survived six attempts on her life, including her car being rammed with children in the back, and a threat to kidnap her son. She went into hiding for a year and she didn’t want to talk to anyone.

“She thought, the only way I’m going to survive is if I stop talking, because when I talk, people want to kill me,” Ladkani says. But she was finally convinced to take a call from him, and from the first moment, he says, he knew he had found the voice for his film. “Her poetry is the thing that stands out – the way she can describe emotions and feelings and put things into context, I felt it was unique. And when she told me the story of how she almost died because of the poisoning, I was in tears.

“I told her I wanted her to be the voice in the film and also offered her the role of producer. Because I knew nothing of indigenous life and I needed her to lead the way.”

An aerial view of the Belo Monte hydroelectric dam in Altamira Credit : CARLOS FABAL

It was a struggle from the word go. Xipaia was not happy about a translator being involved because of security reasons; she couldn’t trust anyone. So Ladkani, who is Austrian, took intensive lessons in Portuguese and within six months was fluent. “It was a key thing to show that I meant business and took her concerns very seriously,” he tells me.

The security budget for the film was huge, they needed the best, most experienced people: safe houses, secure drivers. And the arrangements had to extend for a year after filming was completed – a total of seven years. “Leo was extremely important here because he raised the first third of the budget, and this encouraged other philanthropists to be part of it.”

Filming began in 2020. There was no script and Ladkani didn’t know what he was going to get from it, just that he needed to tell the story of the pillaging of the Amazon via Xipaia’s voice.

And in the end it was a wild ride: it started with Xipaia leading protests against Bolsonaro, but after Lula was elected in 2023, he established a Ministry for Indigenous Rights, of which Xipaia was made state secretary, implementing a series of bills for the protection of the forest and employing lawyers, biologists and engineers to combat the destruction of the Amazon.

Juma Xipata and Leonardo DiCaprio at the Yanuni Premiere during the 2025 Tribeca Festival in New York City. Credit : John Nacion/Getty Images for Tribeca Festival

The film documents her move from her village to set up home in Brasilia with her son; getting together with her husband Hugo Loss, head of special operations for Ibama (the Brazilian Institute of Renewable and Natural Resources), an elite outfit conducting raids on illegal mines; and the birth of their first child, who was called Yanuni.

It was a lengthy, exciting journey, an improvisation which resulted in thousands of hours of film. “I just had to go with the unpredictable. The strength of any documentary is when unforeseen things happen, because a twist in direction is the greatest thing of any film structure.

“And we had that multiple times. I had chosen a woman to be the voice of the Amazon and two years later she became the second most powerful woman in the Indigenous Ministry – I get goosebumps now at the sheer luck. That was the first twist, and then Hugo enters her life, who happens to be this charismatic soldier of an elite force who would take me to the frontline of the Amazon resistance, and then Juma becomes pregnant and gives birth to Yanuni. Holy s**t. If I had written that as a script, everyone would have thrown it out as complete fiction.”

‘I said, how dangerous is it? And he said, “Well, the risk of you dying is 50 per cent”’

Leo DiCaprio was a producer on the film (rather than his usual role of executive producer), which meant he was far more involved. “He not only provided the money, but he gave me meaningful support throughout the production,” says Ladkani. In November 2021 DiCaprio attended Cop 26 in Glasgow, where he met Xipaia for the first time. “That meeting was spectacular – Leo posted a picture of the two of them together and said that she was one of the most incredible people he’d ever met.” The resulting attention helped to protect Xipaia, because a public profile is to some extent a safeguard. “There she is next to DiCaprio, so she’s not just a voiceless indigenous person from somewhere in the Amazon.”

There were many technical challenges. Because of security, Ladkani couldn’t film in the normal way, with lighting and a crew. “I had a second cinematographer, a brilliant guy from Brazil, called Fábio Nascimento, and I took him with me when I could – but that was only 30 per cent of the time. The rest I shot alone. I downsized my gear and basically shot the film with a DSLR, like a photo camera, so I looked like a tourist. To an outsider, I was just a white gringo taking pictures.” Xipaia had a hidden microphone beneath her shirt. If Ladkani was ever confronted, he claimed to be a YouTuber.

“Security demanded that we shot the film incognito, and that became its strength, because I was embedded within the family to the extent that they stopped noticing me,” says Ladkani.

An illegal gold-mining ship destroyed by Ibama in the Brazilian Amazon – it is dangerous work, with agents risking serious injury and even their lives Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

Hugo Loss’s job involved protecting indigenous communities and flying over the forest and rivers of the Amazon routing out illegal goldmines, dredgers and excavators. His small team lands, arrests the miners and sets fire to all the expensive equipment, which is too bulky to confiscate. In the film we see massive plumes of thick black smoke rising above the forest. Penalties for environmental crime are insubstantial, but, says Loss, “It’s not for President Lula to change those things, it’s Congress, and it’s hard to change the law. But destroying the equipment is a real deterrent, because the machines are expensive, so it’s a risky investment.”

An illegal gold mine in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

Loss and Xipaia met when her village was attacked in 2020 by illegal goldminers; she was in Altamira, a two-day boat ride away. She put out a cry for help on social media and Loss, who was also in Altamira, saw it and responded right away. He picked Xipaia up in a helicopter and asked her to take him to the exact location of the miners’ dredger. The attackers spotted them and ran, but Ibama were able to seize their boat and secure the area. “He saved her village and her people and her parents from an immediate attack and they fell in love and have been together ever since,” says Ladkani.

“I’m usually very shy about these things but from the first time I saw her in the helicopter I couldn’t stop thinking about her,” admits Loss. “Three months later I was doing an Ibama operation on land to remove some illegal loggers and I saw a hawk’s nest and I took a picture of it and sent it to her,” says Loss.

“It’s the bird whose feather I wear in my headdress,” interrupts Xipaia, shyly. She admits that she had first met Loss before the helicopter ride, at a meeting, but he was leaving as she arrived. “He shook my hand and I made eye contact with him and something told me – I can’t really explain what – that he was going to be my husband.”

Loss holds a Master’s degree in social anthropology from the University of Brasília and is one of Ibama’s most experienced field agents, yet he spent a good part of his career sidelined by Bolsonaro, who had no interest in protecting the environment. In February 2023, under Lula, he was appointed Ibama’s coordinator of enforcement.

Loss has taken part in hundreds of operations. His job is a dangerous one. We watch him flying helicopters over swathes of forest to spot mines, or patrolling the rivers looking for dredgers. Recently one of his team was killed in an ambush, another got burns over 60 per cent of his body.

Hugo Loss, Xipaia’s husband, on a mission to destroy illegal mining equipment for Ibama, Brazil’s government enforcement agency

Ladkani asked to accompany Loss on a raid. “Hugo told me, it's too dangerous, the risk of you dying is too high. It’s a small team, and you would be taking the place of a soldier on the helicopter so we would be down one security man, which means our job is much harder, and by the way, if we get into a gun fight, we are not your bodyguards, we are there to finish a job. You would have to save yourself.

“I said, how dangerous is it? And he said, ‘Well, the risk of you dying is 50 per cent.’ I laughed – and then I realised he wasn’t joking.

Film-maker Richard Ladkani in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

“Of course I had to think about that – I have a wife and two daughters. My wife and I discussed it. She grew up in a war zone in Beirut, so she understands threats, and how you can mitigate risks as well. She is also the producer of this film. We have had a long journey together – making conflict zone films like Sea of Shadows and The Ivory Game was no joke. But this one felt like a different level because of the 50 per cent quote.” He smiles.”‘I did hostile-environment training and we augmented the security to a degree where I felt it wasn’t 50 per cent any more.”

An illegal airbase in the Brazilian Amazon being destroyed Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

So Ladkani joined the team, and the resulting episode is terrifying: they are patrolling the river when they find a huge illegal dredger, used for gold mining. They board the dredger, its crew of illegal miners are put in a small boat and dispatched, and Loss’s team set fire to it. Attempting to get away, they realise their boat is still attached to the dredger by a chain, and they have only moments before an oxygen tank below the deck of the dredger explodes. Loss has to shoot the chain, but he has to hit it while it is taut, or the bullet would glance off. “The oxygen tank is steel and if it had exploded we would have been killed by the fragments if we were within 100 metres of that boat – and we were six metres away. It was Hugo who shot the chain – it took 50 shots at least. When Juma saw that footage she broke down and sobbed,” says Ladkani.

Do you like your job? I ask Loss.

He smiles. “Yes I do.”

Back in the 1970s, when two major roads were originally carved into the Amazon rainforest, of which 60 per cent is in Brazil, it opened it up for settlers to devastating effects – the population of the Brazilian Amazon quadrupled and millions of acres of trees were cut down for timber or land clearance and farming, and the rivers became polluted. Thousands of garimpeiros (prospectors) arrived, bringing disease, destruction and violence.

Indigenous people from the Mura tribe in a deforested area inside the Amazon rainforest near Humaita, Amazonas State, Brazil Credit : Ueslei Marcelino/REUTERS

Despite the protected reserves created by Lula during his first tenure (2003 to 2011), when Bolsonaro took over, he vowed that he would not demarcate a single millimetre of Indigenous land.

There was reason to be hopeful when Lula was re-elected in 2023, especially when he created the Ministry for Indigenous People. But it was an uphill struggle, and Xipaia left the post of State Secretary after about two years, and retired to her territory, where she still is. “She realised that it would be years, if not decades, before change could happen and she felt that her power was with activism from the front lines rather than being in an office in the city,” says Ladkani. “And what really hurt was her children having to grow up in the city and not having the connection to nature that she had.”

Smoke from illegal fires lit by farmers rises in Manaquiri, Amazonas state Credit : MICHAEL DANTAS

There has been a lot of progress, Juma says, compared to the Bolsonaro years “when it was genocide”. “It is hard to quantify all the changes because even though there was a change in the administration, it is important to understand that the government structure is very colonialist, no matter who is in power, and everything takes time. I entered the ministry when it was just being born.

“It was hard working in an office every day and not spending time with my children, and my son Tuppak [eight] told me that he wanted to go back to the forest, he was having a hard time at school in the city. I did not want to rob my son of that kind of childhood – being in the territory and getting his knowledge from the forest.”

I ask Loss and Xipaia if, with the way things are now, they are more inclined to hope or despair. “Most of the time I don’t think about the future,” says Loss. “I just focus on doing my work, one operation at a time.”

A wildfire consumes land deforested by cattle farmers near Novo Progresso, Para state, Brazil Credit : MICHAEL DANTAS/AFP via Getty Images

Xipaia thinks. “It depends where I am. When I’m in the forest with my family, there is immense fulfilment which is hard to explain; it gives me the hope and energy to keep wanting to protect it, and I want the whole world to get to know it.

“When I walk through the forest and harvest food there with my family and my people, it reminds me of what my ancestors were doing. The innocence of children, the idea of clean water, food without toxins – this gives me hope.”

“I don’t feel despair,” says Ladkani. “I feel like we’re in a war. There are plenty of good people fighting back, and that gives me hope. And there are lives on the line that we need to care about, which is the indigenous people, who are the frontline of our defence. They are defending nature for us so we need to make sure that they are heard and seen and respected. And we hope that the film puts a human face to that.

“We can’t pretend that destroying the biggest ecosystem on the planet is OK. If we lose the Amazon, we all lose.”

Yanuni will be released later this year

News.title: Alexander Isak starts to justify £125m price tag with double
News.content:
Emersonn, Ipswich’s Brazilian striker, did not see the ball in the opening exchanges and, by the time he did, Liverpool had zoomed into the distance to such an extent that you felt it was going to be impossible for them to peg their visitors back.

“I hate having to talk about good performances when you do not get points,” O’Neil declared to a room full of raised eyebrows and you can only assume his message was to ensure that morale in the dressing room was not drooping.

What damage was inflicted with Liverpool’s first significant attack. Gakpo, the subject of an £80m bid from Manchester City, was never going to allow transfer speculation to disrupt his focus and he nudged a perfect little ball into Isak’s path in the sixth minute to show his wellbeing.

The next move announced the return of Isak. One touch gave him an avenue to shoot, the next was a shot with his right foot that was so hard from 16 yards, on an angle, it bent the wrists of Kjell Scherpen as it howled into the net. Critics will feel Ipswich’s keeper should have done better.

Your first thought was to think of the first goal Isak scored in English football in September 2022, a similarly venomous drive, against Liverpool at Anfield. He oozed quality that evening, his pace and skill had Jürgen Klopp’s defenders persistently fretting and this is what he was doing again.

It was no coincidence that three minutes later, he came up with another wonderful goal. This one owed much to the beautiful pass Gakpo presented to him, an inch-perfect through ball with the outside of his right foot, but Isak still showed great poise to bamboozle Scherpen.

News.title: Forced displacement in the West Bank could be ‘crime against humanity’, says UN report
News.content:
Israel’s forced displacement of more than 33,000 Palestinians in the West Bank could amount to a “crime against humanity” and involves “ethnic cleansing”, according to a report published by the UN.

A report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that Israeli actions in the area had sparked the “largest and longest displacement crisis in the West Bank since 1967” – the year in which Israel captured the territory.

The report said “large-scale, long-term and systematic displacement of over 33,000 Palestinians from refugee camps … during Israel’s Operation Iron Wall [which] raises serious concerns of the crime against humanity of forcible transfer”.

It added: “The documented use of airstrikes, armoured bulldozers and controlled detonations, to render entire camps uninhabitable, to force the displacement of their residents and to prevent their return, in the absence of imperative military necessity to justify such destruction and displacement, are not permissible under international law, appear to amount to collective punishment and raise concerns of ethnic cleansing.”

The 27-page report covers the period December 5, 2024 to January 31, 2026.

In January 2025, Israeli forces launched “Operation Iron Wall” in the northern West Bank in a bid to counter what they said were terrorist threats.

They destroyed hundreds of homes, cut off water and electricity, and barred humanitarian access to the Jenin, Nur Sham and Tulkarm refugee camps.

By October 2025, 52 per cent of structures in Jenin camp, 48 per cent in Nur Shams and 36 percent in Tulkarm had been destroyed or damaged.

The three camps are among 19 in the West Bank established to shelter Palestinians after the 1948 Nakba, and are administered by the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA).

Although still referred to as refugee camps, they are in fact now densely packed towns.

News.title: When is Black Friday 2026? This year’s dates and what to expect
News.content:
Five tips for finding genuine Black Friday discounts and deals

Learning how to find the best Black Friday discounts can make a meaningful difference to your festive budget, especially if you’re a keen sale shopper. The following five tips are a good starting point.

1. Don’t over-fixate on Black Friday itself

Although the day of Black Friday brings some of the best discounts of the festive sale season, good deals are likely to be available both before and after it – and some items may sell out.

“When we look at our pricing data on a daily level, you have certain events such as Amazon’s October Prime sale [not yet confirmed for 2026] that are an earlier vector for change in prices,” says Vivek Pandya, a director at Adobe for Business.

“We typically see more significant discounts starting to emerge as we get into late October or early November, and these really kick up a notch as we get into Black Friday week.”

So, while interest in Black Friday deals will peak around the day itself, some of the best deals may have been available since the beginning of the week, or earlier.

2. Expand your search to everyday essentials

At Telegraph Recommended, we’ve picked up on a proliferation of discounts on everyday household items during recent Black Friday sales (and during other occasional events such as Prime Day). If you need a top-up of items such as cleaning products or pet supplies, this could be a thrifty time to buy them.

“These sales have become a spending spree on what retailers frame as ‘everyday essentials’, as well as bigger items and gifts,” says Pandya. Last year’s Cyber Weekend saw a 260 per cent spike in sales of “personal care” items including cosmetics, shampoos, fragrances and toothbrushes, according to Adobe.

3. Use a price tracker

Free price tracking tools such as camelcamelcamel can show you how the price of a product has changed over time. This allows you to identify when a Black Friday deal has actually brought a product’s price significantly lower than usual, or when the retailer’s pricing strategy has artificially made a deal appear to be generous.

Gabrielė Vitkė, product marketing team lead at data-gathering specialist Decodo, warns shoppers to watch out for “anchoring”, where a product’s price is set high prior to Black Friday, allowing the retailer then to reduce it sharply and advertise an eye-catching reduction.

“Discounts on items such as electronics and computing products can seem steep, sometimes exceeding 50 per cent against the list price,” says Vitkė. “However, our data shows that prices in this category rose in the run-up to Black Friday 2025, which is a sign of anchor pricing before the ‘discount’ is applied.”

News.title: Indonesia wildfires trigger 50,000 respiratory infections
News.content:
More than 50,000 people have contracted respiratory infections in Indonesia, as raging wild fires blanket huge swathes of the country in a thick, toxic smoke.

The vast archipelago is only a month into its fire season, but intense blazes have proven hard to control across Sumatra and Indonesian Borneo. There are fears the situation will only get worse, because the “Godzilla” El Niño is set to suppress rains that would normally have helped extinguish the flames.

“Our problems are not over. September is the peak of El Niño,” said Raja Juli Antoni, the forestry minister. “September is the main fight for us.”

Already the toxic haze has spread across Southeast Asia. On Friday Kuching, a city in Malaysian Borneo, was the most polluted city in the world on the IQ Air Index, followed by Jakarta and Singapore.

The wildfires have brought memories of record-breaking blazes in 2015. Then, the smoke was linked to roughly 100,000 excess deaths in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, according to one study. The World Bank said Indonesia alone saw economic losses of $16.1bn, or 2 per cent of GDP.

News.title: Global hunger is a threat to Britain’s national security, report says
News.content:
Global hunger poses a direct threat to Britain’s national security, and tackling it should be a government priority, a new report from the London School of Economics has warned.

It says hunger is a major driver of mass migration, extreme violence and war – events that threaten significant repercussions for Britain and Europe’s national security.

“Hunger prevention is an important part of national security policy, not an optional act of charity,” Stuart Gordon, professor of International Development at LSE and author of the report, told The Telegraph.

Recent hunger crises in places like Sudan, Afghanistan and across North Africa have contributed significantly to rising numbers of people moving to the West.

Between January and November 2025 alone, 12,684 migrants from Sudan – which is facing what has been described as the worst hunger crisis in Africa’s history – arrived in Europe, roughly three times as many as the previous year.

Last year, an estimated 155,000 African refugees arrived in Europe.

“Food insecurity tests one of the most basic expectations people have of government: that it will protect access to the essentials of life,” said Prof Gordon.

“Food price shocks can rapidly escalate into political instability when governments are perceived to have failed to protect access to basic subsistence goods,” he added.

Former Match of the Day host and England star Gary Lineker has candidly opened up about his romantic life

Gary Lineker has opened up on his sad love life, revealing that he "doesn't need" a romantic partner. The 65-year-old has gone from strength to strength since departing Match of the Day in 2025.

‌



The ex-Barcelona forward is thriving as the co-owner of Goalhanger which has been identified as Britain’s fastest-growing business by the Sunday Times. His company, which is worth a staggering £100million, produces four of Spotify’s current top nine podcasts including his very own The Rest is Football show.

‌



Then there's The Box, the brand new game show he’s hosting on ITV from this Saturday night (September 5). With his professional life a benchmark for success, his romantic life seems empty by comparison.

‌



Lineker has disclosed that, despite "the odd date" and a "few short relationships," he’s been largely single since divorcing his ex, Danielle Bux, ten years ago.

In an interview with The Obersever, he said: “I’ve become very comfortable being unanswerable to anyone. Call that selfish if you want I don’t feel I need someone in my life.

"I have a lot of female friends who I get on really well with, so that’s satisfying because I love female company. But it’s the other bit that comes with it. I’m quite happy to be without that."

‌



In 2019 he branded himself as “unbelievably fussy” and even confessed that he's “not massively into sex”. The one-time England hero believes his testosterone levels have dipped in his advanced years and his interest in intimacy has subsequently dissipated.

The media mogul claimed he doesn’t see himself entering another long-term relationship. But he didn't rule it out entirely admitting he would be partial to a “thunderclap”.

View 3 Images Gary Lineker and Danielle Bux wed in 2009 (Image: undefined via Getty Images)

‌



The former Leicester and Everton striker has been married twice. He has four boys, George, Harry, Tobias and Angus, with his first wife, Michelle Cockayne, whom he married in 1986 before divorcing two decades later.

In 2007 the ex-BBC star began a relationship with Bux who was 20 years his junior. The couple later tied the knot in Italy but their marriage lasted just six years before they announced their separation in early 2016.

Sports.content:
Paul Merson singles out the Arsenal weak link that will cost them this season

Arsenal are attempting to defend their Premier League title this season, but former Gunners star Paul Merson feels their squad isn't deep enough to compete across all fronts

View 2 Images Paul Merson has given his take on Arsenal's squad depth (Image: Sky Sports)

Paul Merson has told Arsenal that their failure to sign a world-class forward will cost them the chance to challenge for the Champions League trophy this season.

The Gunners made an attempt to lure Vinicius Junior from Real Madrid before failing to land top target Julian Alvarez from Atletico Madrid. Mikel Arteta decided to sell attackers Gabriel Martinelli, Gabriel Jesus and Leandro Trossard, but only Christos Tzolis arrived this summer to bolster the front line.

It means Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyokeres are the only strikers in the squad, with Tzolis, Bukayo Saka, Noni Madueke, Max Dowman, Martin Odegaard and Eberechi Eze as the other forward-thinking players.

‌



Arsenal signed Tzolis, Bruno Guimaraes, Ezri Konsa, Illan Meslier and Piero Hincapie this summer, but Merson feels the failure to add another attacker will leave them short of crucial depth as the season progresses.

"I think they win the Premier League," he said on Sky Sports. "But they'll be short in the Champions League because of that, not having that extra person up front. You look at Havertz and Gyokeres - I like those two but they're not going to give you sleepless nights.

"And you look on the left and you've got Tzolis and Eze. Eze is a good footballer, but I prefer him in the middle than out wide and Tzolis is an up-and-down, he does what he says on the tin: a very hard-working left winger who is a manager's dream.

"My picture is, when you're playing PSG, Bayern Munich, Inter Milan away, Real Madrid and Barcelona, I can't imagine the right winger tossing and turning in bed at night thinking 'I've got to play against him'. But I can see it when Vinicius Junior is playing for Real Madrid.

‌



View 2 Images Vinicius Junior signed a new contract with Real Madrid after Arsenal's interest (Image: Getty)

"I think that was the one. At the start of the transfer window when they went for Vinicius Junior - and it was serious, it was closer than what people think. I think they concentrated on that too much and things passed them by and they missed out on other people.

"I think that would have taken them to another level. You'd have looked at that and thought 'Arsenal are shopping in a different market to everybody else'. I think they'll be short. I like Bruno Guimaraes - he came on the other day, steadies things, plays nice one-twos. He's a good footballer.

‌



"For me, they've done enough to win the Premier League again but I'd be surprised if they won the Champions League."

Asked if they should have challenged for Morgan Rogers, who joined Chelsea for £117m, or spent big on Vinicius, Merson replied: "I personally would have, especially getting rid of Martinelli and Trossard. I wouldn't have let Trossard go. He's a good football player and played in the big games.

"I always use the same thing: there's a company out there that sell more burgers and chicken nuggets than anyone else, but they still do adverts even though they're the best of the best at what they do. They still do adverts to let you know that. When you're at the top you buy players."

Sports.title: Richard Hughes' 18 Liverpool transfer ranked with best and worst deals decided
Sports.content:
Richard Hughes has left Liverpool after two years at the helm of the club as sporting director. The 47-year-old has decided to leave the club a year early, leaving behind a mixed legacy at Anfield.

Hughes arrived from Bournemouth in the summer of 2024 and was responsible for the decision to appoint Arne Slot as Jurgen Klopp's successor. He therefore took plenty of the plaudits when Slot delivered the Premier League title in his first campaign. But he has also been on the receiving end of his fair share of criticism, given what followed in a disappointing second season.

Liverpool splashed out over £400million on signings last summer, bringing in Alexander Isak (£125m), Florian Wirtz (£116m) and Hugo Ekitike (£79m) as the headline additions which were supposed to help solidify the Reds as the best team in the league. Those deals didn't immediately pay off, with Liverpool finishing fifth in the Premier League.

That cost Slot his job and prompted the hiring of Andoni Iraola for a summer rebuild. Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson and Ibrahima Konate all left on free transfers, leaving Hughes and his colleagues with a major task on their hands.

‌

Sports.title: Mike Dean backtracks on bombshell referee claims in live Sky Sports interview
Sports.content:
Mike Dean backtracks on bombshell referee claims in live Sky Sports interview

Former Premier League official Mike Dean sparked outrage earlier this week when he suggested he would play 'mini-games' while refereeing top-flight games

View 2 Images Mike Dean admitted he regretted the comments which have sparked backlash (Image: Sky Sports)

Former referee Mike Dean regrets his controversial comments on a podcast this week, but insists he always did his job “properly and professionally” during his 25-year career.

Dean sent shockwaves through football when he claimed on the ‘Jamie Vardy’s Having a Party’ podcast he would “joke about” during matches and would see how long he could go without blowing his whistle or leaving the centre circle.

The eye-catching remarks were immediately met with widespread criticism from former officials with the integrity of the game questioned, but Pro Ref – the new name for PGMOL – is yet to make a public comment on Dean’s sentiments.

After Dean started his refereeing career in 1985, he was promoted to the full referees’ list in 1997 before he was appointed to the Select Group of Premier League referees in 2000 until he retired in 2022.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

The 58-year-old from the Wirral released a statement on Friday where he insisted it was never his intention to “criticise or undermine the integrity” of his fellow officials before he reflected on the controversy during his appearance on Sky Sports ’ Soccer Saturday programme.

Asked by presenter Simon Thomas if in 25 years he ever deliberately failed to apply the laws of the game, Dean said: “No, because if I did, I wouldn’t have got as many games as I did.

“And I wouldn’t have been on the list for 25 years. I did my job properly and professionally for the full 25 years.

View 2 Images Mike Dean made the admission on Jamie Vardy's podcast (Image: Getty Images)

“I have no regrets over the way I refereed the game of football. I enjoyed what I did and I think the players enjoyed what I did as well.

“It is one of them comments, if you had your time again, you wouldn’t say it, but it’s been said now and been out there. There is nothing I can do now.

It is understood Dean’s claims have been met with bemusement by those with current involvement in officiating, with some noting a lack of factual detail in his stories.

Dean continued: “It is one of them where as a ref, I like to go out and my threshold was always high as a ref and not to give free-kicks.

“I would give a minimum amount of free-kicks as I can and if I can keep the game flowing, I would keep it flowing. Yes, if I’ve got to step in, I’ll give the free-kick but it is just one of them things you learn by your mistakes.

Article continues below

“Obviously I’ve said something this week that has come out a little bit wrong, I think I could have worded it a bit better than I said but you live and learn. Hopefully we can move on. We’ll see what happens.”

Sports.title: Alejandro Garnacho alarm bells ringing after Bruno Fernandes revealed Man Utd's true feelings
Sports.content:
Alejandro Garnacho alarm bells ringing after Bruno Fernandes revealed Man Utd's true feelings

Alejandro Garnacho's career has severely stalled in recent years

View 3 Images Alejandro Garnacho's attitude was called into question by Bruno Fernandes (Image: Ryan Pierse, Getty Images)

Alejandro Garnacho is at a crossroads in his football career. Once a highly-rated talent with heavy expectations of excellence placed on him, those days seem like a lifetime ago.

‌



The Argentine's form has been on a downward trajectory since the Ruben Amorim era at Manchester United, but questions about his attitude date back to his teenage years.

‌



His career at Old Trafford came to an end when he joined Chelsea for £40million in the 2025/26 campaign, as he went on to endure the worst season of his career, scoring just one goal in 24 Premier League games.

‌



The 22-year-old became surplus to requirements under Xabi Alonso this summer, with Garnacho inking a loan deal with Aston Villa - a move that could make-or-break his career. The winger has been told that he cannot ignore the magnitude of his stint at Villa if he wants to reignite his standing in the game.

Former Villa midfielder Ray Houghton said Garnacho's family have a responsibility to get through to him and make him understand that he won't continue to keep getting chances to impress at the highest level.

Michael Carrick hints he could fill problem Man Utd position without spending a penny READ MORE :

Man Utd striker transfer confirmed despite summer window closing READ MORE :

The 64-year-old told GOAL: "I've got every respect for the kid, but I think the alarm bells should be ringing. His closest people, his family and friends, should be telling him that. What they should be saying to him is: ‘Look where you've been, look what's happened to you and look where you are now, there's a reason this is happening, and it's down to you now.

‌



"This is another club that's going to give you a chance. You've got to seize it. No more excuses. No more saying, 'Oh well, there's something else at that club and someone else at that club.' That's all gone now. It's down to the individual now."

View 3 Images Alejandro Garnacho has played just 16 minutes in Aston Villa's opening two games (Image: Getty Images)

Houghton predicted that Villa boss Unai Emery will give Garnacho "tough love", but warned the winger that he'll be cast aside if he doesn't deliver. He added: "It's down to him as a player to seize it, grasp it and when he gets his chance make sure he's ready to take it. Emery, he's been brilliant at Villa. I love him.

‌



"I think he's a fantastic manager. I love his passion. I love his desire and if anyone's going to get the best out of him, I think it would be him. I think he'll give him some tough love but there'll be an expectation and you've got to live up to that expectation and you've got to deliver. If you don't deliver, he won't hang about with you. He's not that type of manager."

A lack of end product and continuing criticisms of his decision-making have plagued Garnacho in recent years, with questions about his attitude - namely from Bruno Fernandes - being the biggest stain against the Argentine.

‌



Garnacho had spent two years in United's academy before enjoying his breakout season in the 2022/23 campaign under Erik ten Hag. However, he lacked the proper attitude when promoted to the first team, according to the Portuguese star.

"He was good, but he knows we expect a lot from him," Fernandes said to BT Sport in November 2022. "He's still really young, doing really well. At the beginning of the season, he was not at his best.

‌



View 3 Images Bruno Fernandes revealed that his former team-mate didn't have the best attitude (Image: Michael Regan, Getty Images)

"On the [pre-season] tour, he did not have the best attitude. That's why he didn't get his chance until now. He's getting his chances because he's training better, he's having the correct attitude."

Garnacho has had to settle for just 16 minutes of action in Villa's opening two games this season. While opportunities to impress will be available, with the club competing on four fronts, it's up to the player whether his career takes another dramatic decline or if the football world is reintroduced to the star whose potential once seemed endless.

Sports.title: Arsenal vs Chelsea injury news as eight players could miss huge Premier League clash
Sports.content:
Arsenal vs Chelsea injury news as eight players could miss huge Premier League clash

Arsenal vs Chelsea is the standout Premier League fixture this weekend, with both clubs winning their first two games coming into the match at Emirates Stadium

View 2 Images Xabi Alonso and Mikel Arteta have late selection decisions to make on Saturday after their teams' last training sessions (Image: Getty Images)

Arsenal and Chelsea both have late selection decisions to make before meeting at Emirates Stadium in the Premier League this weekend. Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso acknowledged that their teams' final training sessions on Saturday will determine who makes their matchday squads.

‌



The Gunners are worse for wear and could be without as many as five first-team squad members. Multiple players picked up knocks and limped off the pitch during their 1-0 win away to Aston Villa on Monday night.

‌



Arteta's side have just six days to recover from that match. Chelsea, however, had the same Sunday-Monday turnaround last week.

‌



Bruno Guimaraes is among those whose fitness remains uncertain following his appearance as a substitute at Villa Park. Speaking at his pre-match press conference on Friday, the Arsenal boss said: "Yeah, he had a knock against Villa. "He's being assessed, but probably tomorrow (Saturday) he'll be OK for training."

Xabi Alonso rubs salt in Arsenal wounds over Morgan Rogers transfer ahead of clash READ MORE :

8 controversial Mike Dean moments from row with Arsenal manager to celebrating goal READ MORE :

A similar concern surrounds Cristhian Mosquera, who was forced off clutching his thigh before Ezri Konsa came on to make his Gunners debut against his former club. Arteta said of the substitution: "It was more precaution than anything else. So we'll have to see tomorrow (Saturday) in the session to see how he feels."

Declan Rice was also seen limping as Martin Zubimendi replaced him with five minutes remaining. However, the England international was back in training on Thursday and was not mentioned by Arteta during his pre-match briefing.

‌



Jurrien Timber has also returned to training with his teammates and could feature in the matchday squad. Arteta said: "Yeah, he is in really good condition at the moment. As I said, he's been on the pitch for a few weeks, and he's training with us now. We'll decide tomorrow after training [if he will make the squad]."

William Saliba, however, faces a longer spell on the sidelines. Arteta acknowledged: "We don't really know the number of weeks Wilo is going to be out because it's about a healing process and everything is a bit different.

View 2 Images Xabi Alonso and Mikel Arteta previous coached against each other two years ago during the Emirates Cup (Image: David Price, Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

‌



"We know we have to respect certain timings. The progression has been really positive in the last few weeks, but we need to wait and see how that one reacts when we start to put some load into it."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

As for Chelsea, Moises Caicedo's availability is causing concern for Alonso. Speaking during his press conference on Friday, the manager said: "We will check tomorrow (Saturday), as tomorrow is the last decision for the squad on Sunday."

‌



Marco Palestra remains another absentee. Alonso, though, did not refer to the summer arrival during his press conference. Yet, speaking on Wednesday at the Gran Gala del Calcio, held inside Milan's Teatro alla Scala, while collecting an award for making the Serie A Team of the Season, the player said: "I'm fine, it's still a few days away, but I feel much better."

He was absent from training with his teammates on Thursday, however. Jordan Henderson is also set to be absent. Alonso acknowledged last week that they are still awaiting confirmation that he has been given "the green light to play soon."

Sports.title: Constitution Hill tastes Flat defeat as Pride Of Arras scores at Kempton
Sports.content:
Constitution Hill had to settle for an ultimately well-beaten fourth to Pride Of Arras on his eagerly-awaited third Flat outing in the William Hill September Stakes at Kempton Park.

So brilliant at his peak in his hurdling days, Nicky Henderson's superstar has remained one of racing's biggest draws since switching to the level - but this Group Three affair was a major step up from his victories at Southwell and at this track in February and March respectively.

As the odds-on Gethin took early command of the mile-and-a-half contest, Billy Loughnane and Constitution Hill (9-2) sat in a close-up fourth and were still travelling with a degree of menace turning for home.

Asked for his effort just outside the two-furlong pole, there was only a flattering moment of hope before it became clear he was not going to get involved and instead it was the Ralph Beckett-trained Pride Of Arras (11-2) who swept to the front, holding off the rallying Gethin by a length.

Image: Pride Of Arras won the September Stakes under Rossa Ryan

Constitution Hill had arrived at Kempton with the Melbourne Cup a tantalising option for the autumn, but Henderson will now return to the drawing board and said: "Melbourne is gone now sadly. Today was always going to tell us what we were going to do next and I suppose he's posing us another question now.

"I don't think we want to go under a mile and a half, that is for sure, and 12, 13 or 14 furlongs seems to be the range of where we go with him. I do think he is going to come on for the run, what with the way he got there as if it was going to happen, but from a furlong out I think he took a bit of a blow. It will sharpen him up.

"He's going to be eligible to run in handicaps now and it will be interesting to see what the reaction on Tuesday is. It could allow him into some very lucrative handicaps in England, Ireland or wherever you like.

"From two novice stakes of very differing strength and depth it was a big step today and we'll now just wait to see what it does for his mark."

He added: "We'll find a nice race for him somewhere and he's by no means finished yet, I can promise you that."

Australian dreams may have been crushed for Constitution Hill, but for connections of the winner Pride Of Arras, a trip to Canada is now on the cards as last year's Dante and Great Voltigeur scorer showed his class on the Sunbury synthetics.

Beckett said: "He's a good horse and was good in the Dante and Voltigeur last year and a talented individual.

"He had a really bad foot problem that came to light just before the John Porter and he wasn't really ready when he ran against Calandagan in the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud, but I had to run him somewhere.

"I then thought he lugged out when second (to Item) in the York Stakes and was still thinking about his foot.

"I thought he looked a million dollars before the International and hadn't looked better. It was a great disappointment to all of us we couldn't run at York. They loaded him at York before all the other horses had gone behind and I'd say he was looking at the horses walking towards him and that's what set him off

"I thought today he would probably find the surface a touch deeper than he would like so you could probably upgrade it a little bit.

"I think there is a good chance he will really enjoy Toronto when we take him to the Canadian International."

On the impact of Constitution Hill at Kempton, Beckett added: "It's great that the crowds have come out and we're in the entertainment business, but inevitably you have to worry about your own horse.

"I'm delighted there is a crowd and it was a good race. The first two are good horses and Constitution Hill wasn't disgraced."

Sports.title: Villa hold on to earn first WSL point against Chelsea
Sports.content:
Aston Villa came from behind to earn a 1-1 draw against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge as Sonia Bompastor's side were denied a winning start to their Women's Super League campaign.

Lauren James had given Chelsea a deserved lead after just 11 minutes, capitalising on a mistake in the Villa defence before shifting the ball onto her left foot and firing powerfully into the roof of the net.

Chelsea remained on top and Aggie Beever-Jones, making her 100th appearance for the club, was denied by Akane Okuma before Sjoeke Nusken fired over as the hosts went into the break with a slender advantage.

Villa improved after half-time and Amalie Vangsgaard passed up a huge opportunity to equalise when she met Chasity Grant's cross at the near post but fired narrowly wide. Chelsea then went within inches of doubling their advantage as Keira Walsh's long-range effort crashed against the underside of the crossbar.

The visitors made Chelsea pay in the 79th minute. A mix-up inside the home penalty area allowed Noelle Maritz to react quickest and her close-range effort deflected off Veerle Buurman and into the net for an own goal.

Chelsea pushed for a winner and almost found one in the final minute of normal time, but Okuma produced a superb reaction save to somehow turn James' close-range effort over the crossbar and preserve a point for Villa.

The result means Chelsea begin their attempt to reclaim the WSL title with a draw in their first league game since making Stamford Bridge their permanent home, while Villa end a run of 12 successive league defeats against the Blues to make an encouraging start to their campaign.

Image: Katie McCabe made her WSL debut for Chelsea following her summer move from Arsenal

The key moments from Stamford Bridge

5: WIDE! James collects the ball on the left, cuts inside and drives towards the area before creating space for a shot that flashes past the post.

11: GOAL! A mistake at the back gifts the ball to James, who drives towards goal, shifts onto her left foot and fires powerfully into the roof of the net. Chelsea lead!

21: SAVE! Carpenter is played in down the right and crosses towards Beever-Jones at the near post, but Okuma gets down quickly to push her effort behind.

28: BLOCKED! Villa work the ball to McAulay, who cuts inside from the right before seeing her effort blocked and cleared.

32: OVER! Thompson crosses from the left to Beever-Jones, who controls and lays the ball back to Nusken on the edge of the area, but the German fires over.

Image: Lauren James gave Chelsea the lead in the 11th minute at Stamford Bridge

45: CLOSE! Parker produces some fine defending at the near post to turn the ball onto the roof of her own net as Chelsea threaten again.

55: CLOSE FOR VILLA! Grant crosses towards Vangsgaard at the near post, but the Villa striker meets it first time and fires narrowly wide. A huge chance to equalise.

67: OFF THE BAR! Walsh goes close to doubling Chelsea's lead as her stunning effort from outside the area crashes against the underside of the crossbar.

79: GOAL! VILLA ARE LEVEL! A mix-up in the Chelsea box allows Maritz to react quickest and her close-range effort deflects off Buurman and into the net for an own goal.

90: INCREDIBLE SAVE! Okuma somehow pushes James' close-range effort over the bar to deny Chelsea a late winner. A superb save from the Villa goalkeeper.

Sports.title: Russell tops Hamilton at Monza ahead of qualifying
Sports.content:
George Russell established himself as pole position favourite ahead of Italian Grand Prix qualifying as the Mercedes driver topped Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton in final practice.

Mercedes and Ferrari had appeared closely matched in Friday's two practice sessions, and once more led the way on Saturday as Russell's time of 1:22.219s put him just over two tenths of a second clear of Hamilton at Monza.

Russell is shouldering Mercedes' hopes of claiming pole, with his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, the championship leader, serving penalties for taking new engine parts that will leave him starting from the back of the grid regardless of where he qualifies.

Despite being more focused on his long-run setup for Sunday's race, Antonelli, who leads both Russell and Hamilton by 59 points at the top of the standings, was fourth behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

McLaren's Lando Norris, who has closed to within 83 points of Antonelli by winning the last two races, was fifth ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Mercedes tried out using Antonelli to give Russell a highly-beneficial tow around the high-speed circuit, but the Brit's fastest laps came without the help of his team-mate.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton braces for a tight Italian GP qualifying as Mercedes continue to find more pace

Ferrari appear to have reduced their straight-line speed deficit to Mercedes after bringing to Monza their second engine upgrade of the season, but it appears the Italian squad will need to find something extra to claim what would be an extremely popular pole at their home race.

There was drama in the closing moments of the session as Hamilton and Verstappen almost collided at the first corner after a squabble for track position ahead of what should have been their final attempts at flying laps.

Hamilton snuck ahead of Verstappen as they approached the final corner, which angered the Dutchman, prompting him to attempt to race the Ferrari over the start-finish line and then dive up the inside into the first corner.

Hamilton bailed out to prevent contact, avoiding a repeat of the pair's famous collision at the 2021 Italian Grand Prix when they were battling for the drivers' title. The stewards noted the incident but decided an investigation wasn't necessary.

Image: George Russell topped final practice at Monza

Russell has endured a difficult season having started the year of favourite before being outperformed by his far less experience team-mate.

However, the 28-year-old appears to have found a groove at Monza, with pole position having the potential to reignite his championship challenge.

Sky Sports F1's Naomi Schiff said: "George will be very pleased with himself. This is such a psychological sport and with a team-mate leading the championship he does need to switch that momentum.

"This session has been the most positive for Mercedes. They aren't losing much anywhere on deployment through the lap."

Sports.title: Lincoln hit back to hold Southampton
Sports.content:
Mikkel Ladefoged scored his first goal in English football to secure Lincoln a deserved late point against Southampton as they battled to a 1-1 draw with one of the Championship promotion favourites.

Welington had also notched his first effort for the Saints on the stroke of half-time and his thunderbolt looked likely to be good enough for the points at the ProAmpac Stadium before the Imps' record signing struck at the death.

Lincoln handed a first league start to defender Andrei Coubis and the Romanian almost enjoyed an incredible opening to the match, seeing a shot blocked inside 10 seconds after the Imps' 'up-and-under' kick-off caused panic among the Saints defence.

His rebounded shot found its way to Rob Street, whose header was deflected behind for a corner, from which Coubis then headed straight at keeper Daniel Peretz.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Southampton take the lead against Lincoln in spectacular fashion as Welington scores from miles out against Lincoln with a superb strike.

City striker Freddie Draper dragged a shot narrowly wide from 25 yards after five minutes, with Saints winger Kuryu Matsuki's curler then finding the gloves of home stopper George Wickens.

Street found space in the Saints box and nearly squeezed a shot inside the near post, with Peretz getting down quickly to smother his effort.

James Ward-Prowse was handed his first league start upon his return to Southampton, but the set-piece specialist fluffed his first free-kick from 30 yards, pulling a low shot well wide of the target.

Indeed, it was City creating the best chances and 27 minutes in, Adam Reach nodded an Ivan Varfolomeev cross just over the bar.

Ben House missed a golden opportunity from six yards out after Reach's crossfield pass found Coubis on the right flank, but his pinpoint cross to House was met with a swipe at thin air and the chance went begging.

House headed Street's cross over before Southampton struck in the 44th minute. There looked to be no danger when Welington received the ball from Ward-Prowse 25 yards out, but he unleashed a rocket that arrowed into the top corner.

City responded with Peretz's flying saving denying Draper as the half came to an end.

Southampton should have doubled their lead bang on the hour mark, but Leo Scienza's curling effort hit Wickens' left-hand post and bounced across the line to the other post and then into the grateful keeper's arms.

Coubis had a chance to level after 77 minutes when sub Ladefoged's knockdown from Wickens' free-kick dropped perfectly for him, but he blazed his effort well over.

Imps sub Chieo Ogbene was then put into the clear by Ladefoged, but fired a shot straight at Peretz, who saved with his legs, with Draper heading the corner just over the bar.

Ladefoged this time fired over as the Imps poured forward in the closing stages and the pressure finally told when the big Dane nodded home fellow Reeco Hackett's inch-perfect cross in the 87th minute to rescue a point.

The managers

Lincoln's Tom Shaw:

"We've got a player who's a real problem in the penalty area and we've got to help him and he's got to help himself in getting up to speed and understanding what we want, but he's got the physicality and mentality to do that. He's a real nuisance.

"We felt the goal was coming - we sort of reverted to plan B. We created loads of volume, loads of chaos and we're good in the chaos."

Southampton's Tonda Eckert:

"Credit to Lincoln for a performance of courage, manliness and energy. The job was to make sure we brought the ball down quickly and stayed on the floor.

"There were a couple of spells where we did that and not so well, but then we went 1-0 up. I think there's two ways to bring the game home; the first is to score the second goal and if you don't manage that we need to find ways of grinding games out and that was the disappointing thing about today.

"The second half gave us enough moments to score a second goal but we need to do better with balls that come into the box. They showed a lot of physicality but it is up to us to deal with that."

Sports.title: Ramsey rescues draw for Newcastle against Bournemouth
Sports.content:
Newcastle fought back from two goals down as Jacob Ramsey's late strike rescued a 2-2 against Bournemouth at St James' Park.

Bournemouth appeared on track for their first win under Marco Rose after an early strike from Marcus Tavernier and a Malick Thiaw own goal, only to blow a late lead for the third straight game.

Harvey Barnes halved the deficit with a stunning curler 27 seconds after the kick-off following Bournemouth's second goal, before substitute Ramsey found the bottom corner in the 88th minute to continue Newcastle's unbeaten start under Matthias Jaissle.

Bournemouth were the better side overall, attempting 17 shots compared to only eight from the lacklustre hosts, but Ramsey's leveller follows crucial stoppage-time goals conceded in their games against Manchester City and Everton.

The Cherries have lost seven points from winning positions this term. They are the first side in Premier League history to score the opening goal in their first three games and fail to win any of them.

The key moments from St James' Park

9: GOAL! Tavernier is alert to bury the loose ball after Scott's effort is deflected

Tavernier is alert to bury the loose ball after Scott's effort is deflected 35: GOAL! Thiaw turns Scott's cross into his own net after Kluivert's shot hit the post

Thiaw turns Scott's cross into his own net after Kluivert's shot hit the post 37: GOAL! Barnes cuts inside from the left before curling home a brilliant strike

Barnes cuts inside from the left before curling home a brilliant strike 52: CHANCE! A flicked header from Willock bounces inches wide for Newcastle

A flicked header from Willock bounces inches wide for Newcastle 63: WELCOME! Matias Fernandez-Pardo gets a warm reception as he appears for his Newcastle debut

Matias Fernandez-Pardo gets a warm reception as he appears for his Newcastle debut 88: GOAL! Ramsey strokes a composed finish into the bottom corner to equalise

Jaissle pleased with Newcastle spirit

Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle to TNT Sports: "Mixed feelings.

"Happy for that spirit, that belief the lads were showing until the end together with the crowd. I felt the energy and felt if we had five or 10 minutes more we could win this game.

"But the first half was not expected. This is something we need to improve. This is part of the journey.

"We knew Bournemouth would come with everything; they always show great intensity and if you do not compete with that you get problems.

"We struggled with that in the first half but the lads showed the right reaction."

Rose: We need to finish games

Bournemouth boss Marco Rose to TNT Sports: "It is what it is.

"I'm really happy with the confidence the lads brought on the pitch today. Especially in the first half, we were so good. We could have scored even a third goal.

Image: Bournemouth's Marcus Tavernier celebrates his goal at Newcastle

"Then more or less from nothing we conceded a really nice goal to Newcastle, then the game is open here in this stadium. Second half we missed the chances, the transition situations, possession... In the end it's a draw and we have to deal with it.

"It's good that we're in situations to be able to win games. The other things we have to talk about, we have to finish games, we need to defend our own goal like it's the last game in our life.

"If you always concede one or two, you need to score three to win and that's pretty hard in the Premier League."

Positive start for Fernandez-Pardo

Analysis by Sky Sports' Nick Wright:

Ramsey's goal ensured Newcastle remain unbeaten under Eddie Howe's successor, but they might count themselves a little fortunate on this occasion. Bournemouth, by contrast, will wonder how they didn't win.

Jaissle has issues to address but Ramsey's impact showed his value to the side and there was also a positive debut from new £51m signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo, who emerged to warm applause when he came on as a second-half substitute.

The Belgian international is of course new to the Premier League. He was on the receiving end of a couple of meaty challenges to welcome him. But there were glimpses of his talent, too, including a clever drop of the shoulder to escape pressure in the box. He injected some much-needed energy and directness.

Bournemouth undone late again

Analysis by Sky Sports' Peter Smith:

It was 90+1 vs Man City. Then 90+1 vs Everton. And now 88 at Newcastle. Bournemouth's failure to see out the final minutes of matches has cost them dearly in their first three games.

The late goals must be infuriating for Rose, whose side would have been sitting top of the table going into Saturday's 3pm games had they held out in the final minutes of their matches so far.

It will be a particularly galling journey back to the south coast from Newcastle, given how Bournemouth dominated the first half and missed two good chances to add to their tally before the break, with Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson off target.

Rose will also reflect on how his side seemingly allowed the game to fizzle out in that second half before Newcastle's smash-and-grab. Fine margins. Had they held on, it would have looked like a perfect away performance.

But Bournemouth's lack of intensity and focus in the final minutes has seen them give up precious points again.
