Sports.title: Ramsey caps Newcastle fightback for draw as Bournemouth concede late again
Sports.content:
Just as Bournemouth’s Alex Scott seemed to have succeeded in building a personal playground by the Tyne, another midfielder emerged from the shadows and ruined his afternoon.

Since Matthias Jaissle succeeded Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s manager, Jacob Ramsey has been largely shunted to the margins, but substitute’s superbly executed 88th-minute equaliser ensured Scott and his teammates had to settle for a point.

Like Jaissle, Marco Rose is a German graduate of the Red Bull school of management and a former RB Salzburg manager. Big on verticality, intensity and relentless pressing, both men have much in common, but systems are only as good as the players within them and, in Scott, Rose had a player blessed with the brain and vision to dominate central midfield.

By the time Ramsey rose from the bench, Bournemouth should have been certain of their first win under Rose, but once again they proved incapable of retaining a lead and, thanks to Ramsey, Newcastle secured a face-saving draw.

Marcus Tavernier gave Bournemouth a ninth-minute lead. Setting the tone, Scott had started well and, when he advanced into the box, his shot was deflected into Tavernier’s path. Before a rather slapdash Newcastle had time to clear, the latter’s rapid reaction saw his deft finish whizz past Lukas Hornicek.

View image in fullscreen Marcus Tavernier’s second league goal of the season put Bournemouth ahead inside 10 minutes. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

Jaissle attempted to argue that the goal should have been disallowed due to what he perceived as a foul by Adrien Truffert on Anthony Elanga in the buildup, but a video assistant review detected no offence. Meanwhile, Newcastle’s rearguard continued to wobble with Sven Botman looking particularly vulnerable.

As Evanilson spurned a chance to make Rose jump for joy, Jaissle received a reminder why the name Bournemouth is synonymous with “banana skin” on Tyneside. Newcastle, after all, had failed to beat their guests from Dorset in any of their previous eight Premier League meetings.

It is, of course, no longer the “Eddie Howe derby” – Jaissle’s predecessor used to manage Bournemouth – but the new occupant of St James’ Park’s home technical area was confronted with many of the problems that became so painfully familiar to Howe against these particular visitors.

No matter that Rose had replaced Andoni Iraola in the away dugout or that Jaissle started three of his eight summer signings with a further four looking on from the bench, Bournemouth were, again, finding the north-east air hugely restorative.

View image in fullscreen Alex Scott (left) played an important role in the goals that put Bournemouth 2-0 up after 35 minutes. Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters

Indeed as the half-hour mark passed it was possible to wonder if a malicious cyberhacker based on the south coast had somehow programmed Newcastle’s players to forfeit possession at every opportunity. Jaissle’s team appeared at once cowed and overwhelmed by Rose’s ruthlessly clever press.

At this stage the only puzzle was how Bournemouth, with Scott increasingly impressive, were not at least 3-0 ahead. After his teammates had failed to polish off a series of chances, Justin Kluivert took matters into his own hands, unleashing a high-velocity shot from distance that rebounded off a combination of a post and Hornicek before dropping to Scott.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

All that remained was for Malick Thiaw to register an own goal by deflecting Scott’s cross-shot beyond Hornicek. Cue Rose racing down the touchline before exchanging high fives with members of the travelling party.

Pride has an unfortunate habit of preceding falls and, sure enough, less than two minutes later, Bournemouth’s celebrations were rudely interrupted when the previously frustrating Harvey Barnes cut inside from the left and curled a wonderful shot past Djordje Petrovic.

View image in fullscreen Harvey Barnes scored a terrific goal to cut Newcastle’s deficit in half. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

Perhaps galvanised by a Jaissle half-time homily, Newcastle improved a little after the break. They came tantalisingly close to equalising when Joe Willock’s glancing header flashed fractionally off target following Yoane Wissa’s excellent cross and Elanga’s flick. After seeing Bournemouth squander leads during his first two Premier League games in charge, Rose was starting to look distinctly nervous.

With just over an hour gone, Jaissle increased Rose’s growing edginess by introducing his new £51m attacking signing. This time last week Matias Fernandez-Pardo was a Lille forward but now he was making his Newcastle debut in the No 10 role behind Wissa.

Bournemouth, though, refused to fold and Jaissle received a yellow card for persistently stepping outside his technical area as well as, possibly, repeatedly offering the fourth official a piece of his mind.

His mood brightened appreciably in the 88th minute. When Bournemouth failed to clear the fallout from Jacob Murphy’s cross, the ball fell to another home substitute. Ramsey needed no second invitation to make his presence felt, striking the ball low and cleanly into the bottom corner.

Sports.title: Veerle Buurman’s own goal earns Aston Villa WSL draw at wasteful Chelsea
Sports.content:
A Veerle Buurman own goal punished a profligate Chelsea at Stamford Bridge, securing a point for Aston Villa in a frustrating start to their WSL title push.

How Villa came away with a point having conceded 64% possession and having amassed just seven shots to Chelsea’s 32 and five touches in the opposition box to the home team’s 57 is somewhat inexplicable.

Chelsea were creative and Lauren James was at her free-flowing best, but they could not convert their many chances, and the new Aston Villa goalkeeper Akane Okuma’s monumental performance was a big part of that.

Chelsea’s summer has been one of change after a somewhat transitional season, as players moved towards a sort of natural end to their time at the club. Heading into her third season in London, Sonia Bompastor’s stamp is firmly on her Chelsea team after a cautious approach to changes to the successful squad left by Emma Hayes.

However, they have a problem up front, with Melvine Malard, who came off the bench and scored two in their Champions League home leg against Real Sociedad, out with an injury, Mayra Ramírez yet to make her return from a long injury lay-off, and Aggie Beever-Jones failing to make the most of the opportunity to lead the line in their absence.

If there was some rust in Chelsea’s 6-2 defeat of Real Sociedad across two legs it looked to have been firmly shaken off by that competitive appetiser to their new season.

Ushering in a new era in front of 7,900 fans at Stamford Bridge, where they will play all their WSL home games for the first time, the Blues were rampant from the off.

The aggressive and relentless pressing of Bompastor’s side in the opening half-hour caused all sorts of problems for Natalia Arroyo’s team, forcing error after error.

View image in fullscreen Noelle Maritz’s shot led to Veerle Buurman’s own goal and Aston Villa’s leveller. Photograph: Katie Chan/Action Plus/Shutterstock

It was no surprise that that physical effort yielded results. In the 11th minute that pressure caused confusion between Okuma and the target of her pass out from the back and Ellie Carpenter pounced on the loose ball. She worked it to James who glided into the box, shifting her weight as she went, before lashing the ball into the roof of the net.

It was a statement goal from a statement player. James played with the guile, freedom, energy and joy that full fitness brings after a series of niggling issues in recent years that at times left her looking frustrated that her body couldn’t match her ability.

A trip to Chelsea was always going to be tough for Villa, who started five of their eight signings, and they only began to look a little more comfortable and structured as the home team’s pressure eased off towards the end of the first half.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The scoreline at the break flattered the visiting team, who could have been down by more had Chelsea been more clinical.

The profligacy in front of goal was frustrating for Bompastor’s team and Villa were clinging on for swathes of the second half. Okuma, signed from Japanese side INAC Kobe Lionesses, was key to keeping the margin to one goal, producing some fine saves, including pushing away Carpenter’s shot shortly after the hour mark.

The celebrations of Chelsea fans when Beever-Jones finally looked to have scored a goal and extended their lead were edged with a touch of relief but they were short-lived, with the flag raised for offside when she headed home.

At no stage had it felt like the visiting team would take something from the game, but they were patient. Ultimately though Chelsea were the masters of their own downfall by not putting the game to bed and in the 79th minute the ground was silenced when they failed to clear Lynn Wilms’ cross, Noelle Maritz swiped it goalwards from eight yards out and Hannah Hampton’s block sent the ball bouncing off Buurman and over the line.

The home side pushed hard for the winner but Okuma was equal to every attempt, her stunning late block from another James effort a highlight. On the final whistle the Japanese goalkeeper was enveloped in the hugs of her teammates as the players in blue digested how they had ended up with only a point after such a dominant performance.

Sports.title: Championship roundup: Lincoln earn late draw against Southampton, Stoke rout Charlton
Sports.content:
Mikkel Ladefoged scored his first goal in English football to secure Lincoln a deserved late point against Southampton as they battled to a 1-1 draw with one of the Championship promotion favourites.

Welington had also scored his first goal for the Saints on the stroke of half-time and his thunderbolt looked likely to be good enough for the points at the ProAmpac Stadium before the Imps’ record signing struck at the death.

Quick Guide League One roundup: Wednesday make it four wins from five Show Sheffield Wednesday continued their bright start to life in League One with a 2-1 win at Peterborough. Defender Yan Valery scored the winner for the Owls in the 79th minute after Posh’s Ben Woods had cancelled out Josh Feeney’s own goal. It gave Henrik Pedersen’s team a fourth win in five matches, following their relegation from the Championship. Three goals inside the opening quarter sealed the deal as Stockport picked up a convincing 4-0 victory at Wigan. A mistake from Wigan captain Max Power led to Kyle Wootton lashing the ball into the top corner from 25 yards in the 10th minute. County doubled their lead in the 19th minute when Harry Wood broke through the home defence and slipped the ball over the advancing Joe Whitworth. And it was game over two minutes later as Jack Diamond was played in on the home goal, leaving Whitworth completely helpless again. County added a fourth goal they undoubtedly warranted in the last minute through Ryan Glover. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Stoke cruised to a 4-0 win by dismantling 10-man Charlton with a ruthless home performance. The Addicks had not lost a league game this season before their visit to the Bet365 Stadium, but two goals from debutant Justin Devenny and strikes from Ethan Galbraith and George Hirst saw the Potters put the contest to bed before the break.

The second-half substitute Danny McNamara was sent off for two careless yellow cards in the space of three minutes as the afternoon spiralled spectacularly out of control for the visitors. Booked first for pulling back Eric Bocat, the full-back McNamara was dismissed in the 50th minute after berating the referee, Robert Madley.

Quick Guide League Two roundup: Fleetwood continue impressive start Show Fleetwood maintained their unbeaten start to the season with an impressive 2-0 win over struggling Shrewsbury. The Cod Army have now gone six games in all competition – five in League Two – without defeat. In a dull opening, the only chance of note was a powerful shot from outside the area by Josh Davison which was comfortably gathered by Fleetwood goalkeeper Jay Lynch. Six minutes before the break Shrewsbury pressed the self-destruct button. Keeper Will Brook gave away a corner after holding on to the ball for more than eight seconds. The resulting set piece was headed down by Rhys Bennett and Ronan Coughlan managed to guide the ball home from close range with his knee. Shrewsbury started the second half brightly and had two decent penalty shouts turned down, Lewis McCann replying with a left-footed shot that went narrowly wide. The home side secured the points with four minutes to go, on-loan Fulham striker Aaron Loupalo-Bi’s close-range shot taking a wicked deflection on its way in. In the other early kick-off, Joe Powell scored the only goal of the game as Salford secured a 1-0 win against Port Vale. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Stoke should have gone on to score more goals, but the second half was a stroll as both sides played possession football with the result all but confirmed.

“If we could have written a [perfect] script, then that would have been it,” said Stoke manager Mark Robins. “I thought we played really well. There was a lot to be pleased about. All four of the goals were fantastic. We’ve got the penalty and then we’ve scored some good goals. Shooting has been really lacking for a long time, but they did that well today.”

Callum Lang bagged an early double as Preston edged past local rivals Blackburn 2-1 at Deepdale. The 27-year-old opened the scoring with a poacher’s finish in the ninth minute before nodding in a 28th-minute second.

Stanley Mills accidentally halved the arrears early in the second half with an unfortunate own goal on just his second Preston start but his team held on for their first win of the season.

Sports.title: Uefa legal case may be beginning of the end for Infantino as Trump’s support evaporates | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
“Tell Mike it was just business. I always liked him.”

“He understands.”

“Tom, can you get me off the hook? For old times’ sake?”

“Sorry can’t do it.”

I never believed it would actually happen. Not really. Not until this week, when, for the first time, there was a sense, as The Godfather makes so abundantly clear, that you really can get to anyone.

Gianni Infantino is beleaguered. Gianni Infantino is re-beleaguered. Gianni Infantino has been beleaguered for almost six weeks, since news emerged of his grotesque undercover plan to sell off, for related personal gain, the shared global property he’s employed to preserve, protect and safely pass on.

There has been hopeful talk in that time of toxic status attained, a base being hollowed out, a rival presidential candidate next March. But power runs deep. Entrenched dictatorial power runs even deeper. Time passes. The doorway narrows. Infantino is already the man who sold the world, not once, but twice, most recently to Donald Trump in return for a peace prize, a scrunchie and a fawning presence around the sub-table of power.

Give it a month. Chuck in a Football Jesus turn at the lighted lectern a few weeks from now, arms whirling like a street magician, reeling off the usual stuff about caring and sharing, égalité, fraternité, fiscal stimuli. Look deep into those weirdly flat painted-on eyes, cold and hard behind the papier-mache mask of power. You don’t buy me out. I buy you out.

But something has shifted this week. It was never going to be the gnats around his ankles that did for Infantino: another thundering newspaper column, the latest stern denouncement from – whoah, hang on – former Manchester United utility defender Mikaël Silvestre.

Hard power is something else, however. And two things have now happened, both responses to the threat of a Uefa lawsuit, which I believe has no really serious notions of ultimate victory, but which may turn out to be an expert chess move, a zugzwang that leaves the king having to go somewhere, but with no safe spaces left to hide.

View image in fullscreen Josh Kushner said he ‘would not have gotten involved’ in Fifa’s plans had he known the full picture. Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters

The first response was Josh Kushner’s statement this week after being named as a party to discovery in Florida. Kushner was the money guy behind the Fifa Forward fiasco. Nuts isn’t it? The person you come to for finance and macro-favour just happens to be, by an accident of talent and destiny, the brother of the president’s son-in-law.

Kushner said he “would not have gotten involved” in Fifa’s plans had he known the full picture. He said this was all regrettable. Ostensibly mild and reasonable words, but with a sense of distance being carved out, of a cutting loose from the protective apron.

Kushner has also hired a nuclear option lawyer, Alex Spiro, who defended Elon Musk when he called a caver “a pedo” and Alec Baldwin when he accidentally shot someone. It’s a serious defensive move. As is, to a more rattled degree, Fifa’s counter-filing this week, which dismisses the whole episode as a “smear campaign”, then says the quiet thing out loud. Specifically, Fifa mentions discovery and a very urgent intention to resist it.

This is the real point. No one on the Infantino side wants discovery. Which is, to be clear, the sharing of related documents, from internal memos down to relevant emails sent from your smartphone on the golf course after lunch.

This, as Gianni knows, is always a worry to those in power. And you really don’t want to be a worry to anyone in any way connected to Trump. This is why, behind the sabre rattling, there is for the first time a sense of a thinning out, of nobody there on the ward, no cops on the doors, of the old man up there unprotected.

Even Trump’s early support for Infantino was a little over-juiced in the media. The president Truth Socialed his assurances in early August. It still felt a little qualified. “If for any reason” Fifa got rid of Infantino, well, this would be really bad. And nothing since.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There is a vague sense of a shrug here, of an amble away from the stage. We remember the good times for the Gianni-Trump bro-tocracy, laughing together like men in a Brooks Brothers senior knitwear advert, the gleaming bald impresario to power and his tolerant daddy-patron looking as ever like a giant man-size unit of American food, as though something deep-fried, honey-glazed and dished up at an out-of-town hotel conference buffet has somehow learned to walk around in a baggy suit and say things like “a very tall, very handsome man”.

View image in fullscreen ‘Zip it’: Fifa will want to avoid discovery to protect Gianni Infantino’s relationship with Donald Trump. Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPA

This is always brittle. Trump will walk you in, remember your name, glad-hand you by the stairwell. But once you’re gone you really are gone. There is no loyalty, and logically so, because Trumpian politics has no core belief, no substance, just a cold, hard matrix of winners and losers.

And if you lose, or look like you might, then by coincidence bad things tend to happen. The Guardian published a list a while back of Trump enemies who now find themselves subject to charges, exile, security clearances revoked, mortgage fraud investigated. And that list does include some pretty high-profile one-time golden boys.

Michael Cohen, the fiercest of Trump loyalists, who famously stated he would “take a bullet” for the big man? Legal difficulties and fallings-out intervened. Cohen has since been imprisoned, disbarred and sent into exile. The former US attorney general Jeff Sessions was among the first to call Trumpism “a movement”. He’s now not only out of the game, but has apparently been described by Trump, variously, as weak, confused, dumb, an idiot, a disgrace, and “mentally retarded”. There is a pattern here. If you’re in then you’re in. But don’t fly too close to those flames.

The decision of the court on allowing discovery could well be key. Make no mistake, Uefa is accusing Fifa and Infantino of “criminal mismanagement”. The key issue is an alleged undervaluing in the sale of the World Cup. Unrelated, and arguably standard industry practice, Infantino also stood to take a huge personal salary from all this.

It is a clear attempt to peer inside and see what, if anything, is in that box. Uefa wants discovery from Fifa, Thrive Capital and the Trump donor and deal adviser Greg Maffei, all of whom will have paper trails from that period when Infantino was granted intoxicating access to the halls of power. It puts you in mind of the Club World Cup trophy, a weird, frightening-looking thing, all razor-sharp odd nooks and crannies, the secret little drawer full of human toenails. Do you really want to know what’s in there? Is it safe to look?

“Please Mike, don’t do this, don’t do this to me”

“Today I settle all the family business. So don’t tell me you’re innocent.”

How is this going to play out? Infantino is doing what he can, touring his outer provinces and pressing the flesh. Saudi Arabia has offered qualified backing (“at this time …”). There’s a Fifa congress in November. Really, though, you wonder about votes, and to what extent votes are the thing here. It is hard not to muse on how it ended in football for Sepp Blatter and Michel Platini. That one-shot illegal payment allegation really did come out of the blue.

For now the process will simmer on. Legal challenges often fail or melt away. Uefa just needs to keep pressing, to make it clear that coals will be raked. Keep the pressure up and you never know what may fall out, or from where. Mr president, you can have my answer now. Our offer is this. Nothing.

Sports.title: Liverpool look for new sporting director after Richard Hughes formally leaves
Sports.content:
Liverpool are searching for a fourth sporting director in four years after confirming that Richard Hughes has stepped down from the role.

Hughes’s departure has been long expected, with the 47-year-old in line to take up a similar position with the Saudi Pro League club Al-Hilal. He informed Liverpool of his intentions to leave early this year, after the departure of his friend Michael Edwards as chief executive of football for Fenway Sports Group, the club’s owner.

With work already under way on Liverpool’s summer transfer targets – including the signing of Bradley Barcola in a £123m deal – and Hughes enjoying a close working relationship with the new head coach, Andoni Iraola, it was agreed he would continue in the role until the end of the transfer window.

Liverpool say no approach was received from Al-Hilal for Hughes to start work with them this summer and are satisfied the sporting director worked for them alone throughout this period.

The search for Hughes’s replacement is already under way and is being led by FSG’s president, Mike Gordon, who resumed the day-to-day running of the club after Edwards’ exit. The eventual appointment will follow in the footstepsof Edwards, Julian Ward, Jörg Schmadtke and Hughes.

Liverpool’s football structure will otherwise remain intact. That includes Ward as technical director for FSG and Pedro Marques as director of football development at FSG, the assistant sporting director, David Woodfine, the chief scout, Barry Hunter, plus the senior leadership team at the training centre.

Sports.title: Mike Dean insists he refereed ‘properly and professionally’ after podcast claims
Sports.content:
The former referee Mike Dean regrets his controversial comments on a podcast this week, but insists he always did his job “properly and professionally” during his 25-year career.

Dean sent shockwaves through football when he claimed on the Jamie Vardy’s Having a Party podcast he would “joke about” during matches and would see how long he could go without blowing his whistle or leaving the centre circle.

The eye-catching remarks were immediately met with widespread criticism from former officials with the integrity of the game questioned, but Pro Ref – the new name for Professsional Game Match Officials Limited – is yet to make a public comment on Dean’s remarks.

After Dean started his refereeing career in 1985, he was promoted to the full referees’ list in 1997 before he was appointed to the select group of Premier League referees in 2000 until he retired in 2022.

The 58-year-old, from Wirral, released a statement on Friday where he insisted it was never his intention to “criticise or undermine the integrity” of his fellow officials before he reflected on the controversy during his appearance on Sky Sports’ Soccer Saturday programme.

Asked by the presenter Simon Thomas if in 25 years he ever deliberately failed to apply the laws of the game, Dean said: “No, because if I did, I wouldn’t have got as many games as I did.

“And I wouldn’t have been on the list for 25 years. I did my job properly and professionally for the full 25 years. I have no regrets over the way I refereed the game of football. I enjoyed what I did and I think the players enjoyed what I did as well.

“It is one of them comments, if you had your time again, you wouldn’t say it, but it’s been said now and been out there. There is nothing I can do now.

It is understood Dean’s claims have been met with bemusement by those with current involvement in officiating, with some noting a lack of factual detail in his stories.

Dean continued: “It is one of them where as a ref, I like to go out and my threshold was always high as a ref and not to give free-kicks.

View image in fullscreen Mike Dean said he liked to keep games flowing, but is seen here showing a red card to Brentford’s Josh Dasilva. Photograph: Peter Nicholls/Reuters

“I would give a minimum amount of free-kicks as I can and if I can keep the game flowing, I would keep it flowing. Yes, if I’ve got to step in, I’ll give the free-kick but it is just one of them things – you learn by your mistakes.

“Obviously, I’ve said something this week that has come out a little bit wrong, I think I could have worded it a bit better than I said but you live and learn. Hopefully we can move on. We’ll see what happens.”

Sports.title: ‘Reverse bucket list’: Arteta channels Wenger in defence of Arsenal window
Sports.content:
For many people connected to Arsenal, it has been a time to remember the old line from Arsène Wenger. “We live in a society of ‘news’,” the club’s former manager once said, and by that he meant new things – the shinier the better.

Nowhere is the obsession more obvious than in the transfer market, when a club simply has to add new faces. These days, it feels as though some fans prefer them to be signed as late as possible in the summer window to ensure a positive narrative after the deadline; to maximise the potential to generate momentum. Recency bias is powerful.

Wenger’s tone was disapproving. The next big thing is not always thus. What you already have should not be undervalued or taken for granted. It struck a chord with Mikel Arteta, which everybody in the room for his press conference to preview Sunday’s home game against Chelsea could feel because it moved him out of succinct answer territory.

The Arsenal manager enters the match having won three out of three this season – including the Community Shield victory over Manchester City – without conceding a goal. His club, of course, ended their long wait for the Premier League title last May when they chased away all manner of demons. They are hot favourites to win it again.

At Aston Villa on Monday night, Arteta introduced two of Spain’s World Cup winning squad – Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi – from the bench. Plus the marquee summer signing, Bruno Guimarães. Plus Eberechi Eze. Plus another high-profile new boy, Ezri Konsa. Arsenal’s strength in depth is really something.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal were able to add the skill and strength of Bruno Guimarães to an already strong midfield this summer. Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/Reuters

Their squad is surely stronger now than it was at the end of last season. Does Arteta feel that? “Yes I do,” he said. “We are better equipped. We have more players available. We have increased the quality and we have increased the leadership in the team as well, which is very important.”

So, why the angst among supporters after the transfer window closed, which was probably nearer to hysteria in some cases? “It’s human nature,” Arteta said. “When you talk to people and you ask them … normally, it’s: ‘OK, what is on your bucket list?’ People write a lot about the bucket list. And sometimes we forget the reverse bucket list, which is the things that you already have in your life that are incredible. But you put so much emphasis on them [the bucket list items] that nothing seems to be enough.

“It’s very important to value what we have, what we have created together. To have ambition is great, especially to evolve the things we already have within the club. But listen – don’t lose perspective to what we already have, which is amazing.”

Arsenal are indisputably better in defence with Konsa and in midfield with Guimarães. The worry is the front line where it has been one in (Christos Tzolis) and four out (Leandro Trossard, Gabriel Martinelli, Gabriel Jesus and Ethan Nwaneri).

View image in fullscreen The summer window has left Christos Tzolis, himself only recently arrived, as Arsenal’s most natural option on the left wing. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

The reasoning for each departure was difficult to fault. Trossard is 31, he had one year on his contract and Besiktas offered £15.3m. Tzolis felt like a fine replacement for him. Martinelli scored once in the league last season, although he contributed four in the FA Cup and six in the Champions League. Arsenal got £60m from Al-Hilal for him; a club record sale.

As an aside, Arteta mentioned how Arsenal had “made a move last summer” – a reference to their lavish spending – and there has been an acknowledgement within the club that there had to be a balancing this time.

Jesus started nine games in all competitions last season, scoring six goals. He, too, was into the final year of his deal, and he was one of the club’s highest earners. At one stage, it looked as though he might look to see out his contract and in the end, a £8.6m deal with Barcelona rising to £12.9m suited all parties. Nwaneri barely played for Arsenal last season, going to Marseille on loan in January. Another loan, this time to Borussia Dortmund, made sense, particularly as there is a January recall clause.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Yet the weight of the outgoing numbers makes it hard to say Arsenal are stronger in this department and Arteta was in no mood to over-promise here. “It’s another question and we have to prove in that particular position whether we are better or not,” he said. “Let’s see. I understand the point of view [about the number of departures] but we have to understand as well the amount of minutes that those players played. And the ones that were injured last season, especially in the first six months. It is what it is.”There is the belief at Arsenal that Eze can in essence replace Martinelli on the left, albeit he is a different kind of player. Arsenal can perhaps play in a different way, with Riccardo Calafiori stepping up more from left-back. There is the hope that with a reshaped medical staff, the team can have a better run on the injury front – specifically with Bukayo Saka, Martin Ødegaard and Kai Havertz having uninterrupted seasons. The fear is that more problems will undermine them.

What has coloured the post-transfer window vibe is the failure to add a big-name attacker, to make a real statement signing. If Arteta did have a bucket list, then a game-changer for the front line would have been on it. Arsenal did try; they reached for stars such as Vinícius Júnior, Julián Alvarez and Morgan Rogers. Arteta even suggested that this kind of intent was progress. It is a tough sell when the glamour targets remain elusive.

View image in fullscreen Despite a summer-long saga, the transfer window closed with Julián Alvarez still an Atlético Madrid player. Photograph: Chema Moya/EPA

There was a point in July when Arsenal thought there was more of a chance they would get Vinícius than not. Then Real Madrid made him a new contract offer and he signed it. Alvarez just did not want to come, and the case of Rogers boiled down to the numbers. Arsenal offered £80m to Aston Villa for him and no more. Chelsea ended up going to £117m. They overpaid. But then they announced a deal with Villa two days later to loan Alejandro Garnacho there with a conditional purchase obligation, valuing the winger at £40m. Chelsea found a way to get Rogers. Arsenal did not. He will be a major subplot on Sunday .

There were moments when Arteta dropped his usual ultra-positive outlook and offered little peeks behind the curtain, including when he suggested that reporters speak to the sporting director, Andrea Berta, or the co-chair Josh Kroenke about why it was so difficult to close deals for the very elite.

“To get these deals done in this market is complicated,” he said. “I don’t know how it looks from the outside but we have put in everything that we possibly could to make those deals happen and we made most of them happen. We have been very efficient with what Andrea has done in the market again. It has been incredible, the support of all the club and that’s it. It’s not perfect but it doesn’t need to be perfect.”

Arteta believes that Arsenal have enough.

Sports.title: Premier League LIVE: Erling Haaland powers in, Fulham and Palace trade blows, Leeds lead and Tottenham under pressure after early Newcastle-Bournemouth thriller
Sports.content: Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso are the king of the Premier League and the pretender to the throne. This is the story of how their remarkable shared history led them to the same touchline - as very different managers

Sports.title: Ragged in attack, messy in defence - chaotic Newcastle were bettered by Bournemouth for most of their 2-2 draw... but Eden Hazard-like £51m Matias Fernandez-Pardo brings excitement, writes CRAIG HOPE
Sports.content:
Ragged in attack, messy in defence - chaotic Newcastle were bettered by Bournemouth for most of their 2-2 draw... but Eden Hazard-like £51m Matias Fernandez-Pardo brings excitement, writes CRAIG HOPE

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

There remains a little more chaos than cohesion with Newcastle 2.0, but character has survived the reboot.

Without that, they would have lost for the first time this season. On the balance of technical execution, they could have had few complaints.

For new boss Matthias Jaissle, this is a work in progress with a young team. Whilst that work is ongoing, it helps that a summer of change has brought with it renewed optimism on Tyneside.

That is why the mood inside St James’ Park did not sour, despite Bournemouth being the better team. And that is why, from 2-0 down, Newcastle were able to salvage a point.

That they scored with their only two shots on target tells the story of a disjointed attacking display - too many final balls were sloppy, as Jaissle admitted - and they were just as ragged in defence. They lost the midfield battle to the outstanding Alex Scott, too.

Across four matches, they have now faced 74 shots. There is a fragility in the middle of the park that needs to stiffen if those numbers are to improve. Scott out-fought and out-thought adversaries Nico Gonzalez and Lewis Miley.

Jacob Ramsey celebrates scoring Newcastle United's late equaliser against Bournemouth

£51m signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo has draw comparisons with Eden Hazard

Bournemouth led through Marcus Tavernier, followed by an unfortunate Newcastle own goal

Yet, for all of that, Jaissle and his team were applauded from the pitch post match, and rightly so. Newcastle would have - and did - lose this game in seasons past. They did not this time because of their spirt and Jaissle’s changes.

With two minutes remaining, substitute Jacob Ramsey smashed the equalising goal at the Gallowgate End. Newcastle might even have won it when, moments later, Yoane Wissa was inches away from collecting a Sean Steur pass and running clear. St James’ was bouncing by then.

Ramsey’s goal was the fourth from a substitute under Jaissle, who had recognised his team’s drift and addressed it. In every game, his changes have had the desired impact, and how they needed it here.

‘To come back was special and I think there is something we can build on,’ said Jaissle. ‘The desire to win the game was there until the end.

‘But the frustration is also there. In the first half, aspects were missing to be competitive. We could not match Bournemouth. In the Premier League, you need to be at your best over 90 minutes to get three points. But, if there were 10 minutes more at the end, I thought we could have gone for the winner.’

Harvey Barnes curls in his brilliant response to Newcastle going 2-0 down at home

MATCH FACTS NEWCASTLE (4-2-3-1): Hornicek 5; Dedic 5, Thiaw 5, Botman 5, Hall 5 (Livramento 90); Gonzalez 5 (Steur 77, 6), Miley 5 (Ramsey 63, 7); Elanga 4 (Murphy 78, 5), Willock 5 (Fernandez-Pardo 63, 7), Barnes 7; Wissa 6 Subs: Pope, Schar, Bamba, Toure Manager: Matthias Jaissle 6 BOURNEMOUTH (4-2-3-1): Petrovic 6; Smith 6, Hill 6, Antonio Silva 6, Truffert 7; Adams 6 (Cook 76, 5), Scott 0 (Christie 90); Rayan 6 (Doak 89), Kluivert 7 (Brooks 76), Tavernier 7 (Jebbison 89); Evanilson 6 Subs: Soler, Diakite, Di Gregorio, Sanchez Manager: Marco Rose 6 Ref: Rob Jones 5

It was the arrival of £51million debutant Matias Fernandez-Pardo that helped rescue a point as much as Ramsey’s right boot. The Belgian injected an energy and purpose lacking to the point of his 63rd-minute introduction. The comparisons to Eden Hazard are obvious, and you get the feeling the Toon Army are going to enjoy the young forward.

For too much of this match, though, there wasn’t a lot to like about Newcastle. Bournemouth came with the same game-plan from last season, and the one before that. The winning formula is not overly complicated, either - keep the ball, quieten the crowd and pin Newcastle in their own half. With that, use pacey forwards like Marcus Tavernier, Rayan and Justin Kluivert to hurt a backline that had retreated to the point of vulnerability. The hosts knew what was coming but could do little about it. The free beer given to supporters beforehand suddenly felt as flat at the lunchtime atmosphere.

By the 35th minute, Bournemouth were two goals in front and it was entirely deserved, even if a deflection presented Tavernier with the chance for his opener and the second was an own goal via a looping ricochet off Malick Thiaw.

They were still showing replays of that bizarre concession on the monitors in the ground when Harvey Barnes raced up the other end from the restart and curled in a trademark reply from 18 yards.

‘A world class goal,’ said Jaissle. ‘I could not have wished for that goal more in that moment.’

If the reprieve was supposed to signal a home improvement, it did not. Bournemouth were the more organised and looked to have kept Newcastle at bay until the ball bounced around the penalty area and Ramsey took it off the toe of Fernandez-Pardo to score. The two subs queuing up to convert spoke of their eagerness to impress.

It was the third game on the spin that Marco Rose’s side had conceded late goals to forgo Premier League victories, but they still look like a very competent team.

As for Newcastle, it is hard to know what their season will look like. Good, bad or indifferent, it sure promises to be fun.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo in line to play TOGETHER for the first time ever as their former team-mate plots star-studded farewell match
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo in line to play TOGETHER for the first time ever as their former team-mate plots star-studded farewell match

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo will line up for the same team for the first time ever later this year... if Carlos Tevez gets his way.

The world superstars have gone head to head over the years with their biggest tussles coming while they were at the top of the game with Barcelona and Real Madrid.

Messi and Ronaldo were pitted as rivals as they vied for the Ballon d'Or with either player winning the honour an incredible 10 years in a row between 2008 and 2017.

With Messi now plying his trade in the United States with Inter Miami and Cristiano Ronaldo happy in Saudi Arabia with Al Nassr, it doesn't look like they will be club team-mates before they retire in the not so distant future.

However fans of both players might finally see the duo share a dressing room as Tevez, who is a former team-mate of both players, plans to invite them to his testimonial match in December.

'Leo Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo will be there,' promised Tevez.

'I'll go pick them myself if I have to. I have both of them on WhatsApp.'

Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi could finally line up as team-mates in December

Carlos Tevez is planning to invite Wayne Rooney and Ronaldo to his testimonial match

Tevez lined up alongside Messi when representing Argentina's national team

Tevez hung up his boots back in 2021 but is yet to host a celebratory match to honour his career despite achieving great success with the likes of Manchester United, Manchester City, Juventus and Boca Juniors.

Juan Roman Riquelme has granted Tevez his wish of hosting his testimonial match at Boca Juniors' legendary La Bombonera Stadium, according to A Bola.

And both Messi and Ronaldo are set to top the guestlist of stars taking part, along with Wayne Rooney, Rio Ferdinand, Andrea Pirlo and Gianluigi Buffon.

Messi, who retired from international duty with Argentina on Monday, represented his country alongside Tevez between 2005 and 2015.

Ronaldo and Tevez formed a deadly three-pronged attack alongside Rooney during the Argentine's two-year spell at Old Trafford between 2007 and 2009.

They won back-to-back Premier League titles as well as the Champions League, League Cup and Club World Cup.

Tevez didn't win a major honour with Argentina's national team but did finish as a Copa America runner-up in 2004, 2007 and 2015. He also won a gold medal with Argentina's Olympic team in 2004.

Sports.title: Humiliating moment college football star is caught with his pants down on live TV after opponent's bruising tackle
Sports.content:
A college football player suffered the ultimate live TV nightmare on Friday after having his pants pulled down during a tackle – leaving his backside exposed to viewers.

Michigan State running back Cam Edwards endured the unfortunate disaster during the first quarter of the Spartans' season opener against Toledo in East Lansing.

Taking a handoff on a run up the middle, Edwards was swallowed up by a swarm of Toledo defenders near the line of scrimmage.

However, as Toledo's Lucas Lambert-Pipkin dragged him to the turf, the defender's hand got caught on Edwards' pants, pulling them down beyond his backside.

As Edwards lay on the turf, the FS1 broadcast camera zoomed right in on the downed running back as he struggled to pull his pants back up.

To make matters worse, Edwards' compression shorts had also ridden down, briefly exposing his bare backside to the viewers at home.

Michigan State running back Cam Edwards suffered the ultimate live TV nightmare after having his pants pulled down and his backside exposed following a tackle on Friday evening

Toledo's Lucas Lambert-Pipkin dragged him to the turf, pulling his pants down in the process

He did whatever it took to make the tackle happen… pants included 🤣 pic.twitter.com/V2yp0F2Epi — FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) September 5, 2026

The camera lingered for several excruciating seconds while Edwards scrambled on the turf to fix his uniform, sparking disbelief and jokes across social media.

One fan on X wrote: 'No model has a variable for losing your pants during a tackle. Week 1 remains undefeated.'

Meanwhile, another said: 'Michigan State RB Cam Edwards just got pantsed in front of 75,000+ people. This is why we love college football!'

Despite the mortifying on-field moment, Edwards brushed off the mishap to lead the Spartans' ground attack in his Michigan State debut.

The UConn transfer carried the ball 27 times for 98 yards and scored a touchdown, helping propel Michigan State to a 30-20 victory in front of the home crowd.

Edwards arrived in East Lansing during the offseason after a four-year stint at UConn, where he established himself as the Huskies' primary offensive weapon.

Sports.title: US Open chiefs reveal real reason why entitled influencers were kicked out and stripped of their free passes
Sports.content:
US Open chiefs have revealed why two entitled influencers were kicked out of the tournament and stripped of their access after they claimed it was because they shared images of their credentials online.

Meg Radice and Audrey Jongens, two NYC-based influencers who run the social media account The VIP List, said their passes were revoked just hours after they committed the cardinal sin.

The pair posted photos of their credentials on social media when they went to have dinner at a restaurant they had partnered with for the tournament.

'We post our credentials on our story. We go to our favorite restaurant. Have a nice steak dinner. We're downing Honey Deuces. We're having a great time, haven't even made it to court yet,' Redice told TMZ.

'Within two hours of us leaving, we were told we could no longer use our credentials. We were heartbroken and we still are,' Jongens added.

However, the USTA has now hit back with their own version of events, saying that their access was revoked because they had been improperly submitted as vendor staff.

Meg Radice and Audrey Jongens had their US Open credentials revoked earlier this week

Radice and Jongens are NYC-based influencers who run the social media account The VIP List

'These individuals were not credentialed as media or content creators,' the USTA said in a statement to The New York Post.

'They were improperly submitted for credentials on a staff list provided by a food vendor. Vendors are not permitted to credential media, content creators, or outside individuals as part of their staff.

'We review credentials throughout the tournament to ensure compliance with all US Open policies.

'When we identified that these individuals had been improperly credentialed, their access was revoked and vendors were reminded of our policy.'

Redice and Jongens have described themselves as 'diehard' tennis fans and said that they had intended to film content at the Grand Slam over the course of the two weeks, branding it a 'dream' opportunity.

'We were there to be respectful and follow the rules and just have a good time and show content to our followers about how amazing the US Open is,' Jongens added to TMZ.

'We were like, what do you mean? We had our credentials just stripped away within two hours before we even get to see a match. How does this happen?' Radice questioned.

'It was taken away like that. Just because we wanted to show how hot we looked in our credentials,' Radice added.

The pair pleaded with the USTA to allow them to return, saying: 'We don't even need an apology, we just want to go back.'

They bemoaned the fact that they had cancelled plans for the two weeks and planned their outfits to be able to attend the event.

US Open chiefs said the duo were removed after being wrongly submitted as vendor staff

One social media user called out 'influencers' for taking pictures while action was ongoing

Guests of a US Open hospitality suite were told off by a chair umpire for taking pictures during a game, seemingly using a portable light (ringed)

This year's tournament has seen the number of influencers at the event almost boule with the USTA credentialing 100 content creators.

Yet, the impromptu photoshoot between points, chatting and moving around have caused quite the stir at Arthur Ashe, leaving traditional tennis fans disgruntled over the lack of etiquette.

Earlier in the week, Naomi Osaka was forced to wait until the chair umpire had chided a group of spectators in one of Arthur Ashe's hospitality suites.

'Guys, please, in the suite behind me, please thank you guys, please take your seat,' the chair umpire announced to the stadium, as the broadcast camera panned to a group milling freely within their prime seats, taking pictures and talking.

Elsewhere in the stands, another spectator was heard calling out: 'The players are ready!'

When the stadium had stilled somewhat, Osaka returned to her serve but struggled with her ball toss, apologizing as she reset.

Footage captured from another spectator of the group on social media later showed them posing as a group, allegedly during a game, with a person who appeared to be a member of US Open staff holding up a portable light to help them capture the shot.

The social media clip showed another spectator on the same evening posing in front of the court with a portable light, also allegedly during live matchplay.

When contacted by Daily Mail Sport for comment on the incident, Brendan McIntyre, head of US Open communications said: 'We want our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend the US Open, but we also need to ensure that does not interfere with the action and competition on the court.

'These instances happen infrequently, and similar to when crowd noise reaches a certain level, our chair umpires have the ability to address the crowd when they occur.'

Sports.title: Richard Hughes, mastermind of Liverpool's £700m transfer rebuild, QUITS to move to Saudi Arabia
Sports.content:
Richard Hughes, mastermind of Liverpool's £700m transfer rebuild, QUITS to move to Saudi Arabia

Big-spending Richard Hughes has officially left his post as Liverpool sporting director.

The Scottish transfer chief informed the club of his desire to seek a new challenge earlier this year but agreed to stay in situ until the end of this summer window.

Hughes and Liverpool also agreed that he would work for only the Premier League club and not simultaneously conduct business for Saudi Arabian side Al Hilal, where he is expected to join.

The Reds hierarchy are satisfied Hughes honoured this agreement.

Hughes spent more than £700million at Anfield on big-money players like Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola.

He was also the man that identified Arne Slot and Andoni Iraola as head coach after Jurgen Klopp's exits.

He joined the club from Bournemouth in June 2024.

But he leaves with some fans frustrated at his business which has left Liverpool exposed in certain positions.

Richard Hughes has left Liverpool with the transfer chief set to move to Saudi Arabia

Alexander Isak was signed under Hughes' watch for an initial £125million in September 2025

Bradley Barcola made his debut for Liverpool against Ipswich Town on Friday night

Hughes said of his departure: 'First and foremost, I would like to reiterate what I said upon my arrival – it has been a source of great pride to have been given the opportunity to serve this incredible and unique institution. That is something I will always be grateful for.

'My appreciation extends to ownership for their support and leadership, to club staff at all levels who give so much to make Liverpool FC what it is, to the players who make such an enormous contribution and to the fans who support the team in great numbers whenever and wherever games take place.

'I'll always follow and support the club with great affection, and I wish everyone involved nothing but success for this season and beyond.'

Hughes (centre) played a key role in bringing manager Andoni Iraola (right) to Liverpool

LIVERPOOL'S BIGGEST DEALS UNDER HUGHES Alexander Isak - £125m Bradley Barcola - £123m Florian Wirtz - £116m Hugo Ekitike - £79m Jeremy Jacquet - £60m

Fenway Sports Group president Mike Gordon added: 'Richard joined us at the start of a period of change, embracing that responsibility by leading our football operations department and overseeing recruitment while also providing valuable support to our coaching staff.

'The results we achieved in these areas during this period are testament to this contribution. Nevertheless, we respect Richard's life choices and wish him and his family well in their next venture.'

The news comes a day after Liverpool claimed their first win of the season by defeating Ipswich Town 2-0.

Isak, who cost the club an initial £125million in September 2025, scored a first-half double against the Premier League new boys.

Bradley Barcola, signed from Paris Saint-Germain for £123m, made his debut on Friday night.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua's conqueror Andy Ruiz is PUMMELLED with punches and brutally beaten on his return to the ring after two years - but incredibly insists he WILL keep fighting
Sports.content:
Andy Ruiz, the man who condemned Anthony Joshua to his first ever professional defeat, suffered a horrific loss of his own on Friday night.

The 36-year-old Mexican was left bruised and bloodied as he lost to Poland's Damian Knyba on his return to the ring after two years out.

Knyba unleashed heavy punch after punch in the seventh round but Ruiz managed to ride it out, after being saved by the bell, to lose by a unanimous points decision.

Ruiz, who is now signed to British promoter Eddie Hearn, vowed to carry on despite losing his comeback fight to Knyba. The Pole now has a record of 18 wins and one defeat.

Rewind to June 2019, and Ruiz shocked the boxing world by upsetting the odds to knock Joshua out in the seventh round at Madison Square Garden.

Ruiz was a late stand-in for Jarrell Miller, who had failed a drugs test, and wasn't seen as a threat to Joshua's chances of remaining unbeaten and hanging on to his then IBF, WBO and WBA world heavyweight titles.

ANDY RUIZ IS SAVED BY THE BELL 🤯🤯🤯#TheFight | #RuizKnyba | Live NOW on DAZN and TNT ▪️ pic.twitter.com/JVQjG3KQM3 — DAZN Boxing (@DAZNBoxing) September 5, 2026

Andy Ruiz kneels down in front of the referee after being on the receiving end of heavy blows

Ruiz feels the full force of Poland's Damian Knyba during Friday's fight in New Jersey

Ruiz famously defeated the then undefeated Anthony Joshua back in June 2019

Joshua exacted revenge six months later and Ruiz has gone on to have just four more fights since due to injury problems, beating Chris Arreola and Luis Ortiz before drawing with Miller and now suffering his third loss.

Ruiz said after Friday's defeat in New Jersey: 'It was just a long layoff, and it was a great opponent.

'I didn't want to take an easy fight, so that's why I took Damian. He's a big guy. But we've got to take risks. I've still got it in me, man. I've just got to stay active and I want to fight again.

'Every time I tried to come in, he'd hold me really tight, and I just couldn't let my combinations go.

'He played a good game plan, but I'd love to run it back and do things a lot different.'

The judges scored the fight 117-110, 114-113 and 114-113 in Knyba's favour.

It wasn't the night Hearn was hoping for after signing Ruiz this summer but much of his current focus is on trying to finalise Joshua's highly anticipated fight against British rival Tyson Fury.

The bout has been proposed to take place in November after years of negotiations but the location of the fight appears to be a major sticking point.

Hearn and Joshua are said to want the fight to take place at Wembley Stadium in London while the Fury camp are reportedly leaning towards Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Sports.title: Andy Gray is handed return to UK broadcasting - covering Liverpool in his first game back - over a decade after leaving the country with Richard Keys in wake of Sky Sports sexism row
Sports.content:
Andy Gray is back working in football broadcasting in the United Kingdom after being handed a new role commentating for talkSPORT.

Scottish pundit Gray, 70, has been absent from UK television and radio for 12 years. He was sacked by Sky Sports in 2011 after being caught making sexist comments about a female assistant referee. He then worked alongside Richard Keys on a talkSPORT radio show and briefly appeared as a commentator on the FA Cup for BT Sport in 2014.

Gray and Keys had moved to Qatar in 2013 to front beIN Sports' coverage of the Premier League but returned earlier this year amid war in the Middle East and have been publishing their own podcast.

And now Gray has landed a more mainstream role: talkSPORT have hired him to commentate on their coverage of the UEFA Champions League. Gray is partnered with Jim Proudfoot on commentary for Liverpool vs Atletico Madrid this coming Wednesday - an 8pm kick-off at Anfield.

Speaking to Daily Mail Sport in an exclusive interview last month Gray had hinted he had a desire to return to the commentary box. 'I'd like to think, somewhere, I could do a bit of commentary,' he said. 'Not television, maybe, but radio. Just to see what it feels like again. I would like that.'

Keys, his long-time friend and colleague had said: 'I would be happy for you if that happened. I think you deserve it. To hear him back, analysing a football match, that would be special. He's the best I've ever known.'

Andy Gray, pictured with long-time colleague Richard Keys, is heading back to UK radio

talkSPORT say their hiring of Gray is 'not just a cameo appearance' and in the announcement revelled in Gray's iconic commentary line 'Oh you beauty! What a hit, son! What a hit' - recorded at the same venue, Anfield, in 2004.

Gray was sacked by Sky in 2011 after an off-air conversation between him and Keys was leaked to the press in which they questioned whether female assistant referee Sian Massey understood the offside rule. Keys resigned soon after as further off-air footage emerged, including his infamous 'Did you smash it?' remark about Jamie Redknapp's love life.

Today, Gray says: 'I can't imagine saying today what I said then, I just can't. I think we were two of the first people ever cancelled. I had 20 reporters outside my house for weeks.'

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
