World.title: Dolly Parton: Another candle in the wind, By Osmund Agbo
World.content:
It was in late spring of 1964, just a day after graduating from high school, that a diminutive farm girl packed her belongings and bade farewell to the life she had known in the Smoky Mountains of rural Tennessee. Her destination? Nashville, the undisputed Mecca of country music. She left behind the two-bedroom cottage where she had lived with her parents and eleven siblings, carrying little more than a dream and the audacious belief that she could make something of herself.

Like most people who dare to pursue improbable dreams, Dolly Parton wandered through a period of uncertainty, chasing fame and fortune while occasionally wondering whether she had made the right choice. Then, three years later, her fortunes changed dramatically. Country music star Porter Wagoner invited the twenty one year old Dolly to become the “girl singer” on his immensely popular, nationally syndicated television program, The Porter Wagoner Show.

Wagoner had been searching for someone to replace his female vocalist, Norma Jean, who had left the program after marrying and moving away. He recognized something in Dolly that others had not yet fully appreciated and gave the young singer what was, at that stage of her career, an invaluable gift: a national platform. Dolly repaid his confidence with exceptional songwriting, musicianship, charisma, and a full stage presence. Together, they became one of the most consequential partnerships in country music.

But Dolly Parton was never destined to remain someone else’s “girl singer.” Before long, the protégé was emerging as a formidable artist in her own right. Eventually, the student had to outgrow the teacher. In 1974, after seven years on the program, Dolly concluded that the time had come to leave.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

To articulate what she was feeling, she wrote Porter a song: “I Will Always Love You.” What began as a deeply personal farewell would, decades later, become one of the most recognizable songs in the history of popular music, when Whitney Houston’s rendition transformed it into a global phenomenon. But we’ll return to that later.

Porter did not receive Dolly’s departure graciously. Their relationship soured, and he eventually sued her for breach of contract, seeking $3 million in damages. The dispute was ultimately settled out of court for $1 million, which Dolly paid in installments because she could not satisfy the obligation in a single payment.

For many people, such an episode might have marked the definitive end of a relationship. Not Dolly. The lawsuit was undoubtedly painful, but she refused to allow one painful chapter to obliterate all the chapters that had preceded it.

Some people become famous because they master the art of giving the world precisely what it wants. Dolly Parton became extraordinary because she seemed remarkably uninterested in conforming to anyone else’s expectations of who she should be. She gave the world Dolly, unfiltered and unapologetic, adorned in rhinestones, crowned with towering hair, wrapped in extravagant femininity, and possessed of a heart as enormous as her public persona. Beneath all the glitter, millions of people recognized something far more enduring: authenticity.

Long before Dolly Parton became a global icon, she had already begun constructing the woman she would eventually become. Dolly once recounted how, as a young girl, she became fascinated by a woman in her community who was regarded with considerable disdain and described as promiscuous, even a prostitute. Yet Dolly noticed something beyond the gossip. The woman was always impeccably presented, with carefully styled hair, manicured nails, and clothing that announced her presence.

Young Dolly looked beyond the judgment and saw the glamour. She decided that when she grew up, she wanted to look just like that woman. And she did.

There is something profoundly revealing about that story. Dolly understood at an extraordinarily young age that other people’s judgments did not have to dictate the boundaries of her identity. She would totally define herself.

And so she embraced the towering hair, extravagant makeup, acrylic nails, plunging dresses, impossibly high heels, and, of course, rhinestones. She also openly acknowledged her cosmetic procedures. Dolly Parton quite literally fashioned herself into the woman she wanted to be, and the world had plenty to say about it.

People mocked her appearance. They speculated about the extent of her cosmetic surgery. They questioned why any woman would deliberately cultivate such an exaggerated, artificial, and unapologetically feminine image. Dolly’s response was remarkably simple: she liked it. She famously quipped that it costs a fortune to look this cheap.

Yet for all the glitz, glamour, fame, and fortune associated with Dolly Parton, there was one quality that elevated her above many of her contemporaries: her extraordinary humanity and almost inexhaustible instinct to find people in distress and do something meaningful to alleviate their suffering. And remarkably, she often did so without seeking the spotlight.

In November 2016, devastating wildfires swept through Sevier County, Tennessee, the very region where Dolly had been born and raised. Fourteen people died, and thousands of structures were destroyed or damaged. Dolly did not merely issue a statement of sympathy. She acted.

Within forty eight hours of the disaster, Dolly and the Dollywood Foundation established the My People Fund. Families whose primary residences had been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable were promised $1,000 every month for six months. Ultimately, 921 families benefitted.

For Dolly, this was not charity performed from a comfortable distance. These were her people, from the mountains that had shaped her childhood and given her the identity she carried into the world.

Then there was the song. Dolly wrote “I Will Always Love You” when she was still a young songwriter. Nearly two decades later, Whitney Houston recorded it for The Bodyguardand transformed it into something almost otherworldly. The song Dolly had written as an intimate farewell became an international cultural phenomenon.

Because Dolly had retained her songwriting and publishing rights, Whitney’s extraordinary success generated enormous royalties for her, reportedly about $10 million in the 1990s alone. What Dolly did with that fortune is one of the most touching footnotes in music history.

She purchased a substantial office and studio complex in a predominantly Black neighborhood in Nashville, an area that was then considerably removed from the traditional center of the city’s music establishment. She could have invested her money anywhere. Instead, she chose to invest in a community that was overwhelmingly Black and gave the property a name that was both humorous and deeply affectionate: “The House That Whitney Built.”

Dolly explained that she loved being there because it was Whitney’s community, and, in her words, it was also her community. That instinct to give rather than merely accumulate was evident even in her complicated relationship with Porter Wagoner.

Decades after their famous professional partnership had dissolved acrimoniously, Porter found himself in serious financial difficulty. The IRS was pursuing him for unpaid taxes, and he began liquidating his assets to address his debts. Among the assets he contemplated selling was a small publishing catalog containing songs he had accumulated over the years. Dolly could easily have watched from a distance. After all, this was the same man who had once sued her. Instead, she intervened.

Dolly Parton purchased the publishing company that owned Porter Wagoner’s songs, providing him with desperately needed financial relief. Then she did something extraordinary: she gave the company back to him. She understood the sentimental and historical value those songs held for Porter. She wanted him to retain them and, ultimately, to pass them on to his children. That is vintage Dolly Parton.

There are countless other acts of generosity that she championed, both in public and far from the glare of cameras. Through her Imagination Library, Dolly has promoted childhood literacy on an extraordinary scale, providing free, high quality books to children from birth to age five, irrespective of their families’ financial circumstances.

When Dolly partnered with the Herschend family in 1986, the existing Silver Dollar City attraction in Pigeon Forge was transformed into Dollywood. Her motivation was not merely commercial. She wanted the world to discover the beauty of the Smoky Mountains she had loved since childhood, while simultaneously creating meaningful employment and economic opportunity for the people of her native community.

In more ways than one, Dolly’s story has always felt strangely familiar to me. I, too, grew up among eight siblings in a small village tucked away in the hinterland of Eastern Nigeria, where we lived largely from the harvest of the family farm. Like Dolly’s hometown, it was a place where dreams could sometimes appear impossibly distant, yet somehow remained tantalisingly within reach.

After coming to America, I spent considerable time working in the coal country of Appalachia, a rugged and beautiful part of the country that bears more than a passing resemblance to the Smoky Mountains where Dolly was born and raised. Perhaps that is why her story resonates so deeply with me.

Beneath the rhinestones, the towering hair, the fame, the fortune, and the larger than life persona lies a story I recognize. It is the story of a child born into modest circumstances who refused to allow the limitations of her beginnings to determine the magnitude of her dreams. Dolly Parton did not merely escape poverty. She transcended it without becoming ashamed of where she came from. She did not abandon her people when success finally arrived. She went back for them.

Success can make a person famous. Wealth can make a person powerful. But neither necessarily makes a person generous. Dolly Parton managed to become all three while remaining recognizably human.

Dolly Parton, we are forever grateful for the love, laughter, music, generosity, and humanity you shared with the world.

Now that you have your wings, we wish you all the best as you join the rest of Heaven’s Angels. There will never be another Dolly Parton, and we will always love you.

Osmund Agbo is a medical doctor, author, and the 2026 recipient of the Thabo Mbeki Prize for Scholarship and Public Service.

World.title: University lifts suspension on lecturer who claimed tricyclists earn more than professors
World.content:
The management of Abia State University (ABSU) has lifted the suspension of a lecturer, Nnamdi Nwaeze, from the Department of Economics, Faculty of Economics and Management Sciences.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that Mr Nwaeze, a professor, was suspended for his Facebook post in August in which the lecturer claimed that professors in ABSU earn less than N400,000 as monthly salaries.

The professor’s post was addressing the the industrial action declared at that time by the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) at ABSU.

Lifting of suspension

In a letter dated 3 September and signed by the Acting Registrar of the ABSU, Joy Nwankwo, the university announced the lifting of the lecturer’s suspension.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Following a written plea from ASUU-ABSU, the university management hereby lifts your suspension effective immediately,” Ms Nwankwo said.

The acting registrar, however, said the lifting of the suspension was without prejudice to the investigative panel set up to probe allegations of misconduct against the lecturer.

She said the “ultimate report” of the investigative panel was still being awaited by the university management.

‘Momentary reprieve’

In a long Facebook post on Saturday, Mr Nwaeze expressed gratitude to Nigerians who supported, showed solidarity, and advocated against his suspension which he said helped him to achieve “this momentary victory.”

The lecturer, however, said the university’s reference to the continued investigation against him suggested that the recall was “a momentary reprieve.”

“While it has become difficult and unfashionable to continue with the ill-fated and provocative suspension, they have merely retreated but haven’t surrendered to good conscience and justice,” he said.

‘It’s geek gift, my initial suspension politically motivated’

Mr Nwaeze praised Governor Alex Otti of Abia State for facilitating his recall, explaining that the governor might not have instructed anyone to oppress him.

While appealing to Mr Otti to call those oppressing him to order, he reminded the governor that the journey to justice and fairness was still ahead despite his intervention.

The lecturer, however, claimed the lifting of the suspension was “a mere greek gift” offered to firstly prevent ASUU-ABSU from resuming the suspended strike at the expiration of the 4 September ultimatum.

“Secondly, but more importantly, they offered this greek gift in order to buy time and continue to shop for non-existent offences that could be ascribed to me in order to achieve a premeditated and prejudiced outcome, either to silence me, sack me, or drag my highly reputed name through the mud,” he said.

The professor said while he is neither infallible nor above investigations, he believes that he did not commit any offence against the university or the Abia State Government.

“My ordeal is politically engineered. Let me put it on record that before now, I have been hunted and subjected to several different panels in the past two to three years; of which fortunately none has indicted me.

READ ALSO: Nigerian university suspends lecturer for claiming tricyclists earn more than professors

“Unfortunately, rather than embracing peace and harmony, these persecutions have continued, which culminated in the ill-fated suspension,” he said.

“I, therefore, wish to put the world on notice that all these are politically premeditated and sponsored, using ABSU as the machinery.”

Mr Nwaeze insisted that, in his engagements on topical issues and governance, he has not only remained civil and respectful, but has never disrespected, maligned, or defamed the governor as a person or his esteemed office.

“Let me state here that I will stoutly resist every attempt to intimidate, hoodwink, malign, victimize, or cow me into silence and oblivion.

“I believe that I have the legal, mental, and moral fortitude to defend myself and guard my hard-earned credibility and integrity,” he said.

The lecturer expressed fears that his safety in ABSU and Abia State was no longer guaranteed.

“However, lawful measures are being taken to protect and preserve my life,” he said.

World.title: Plateau shuts schools over suspected diphtheria outbreak
World.content:
The Plateau State Government has ordered the temporary closure of all public and private primary and secondary schools as part of measures to contain suspected cases of diphtheria in the state.

The Commissioner for Information and Communication, Joyce Ramnap, announced the directive in a statement on Saturday, saying the closure would take effect from Monday, September 7.

The government said the measure followed the reporting of suspected diphtheria cases in Jos North, Wase, Jos South, and Bassa Local Government Areas.

Schools that have resumed academic activities are required to close from Monday and remain shut until further notice, the statement said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The government directed school proprietors, administrators, teachers, parents and guardians to comply with the order and ensure that pupils and students remain at home during the period.

It said the measure was intended to protect pupils, students, teaching and non-teaching staff while health authorities assess and respond to the outbreak.

The government said further information on the resumption of academic activities would be communicated to the public.

Death toll rises

The school closure comes amid concerns over the increasing number of deaths linked to the outbreak in Plateau.

PREMIUM TIMES gathered on September 3 that the Plateau State Commissioner for Health, Nicholas Baamlong, said 143 suspected diphtheria cases had been recorded in the state, with 23 deaths and nine patients receiving treatment at the Jos University Teaching Hospital and Plateau Specialist Hospital.

However, a resident of Jos North, Usman Sheidu, told the Guardian newspaper that four additional deaths had been recorded in the local government, bringing the reported death toll to 27.

Mr Baamlong said patients identified with the disease were being quarantined at the two hospitals as part of efforts to prevent further spread.

“So far, we have 143 suspected cases; we have had 23 deaths and nine are currently on admission at JUTH and the Plateau Specialist Hospital, Jos,” he said.

He identified late presentation of patients and difficulties in obtaining diphtheria antitoxin as major challenges to the state’s response.

Vaccination urged

Diphtheria is a potentially fatal bacterial infection that can spread through respiratory droplets and close contact. Vaccination is the main means of preventing the disease.

The Plateau government’s decision to shut schools comes as health authorities continue to encourage vaccination and early reporting of suspected cases.

In Kano State, the Kano State Centre for Disease Control recently urged traditional rulers to intensify community sensitisation and encourage residents to accept vaccination against diphtheria and other vaccine-preventable diseases.

The centre’s Director-General, Muhammad Adamu-Abbas, also urged traditional medicine practitioners and barbers to avoid treating suspected diphtheria cases and instead refer them promptly to health facilities.

The Plateau government urged all stakeholders to cooperate with the temporary closure and other measures being taken to protect residents while the situation is being monitored.

World.title: Queen Sarraounia: Hausa guerrilla warrior who took on barbaric France, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
Niger Republic was rocked by an attempted coup from 29 to 30 August. The plotters invaded the Diori Hamani International Airport, where Air Base 101 is stationed. They also stormed the state broadcaster and the presidential palace.

They were defeated, and the populace took to the streets in protest against the attempt to return France to its position of dominance in the country. France had, in 1898, invaded, destroyed and colonised territories that now constitute Niger Republic. It virtually dictated to that country for 125 years until the 2023 coup led by General Abdourahamane Tiani.

Interestingly, it was in Niger Republic that France met one of the stiffest resistances to its military colonisation of Africa. That resistance, which also exposed one of France’s most bestial expeditions, was led by Queen Sarraounia Mangou, leader, priestess and military commander of the Hausa Azna nation.

Before invading Azna, France had subjugated Algeria and Tunisia in North Africa; Gabon and French Congo in Central Africa; Madagascar and Djibouti in the East; and Mali, Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina Faso and Benin Republic in West Africa. In 1898, it set out on one of its most brutal campaigns to seize the Chad Basin, including Niger.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

To do so, France sent out its Central African-Chad Mission, or Voulet–Chanoine Mission.

It set out from conquered Senegal in November 1898. It was fused with two other missions: the Gentil, which advanced from Congo, and the Foureau-Lamy, which came in from Algeria. It was led by bestial military leaders for whom human life, especially African life, meant little or nothing. In command was Captain Paul Voulet, who was reputed in the army as a human vampire with “a true love of blood and cruelty coupled with a sometimes foolish sensitivity”. His Adjutant Lieutenant, Julien Chanoine, was reputed as being: “cruel out of cold-bloodedness as well as for pleasure”. Both officers had apparently been deliberately paired, as they had shown their level of depravity back in 1896 when they laid waste to the Mossi Kingdoms, including Ouagadougou, the capital. The officers were deliberately given vague orders on how to carry out the mission of bringing the African territories “under French protection.”

The Minister of Colonies, Andre Lebon, told them: “I don’t pretend to be able to give you any instructions on which route to choose or how you are to behave towards the native chieftains.” The officers saw their mission as the annihilation of peoples, including the burning down of villages and towns on their path. They left in their trail destruction and massacres, regardless of the age and gender of their victims. When, on 8 January, 1898, some soldiers were wounded in the village of Sansanné-Haoussa, the French officers, in retaliation, executed 101 persons, including thirty women and children. Their bestiality preceded them, and the various territories on their path simply surrendered. So, they were shocked when Sarraounia, who led just six Hausa villages, refused to surrender to the heavily armed French army of two thousand.

As the furious French army marched towards Azna, she moved the women and children into the dense forest. The battles went on for months until 16 April, 1899, when, at the Battle of Lougou, the French were victorious—or so they thought.

But Sarraounia and her army did not surrender. Rather, they melted into the thick forests, where they began a guerrilla war that was to force the French into retreat, destroy the morale of its army and lead to mutiny.

The French military was faced with a seemingly invisible Azna army that attacked at will, food shortages, growing restlessness and frustration in finding Sarraounia.

So, the pursuit was abandoned because even some of the Africans in the French military had begun to believe that she was indeed a spirit. The reports of the bestiality of the French military had also started circulating in France, and a diplomatic dispute with Britain was brewing, as the French expedition was also carrying out its brutality in Sokoto, which was British territory. A decision was taken to change the leadership. Governor-General of French Sudan, Colonel Vimard, was instructed to have them replaced.

The French Governor of Timbuktu, Lieutenant Colonel Jean-Francois Klobb, was appointed to take over the command.

In his book, Exterminate All the Brutes, S Lindqvist reported that when Klobb went to replace the officers, he found: “a trail of burned villages and charred corpses. He passed trees where women had been hanged, and cooking fires where children had been roasted. He also found the corpses of the expedition’s guides; those that had displeased Voulet had been strung up alive in a position that the foot went to the hyenas and the rest of the body to the vultures.” Meanwhile, the French officers continued their mindless massacres. In reaction to the sustained guerrilla warfare of Sarraounia, the French, led by Voulet, massacred thousands of persons on 8 May, 1899, including wiping out the village of Birni-N’Konni.

Even by the brutal standards of French colonialism, this was one of the most brutal massacres in its history. When, after being on the trail of the French Mission for about 2,000 kilometres, Klobb caught up with it on 10 July, 1899, he sent Voulet a letter informing him of his replacement and recall home. But Voulet replied that Klobb had only fifty guns, while he had 600, and would not hesitate to use them if Klobb dared come to his base. Then, Voulet went on with the massacres. On 13 July, 1899, the French military, in retaliation for two of its soldiers killed by a villager, executed 150 women and children.

Klobb, on 14 July, 1899 appeared at the French base in full-dress uniform. He addressed the Mission, reminding the soldiers of their duties to the military and country. Voulet ordered his men to shoot Klobb. They did. When he did not die immediately, another salvo was released, killing him. After Klobb’s assassination, Voulet declared: “I’m no longer a Frenchman; I’m a Black chief. With you, I will found an empire.”

On 16 July, 1899, Voulet and Chanoine assembled the soldiers, told them that duty was to obey orders, and released some shots. A Senegalese soldier then shot Chanoine dead. Voulet escaped but returned the next morning and was killed by the sentry. The new commander, Lieutenant Pallier, tried to continue the Mission but was forced to rescind his decision as the soldiers threatened mutiny. Queen Sarraounia Mangou was never found. But the locals believed she had used her spiritual powers to confuse the French invaders, cause the officers to execute one of their own, and make the soldiers turn their service weapons on their officers. The French were so ashamed of their war against the African Queen that, for a century, they tried to blank her out of history. But, as you can see, they failed.

World.title: JAMB releases 2026 UTME results of underage candidates
World.content:
The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) has released the 2026 Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) results of candidates who are below the prescribed minimum admission age of 16 years.

The board, however, said the release of the results is only to enable the candidates and their parents or guardians to know their performance and does not confer eligibility for admission.

In a statement by its spokesperson, Fabian Benjamin, JAMB said an underage candidate for the 2026 admission exercise is anyone who will be less than 16 years old by 30 September.

Candidates can check their results by sending RESULT to 55019 or 66019, using the same telephone number they used to register for the UTME.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

JAMB said results released under the arrangement could not be used for admission or any other official purpose, except for candidates who meet the requirements for exceptional consideration.

“Participation in the UTME and the release of a candidate’s result do not, in themselves, guarantee admission,” the statement said.

Why JAMB withheld the results

The release follows months of withholding the results of underage candidates who sat for the 2026 UTME.

JAMB said more than 38,000 underage candidates registered for the 2026 UTME. Last year, 41,027 candidates sought consideration under the special underage category in the 2025 UTME.

When JAMB began releasing the 2026 UTME results in April, candidates below the age threshold who attempted to check their scores received a “No Result Yet” message.

The board said the decision was deliberate and in line with its policy that only candidates who will be at least 16 years old by 30 September are ordinarily eligible to register for and sit the UTME.

However, JAMB allows a narrow exception for exceptionally brilliant candidates who are below 16 but can demonstrate that they are academically and otherwise ready for tertiary education.

The board had therefore said the results of the underage candidates would remain withheld until the exceptional admission assessment was completed.

How the exceptional admission process works

JAMB said candidates must first score at least 320 out of 400 in the UTME to proceed to the next stage.

They must then demonstrate strong performance in other areas, including at least 80 per cent in the relevant Senior Secondary School Certificate Examination (SSCE) subjects, where applicable, and meet the required Post-UTME standards of their chosen institutions.

They must also undergo a final assessment conducted by experts before they can be classified as exceptionally gifted and considered for admission.

JAMB has also said that underage candidates are required to undergo dedicated Post-UTME screening, even in universities where the general Post-UTME exercise has been suspended.

How JAMB selected gifted candidates in 2025

Last year, only 85 of the 41,027 underage candidates who sought consideration for admission eventually qualified.

JAMB explained that the process began with the selection of 599 candidates out of the 41,027 who scored at least 80 per cent (or 320) in the UTME, making them eligible to proceed to further assessment.

The 599 candidates were subjected to further scrutiny, including verification of their school certificates and Post-UTME performance. That process produced 182 finalists, who subsequently underwent verification, interviews and further screening.

JAMB eventually cleared 85 candidates for exceptional admission after the final assessment, which included written assessments and face-to-face interviews.

READ ALSO: INEC to support JAMB with biometric verification technology

2026 assessment still ongoing

JAMB said the 2026 exceptional admission process has not been concluded.

The board said it would wait for the release of this year’s National Examinations Council (NECO) results before proceeding to the final stage of the assessment.

It added that a date for the final assessment will be announced after the release of the NECO results.

JAMB said only candidates who successfully complete all stages of the exceptional admission process and satisfy the prescribed requirements will be considered for admission.

World.title: Jos University Teaching Hospital’s psychiatric facility stretched as mental health cases rise
World.content:
For three days, Emmanuel John waited anxiously in the psychiatric emergency unit of the Jos University Teaching Hospital (JUTH), hoping a bed would become available for his daughter.

She had been referred to the hospital after suffering a severe mental health episode, but every bed in the psychiatric ward was occupied. She remained in the emergency unit, where doctors and nurses monitored her condition while the family waited for a vacant bed.

“We spent three days there because there was no bed,” Mr John told PREMIUM TIMES.

When a bed eventually became available, the family’s relief was short-lived. According to Mr John, his daughter was discharged early to yield her bed space to patients in more critical condition.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I was disappointed, but I didn’t blame the doctors,” he said. “They were doing everything they could. The real problem is that there are too many patients and too few beds.”

Mr John’s experience illustrates the growing strain on one of North-central Nigeria’s major referral centres for mental healthcare.

John’s experience is becoming increasingly common at JUTH. As more Nigerians seek treatment for mental illness, the hospital’s psychiatric department is struggling to cope with demand, leaving patients waiting for admission, stretching healthcare workers and exposing wider weaknesses in Nigeria’s mental healthcare system.

A PREMIUM TIMES investigation, based on interviews with patients’ relatives, healthcare workers, hospital management and mental health experts, found that rising demand for psychiatric services is stretching JUTH’s capacity, forcing clinicians to make difficult decisions about admissions and discharges.

Although JUTH has not publicly released annual psychiatric admission figures, hospital officials and mental health workers interviewed by PREMIUM TIMES said they have witnessed a steady increase in patients over recent years.

They attributed the trend largely to rising substance abuse, worsening economic hardship, insecurity and increased public awareness that has encouraged more people to seek treatment.

Families caught in crisis

Mr John’s family is not alone.

Patience Samuel recalled a similar ordeal after her son developed a severe mental health condition and was taken to JUTH for specialist care.

Following an assessment, the family was informed that no admission bed was available.

“They attended to him, but they couldn’t admit him because there was no bed,” she said.

With no alternative, the family sought treatment at a private hospital, where the cost of care placed a heavy financial burden on them.

“If there had been space at JUTH, we would have stayed because treatment there is more affordable,” she said.

Their experiences highlight the difficult choices confronting many Nigerian families who depend on public hospitals for mental healthcare.

An overstretched facility

During several visits to JUTH’s psychiatric department, this reporter observed anxious relatives waiting around the emergency unit as healthcare workers attended to patients awaiting admission.

Hospital management confirmed that the department currently operates only two inpatient wards, a 20-bed male ward and a 15-bed female ward. Once the wards reach capacity, newly referred patients remain in the emergency section until space becomes available.

Healthcare workers, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly, described the shortage as a persistent challenge.

According to them, clinicians are frequently compelled to balance the needs of patients already on admission with those arriving in critical condition. As a result, patients whose conditions have stabilised may be discharged earlier than doctors would ordinarily prefer to create room for emergency cases.

For many families, the alternatives are limited: endure days of uncertainty while waiting for admission or seek treatment at private facilities where the cost of care is often beyond their means.

A national challenge

The pressure on JUTH mirrors a wider crisis confronting Nigeria’s mental healthcare system.

According to the Federal Ministry of Health, only about one in five Nigerians living with severe mental illness receives appropriate treatment, leaving an estimated treatment gap of about 80 per cent.

A shortage of specialists has further weakened access to care. Nigeria has fewer than 300 practising psychiatrists serving a population of more than 200 million people, with most concentrated in major urban centres.

Mental health advocates attribute the situation to years of inadequate funding, persistent stigma, limited community-based services and the migration of healthcare professionals.

These challenges have increased pressure on tertiary hospitals such as JUTH, which now receive referrals from neighbouring states, even as their resources remain limited.

The growing burden comes despite recent policy reforms aimed at improving mental healthcare. The National Mental Health Act replaced decades-old legislation and seeks to strengthen mental health services, promote community-based care and protect the rights of people living with mental illness.

However, experts say meaningful implementation will require sustained funding, improved infrastructure and the recruitment of more specialised personnel.

Against this backdrop, JUTH has become a critical lifeline for many families seeking affordable psychiatric care, making the pressure on its limited facilities increasingly difficult to manage.

Hospital management responds

The Chief Medical Director of Jos JUTH), Pokop Bupwatda, acknowledged that the psychiatric department is operating under immense pressure but said the hospital has begun taking steps to improve capacity and service delivery.

In an interview with PREMIUM TIMES, he linked much of the increase in psychiatric admissions to the growing abuse of psychoactive substances, particularly among young people.

“We have seen many cases related to substance abuse, especially among young people,” he said. “It is one of the biggest challenges confronting mental healthcare today.”

Mr Bupwatda said the problem extends beyond patients seeking treatment.

“We have even discovered some members of our staff abusing substances. Whenever such cases arise, we ensure they receive appropriate rehabilitation because our priority is to help them recover.”

He stressed that tackling substance abuse requires a coordinated response involving families, schools, religious institutions, communities and government, arguing that hospitals alone cannot reverse the trend.

His concerns are consistent with national findings.

According to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), an estimated 14.3 million Nigerians aged 15 to 64 used psychoactive substances in 2018, representing a prevalence rate of 14.4 per cent—more than twice the global average at the time.

The survey remains Nigeria’s most comprehensive national assessment of drug use and continues to inform policy discussions on substance abuse and mental health. Cannabis remains the most commonly used illicit drug, while the non-medical use of opioids such as tramadol and codeine continues to drive addiction and psychiatric disorders across the country.

Mental health specialists say prolonged drug abuse can trigger psychosis, worsen existing psychiatric illnesses and increase the likelihood of relapse, making treatment more difficult and recovery longer.

Mr Bupwatda said the Federal Government’s policy requiring drug tests for prospective employees of federal health institutions is one of several measures aimed at addressing the challenge.

“The objective is to identify those who need help before they enter the workforce,” he said. “Where necessary, rehabilitation is provided because the goal is not punishment but recovery.”

Shortage of specialists

Beyond inadequate bed space, the hospital is also struggling with a shortage of specialised personnel.

Mr Bupwatda admitted that the psychiatric department is overwhelmed, describing the challenge as part of a wider healthcare workforce crisis affecting Nigeria.

“Yes, they are overwhelmed,” he said. “But this reflects the broader shortage of healthcare workers across the country. It is not a challenge peculiar to psychiatry.”

He explained that psychiatric care requires specialised training, making recruitment considerably more difficult than in many other areas of medicine.

“It is not every doctor or nurse that can work in psychiatry,” he said. “We are training more psychiatric nurses to strengthen the department and improve service delivery.”

During visits to the psychiatric department, this reporter observed relatives sitting quietly outside the emergency unit while nurses moved between patients awaiting admission. Inside, clinicians attended to new referrals even though the inpatient wards were already full, highlighting the pressure facing the department.

Despite these constraints, relatives of patients praised the commitment of doctors and nurses, saying staff continued to provide compassionate care despite limited resources.

Security concerns

The investigation also uncovered concerns about security within parts of the psychiatric complex.

This reporter observed sections of the complex that were not fully enclosed. Some healthcare workers, who requested anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly, expressed concern that the layout could make it easier for patients to leave the premises without authorisation.

Others alleged that prohibited substances occasionally find their way into the facility through visitors, potentially undermining the rehabilitation of patients receiving treatment for drug-related mental health conditions.

Responding to the allegations, Mr Bupwatda said he was unaware of the concerns but promised to investigate them.

“I am hearing that for the first time,” he said. “I will discuss it with the Head of Department. If there are security lapses, we will address them because the safety of our patients remains our priority.”

He added that strengthening security forms part of the hospital’s broader expansion plans, which are expected to improve both patient safety and the quality of psychiatric care.

Expansion offers hope, but challenges remain

Mr Bupwatda said the ongoing expansion of JUTH’s psychiatric complex is expected to ease pressure on the department by increasing admission capacity and improving the treatment environment.

According to him, the complex was designed to be developed in phases, with the existing wards representing only the first stage of the project.

He disclosed that the second phase is between 90 and 95 per cent complete and will provide additional wards and treatment spaces once commissioned.

“Our goal is to ensure that more patients receive timely care in a safer and more conducive environment,” he said.

The CMD added that JUTH’s relatively affordable treatment costs, compared with many private hospitals, have also contributed to the growing number of referrals from Plateau and neighbouring states.

“For many families, this hospital remains the most affordable option,” he said. “That is why we must continue expanding our facilities to meet the increasing demand.”

Experts call for wider reforms

Mental health experts, however, say expanding one hospital will not be enough to address Nigeria’s widening mental healthcare gap.

A Jos-based mental health expert, Mary-Jane Samuel, described the experiences of patients and their families as evidence of years of underinvestment in mental health services.

“The burden of mental illness is increasing, but investment in mental healthcare has remained inadequate,” she told PREMIUM TIMES.

While welcoming JUTH’s expansion project, she said the country must also invest in human resources by recruiting more psychiatrists, psychologists, psychiatric nurses, occupational therapists and social workers.

READ ALSO: Tinubu reappoints JUTH chief medical director

According to her, strengthening mental healthcare at primary and secondary health facilities would reduce unnecessary referrals to tertiary hospitals.

“Many patients should be able to access treatment closer to their communities instead of travelling long distances to referral hospitals,” she said. “Early diagnosis and treatment at lower levels of care will reduce the burden on facilities like JUTH.”

Mrs Samuel also advocated increased funding for psychiatric medicines, counselling services and rehabilitation programmes, stressing that effective mental healthcare extends beyond hospital admission.

Although the National Mental Health Act provides a legal framework for improving access to care, protecting patients’ rights and promoting community-based treatment, Mrs Samuel, however, cautioned that legislation alone will not transform services without increased funding.

She said that expanding psychiatric units, recruiting specialists and strengthening mental healthcare at primary and secondary facilities are essential if tertiary hospitals such as JUTH are to avoid becoming overwhelmed.

Waiting for change

For Emmanuel John, the debate over mental health funding is deeply personal.

He still remembers the anxiety of watching his daughter spend three days in JUTH’s emergency unit because no bed was available.

Although he commended the doctors and nurses for their professionalism, he believes no family should have to endure such an experience before receiving specialist care.

“I hope the government completes the new building quickly,” he said. “If there are more beds, other families will not have to go through what we experienced.”

Mrs Samuel expressed a similar hope.

“If there are more wards and more doctors, it will help families like ours,” she said.

Months after his daughter’s admission, Emmanuel John still remembers the uncertainty of waiting three days for a hospital bed. While he remains grateful for the care she received, he believes no family should have to wait during a mental health emergency because of inadequate facilities.

His experience reflects a challenge extending far beyond JUTH. As mental health needs continue to grow across Nigeria, experts say improving access to care will require more than new laws. It will demand sustained investment in specialist personnel, hospital infrastructure and community-based services to ensure that families seeking help can receive timely treatment when they need it most.

World.title: INEC offers biometric support to JAMB
World.content:
Amupitan

By Olayinka Ajayi

The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, has expressed its readiness to support the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board, JAMB, with biometric verification technology as part of efforts to deepen collaboration between the two federal agencies.

Speaking during a courtesy visit to the INEC headquarters in Abuja at the weekend, JAMB Registrar, Prof. Segun Aina, led members of the board’s management team and said JAMB approached INEC as a sister agency with considerable experience in the deployment of biometric technology for the identification and verification of large numbers of Nigerians.

He said the Board was seeking to further strengthen the integrity of its examination processes and had learned that INEC had biometric verification equipment that might no longer be in active use.

Aina therefore appealed to the Commission to consider making some of the equipment available to JAMB to support its efforts to enhance biometric verification.

Responding, INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, SAN, welcomed the delegation and commended JAMB for its statutory responsibilities, describing the Board as a critical institution in Nigeria’s education system and the development of the country’s youth.

The Chairman received the delegation alongside the National Commissioner in charge of Outreach and Partnerships, Prof. Abdullahi Abdu-Zuru; the Directors of Information and Communications Technology (ICT), Dr. Lawrence Bayode; Human Resources Management, Umar M. Bashar; and Voter Education and Publicity (VEP), Mrs Victoria Eta-Messi; as well as the Chief Press Secretary to the Chairman, Adedayo Oketola.

Amupitan said INEC’s recent electoral engagements, including the Anambra and Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Area Council elections, the Ekiti and Osun governorship elections, as well as bye-elections conducted across the country, had further demonstrated the Commission’s growing technological capacity.

According to him, the deployment of technology in recent elections had attracted commendations from stakeholders, including the Office of the National Security Adviser and the United Kingdom High Commission, particularly for the credibility and peaceful conduct of the exercises.

The INEC Chairman directed the Director of ICT to review JAMB’s request and undertake a proof-of-concept assessment to determine the availability, technical condition and suitability of any biometric verification equipment that could potentially be deployed by the Board.

He described the visit as a reflection of the growing importance of inter-agency collaboration and the need for government institutions to leverage their respective expertise and resources in advancing national development.

Amupitan assured the JAMB delegation that INEC remained willing to explore further areas of cooperation that could strengthen the capacity of both institutions to deliver on their respective mandates.

In his response, Aina expressed appreciation to the INEC Chairman and management for the warm reception accorded him and his team, reaffirming JAMB’s interest in strengthening institutional collaboration with the Commission.

World.title: Tinubu grants ₦450m relief to SPAR Mall fire victims
World.content:
President Tinubu

By Ike Uchechukwu

Eighteen business owners affected by the fire that razed the Calabar Mall, popularly known as SPAR Mall, are to receive ₦25 million each from the Federal Government, amounting to ₦450 million.

The First Lady of Nigeria, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, disclosed this on Friday in Calabar, saying President Bola Tinubu approved the intervention to cushion the effect of the inferno on the victims.

According to her, an additional ₦50 million was presented to the Wife of the Governor of Cross River State, Bishop Eyoanwan Otu, to support women’s groups, while ₦15 million was given to women who received her in the state, bringing the total intervention to ₦515 million.

“Mr President commiserates with the government and people of Cross River over this unfortunate incident that destroyed many businesses and livelihoods.

“This intervention is to provide immediate support and help victims recover from their losses,” Senator Tinubu said.

The intervention followed the August 22 fire outbreak at the shopping mall, which affected several businesses and destroyed properties worth billions of naira, leaving business owners with substantial losses.

Senator Tinubu said the Federal Government’s gesture was aimed at providing immediate relief to affected entrepreneurs and helping them recover from the losses suffered in the disaster.

Receiving the First Lady, Governor Bassey Otu expressed appreciation to President Tinubu and Senator Tinubu for the intervention, describing it as a timely gesture that would bring succour to victims of the fire disaster.

The governor said the relief package would provide meaningful assistance to the affected business owners as they begin the process of rebuilding their businesses and livelihoods.

World.title: US military says it destroyed 3 Iranian oil tankers
World.content:
The US military said Saturday it had struck and destroyed three oil tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps after the Iranian military organization fired on American warships.

“Following Iran’s failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask,” Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement on X.

“American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo… in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship,” it continued.

Video posted by CENTCOM showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.

The three ships targeted were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies,” it said.

“Iran has no means by which to defend them,” it added.

No US soldiers were hurt after a destroyer and aircraft carrier “successfully evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks,” it said.

CENTCOM’s commander, Admiral Brad Cooper, said: “Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours.”

The strikes come as Washington insists that it is working to economically strangle Iran, including a blockade of its ports, while keeping alive the threat of military action.

Iran, for its part, has blocked commercial traffic through the critical Strait of Hormuz by threatening shipping that doesn’t have its permission to transit.

The two sides exchanged fire earlier this week, with the US saying it was targeting the IRGC’s ability to attack commercial shipping while Iran fired on US military bases in nearby Jordan.

AFP

World.title: Newcastle rally from two goals down to earn Bournemouth draw
World.content:
File. Photo by ANDY BUCHANAN / AFP.

Newcastle surged back from a two-goal deficit against Bournemouth on Saturday to draw 2-2 and extend their unbeaten start to the season after a period of intense upheaval at the club.

Matthias Jaissle’s team found themselves 2-0 down in the 35th minute after Marcus Tavernier’s close-range effort and an own goal from Malick Thiaw, both helped by deflections.

Newcastle winger Harvey Barnes changed the complexion of the match with a stunning curling effort less than two minutes later.

The home team struggled to find momentum in the second half but substitute Jacob Ramsey steered home in the 88th minute to ensure the points were shared.

Newcastle, who remain unbeaten in all competitions this season, drew 2-2 against Liverpool in their Premier League opener before brushing Tottenham aside 2-0.

The club appointed German boss Jaissle last month after the departure of the long-serving Eddie Howe, who also previously managed Bournemouth.

Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon have all left but the club have made eight new signings in what they described as a “transformational” summer transfer window.

Bournemouth, also under a new head coach, Marco Rose, following the departure of Andoni Iraola to Liverpool, started brightly at St James’ Park, taking a deserved early lead.

Alex Scott’s shot took a significant deflection and fell kindly for Tavernier, who showed impressive anticipation to poke the ball home past Lukas Hornicek.

Bournemouth doubled their lead when Justin Kluivert’s shot from distance smashed against the post and came back off the back of Hornicek before Scott’s cross hit Thiaw and looped over the line.

But the home side gave themselves renewed hope when Barnes surged down the left before cutting inside and curling a wonderful effort past the outstretched hands of Djordje Petrovic.

New signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo came on in the 63rd minute to warm applause and Jaissle made further substitutions as he searched for an equaliser.

The visitors, who have developed an unwelcome habit of conceding late goals, failed to clear and Ramsey stayed cool to earn a point.

World.title: Military aircraft crashes during airshow
World.content:
File: Photo by Punit PARANJPE / AFP

An F-4 Phantom military aircraft crashed Saturday at a base outside Athens during an airshow, Greek news agency ANA reported.

The circumstances of the crash were unclear, as was the fate of the two pilots aboard, local media said.

The aircraft had just taken off when it suddenly lost altitude and crashed, said a journalist from public broadcaster ERT who was at the scene.

There was an explosion immediately after the crash, which happened before thousands of visitors watching the annual “Athens Flying Week”.

A fire service helicopter was dispatched to the scene to extinguish the blaze caused by the crash, ERT reported.

Defence Minister Nikos Dendias cancelled a trip to Thessaloniki’s International Fair to visit the scene of the accident.

World.title: Nigeria,​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‌‍‌⁠​‍​‌⁠‌​ 163 countries to back UN resolution for larger Africa on world map
World.content:
President Tinubu

Nigeria has joined 163 other countries to endorse an African-led UN resolution seeking fairer world maps that accurately reflect Africa’s true geographical size.

The UN General Assembly adopted the historic “Correct the Map” resolution by 164 votes to one, with six abstentions.

The United States cast the sole opposing vote, while Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine abstained.

The resolution is formally titled “Correct the Map: Rebalancing global cartographic representation and promoting equitable representation of the world’s regions, particularly Africa.”

The African Union-backed campaign challenged centuries of cartographic representation that makes the African continent appear disproportionately small.

Africa covers approximately 30 million square kilometres and is the world’s second-largest continent by both land area and population.

However, advocates say conventional Mercator maps have historically presented the continent visually as considerably less imposing than its actual dimensions.

The vote enjoyed an overwhelming majority of UN members endorsing the continent’s demand for more accurate global geographical representation.

Togo led negotiations on behalf of the African Group, building on an AU-supported initiative that Africa needs to stop being represented as smaller than it actually is.

Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the UN General Assembly that maps were not merely technical illustrations but powerful instruments influencing how people understand the world.

“Maps shape our understanding of the world. They guide education, nourish the imagination and influence collective perceptions,” Dussey said.

The resolution promotes wider use of the Equal Earth projection and other equal-area maps where accurate comparison of the relative sizes of continents and countries is important.

It describes the consequences as contributing to the “symbolic minimisation” of Africa and other regions in the global collective imagination.

“A fair map does not change the geography of the world; it changes how we see the world,” said, adding, “a fair world begins with a fair map.”

The Equal Earth projection, developed in 2018, seeks to preserve the relative area of countries and continents, thereby presenting Africa much closer to its actual scale.

Unlike Mercator, equal-area projections do not enlarge Africa; rather, they remove the artificial enlargement given to territories nearer the poles.

The United States strongly rejected the initiative, arguing that the General Assembly should focus on more pressing global challenges.

France, however, supported the resolution, announcing plans to move away from Mercator in its official world maps.
