He said when he eventually saw people searching for him on a road, they were crying too — reflecting how much they had hoped to find him.

Security cameras capture Stanislav Volo exiting the Sea-to-Sky Gondola around 11:30 a.m. PT on Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (Squamish RCMP)

Volo said he got injured while on the hike, and had to wait a few cold nights for his foot to heal.

He said he learned a lot about survival in the wilderness during, and was determined to not spend the rest of his time on the mountain.

Volo survived by eating twigs and wildflowers.

"When you still have some sort of stamina, some energy, and you can actually do something and that's why ... I decided to, like, keep going," he said.

Stanislav Volo is seen in this handout image from authorities. (Yana Geng, Squamish RCMP)

His sister Ola Volo confirmed her brother was found earlier Friday.

"We found him," she said. "He walked out on the road on his two feet."

She eventually went to see her brother in hospital, where she connected him with CBC News.

He celebrated by eating pizza, calling it "very tasty."

'Remarkable that he survived'

Squamish Search and Rescue also confirmed that Volo had been found alive.

"It's absolutely remarkable that he survived," said search manager Tyler Duncan.

Volo managed to walk out onto the Indian Arm Forest Service Road where search and rescue had been flying a drone to look for him.

"He walked out of the forest onto the road and [we] were able to meet him and get in contact with him and provide him with some very basic first aid," Duncan said.

Volo was tired, hungry, cold and wet but overall he was doing well and wasn't injured, Duncan said.

The road he was walking on is on the backside of Mount Habrich Loop and he would have gone through difficult and technical terrain to reach the road.

"I would absolutely love to sit down with Stas and have a good conversation about what he has been up to for the last six days," Duncan said. "It's got to be a remarkable story."

WATCH | Search teams looking for missing hiker in Sea-to-Sky region: Search teams looking for missing hiker in Sea-to-Sky region | Duration 2:08

Duncan said it was one of the most "involved" searches he had been a part of in his 15 years in search and rescue.

"He was out in that storm. It must have been an absolutely horrendous experience for him," Duncan said.

Went hiking above the Sea-to-Sky Gondola

Volo planned to hike the Mount Habrich Loop and surveillance footage showed him getting off at the top of the Sea-to-Sky Gondola in Squamish around 11:30 a.m. PT on Sunday.

Drones, helicopters and police dogs joined in the search along with many volunteers from multiple search-and-rescue agencies.

The search for the missing Squamish man focused around Mount Habrich Loop. (Squamish Search and Rescue)

On Tuesday, Volo made a call to 911 saying he was stuck on the mountain.

RCMP Sgt. Katrina Boehmer said Volo was transported to hospital and is being treated for what is believed to be minor injuries.

World.title: A month after migrants surged into Ceuta, thousands of kids are still stranded on the streets
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

"I'm back on the street," 17-year-old Ikram wrote in a text message to CBC on Monday.

For a brief period, Ikram had felt relief in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. After spending almost a month sleeping in a forest, an abandoned bathhouse and on the street, the young Moroccan had finally found somewhere to stay. For three days, a family had hosted her as she helped look after their young children.

Then the work ran out.

Ikram left the Moroccan coastal town of Fnideq at the end of July, when an estimated 80,000 Moroccans and migrants from countries further south travelled to the north, hoping to cross into Ceuta. For many, the Spanish territory represents a possible route toward legal residency in Europe.

"In Morocco we are living, but not living the life we want," she said. Her father works as a tailor but earns little.

Most of the migrants who arrived during the July surge returned to Morocco within hours. But Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said 5,000 remain in Ceuta. Local authorities estimate 9,000 remain in and around the small enclave, whose population is roughly 80,000.

Among those who remain are hundreds of unaccompanied minors, including Ikram, living in extremely vulnerable conditions.

Ikram looks out toward the sea as she stands on a bridge in Ceuta near the border checkpoint through which migrants enter the city. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

Many minors under 13, Spain says

According to Jennifer Zuppiroli, a migration specialist at Save the Children Spain, the Spanish Ministry of the Interior has registered 2,500 "children and adolescents" in Ceuta so far.

The actual number could be considerably higher.

"Various social and neighborhood organizations estimate that there could still be thousands of minors awaiting identification and referral to protection services," Zuppiroli told CBC News. Spain's Minister for Youth and Children, Sira Rego, said many of the minors are under the age of 13 and that around 700 of the migrant minors were girls.

WATCH | The humanitarian challenge in Ceuta: Ceuta faces humanitarian challenge after surge of migrants | Duration 2:06 Roughly 2,000 migrants are left in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after 70,000 surged into the autonomous city last week, leaving humanitarian organizations stretched to their limits.

Most of the children and adolescents in Ceuta are from Morocco, Zuppiroli says, although minors from other countries are also there, particularly from sub-Saharan Africa, including Sudan.

(CBC is not using the last names of the migrants in this story because they fear deportation and reprisals from locals. For this reason, CBC is also not showing the faces of some of the migrants.)

Rego has reiterated that family reunification is the priority while acknowledging that "in most cases, there is no possibility of return." Under international law, the removal of unaccompanied minors is subject to strict safeguards, including the requirement to consider the child's best interests.

Ikram had tried to reach Ceuta alone during a previous mass crossing attempt in 2024. This time, however, she hadn't actually planned to go.

"My mom told me in the morning that people were crossing. Then, on my way to work, I met a friend who told me to go. I told her, 'No, I have a job.' She said, 'Let's just go and see.' And then I said, 'OK, let's go,' and we went."

At the border, they were confronted with a scene of chaos, with hundreds of people trying to swim around the border fence.

"We saw so many dead people," Ikram said. "Still I said, let me try my luck, and I went in. I almost died, too. I kept crying, and then I couldn't go on anymore."

One boy helped keep her afloat. "He kept pushing me, pushing me until I reached the shore."

When Ikram eventually reached the beach, she fainted and was taken to hospital. She was released the following day.

Her 15-year-old brother, Marwan, had crossed the land border earlier that day but left shortly afterward.

"He couldn't handle it," Ikram said, referring to the dire situation for migrants in Ceuta.

A scene from a recent protest against migrants in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

Ikram, however, insists she'll stay in Ceuta despite not having a place in any official accommodation or child-protection facility.

"I wish to build my future abroad, so I can help my mom and dad," she said. "Because right now, they're the ones counting on me."

For unaccompanied minors, Ceuta is 'a war zone'

Khadija Toufik, a French independent journalist who has reported for France Télévisions and TV5Monde, has seen how many minors are on the streets of Ceuta.

"They sleep alone outside," she said. "Every night is a night of terror, as soldiers come to wake them up, and very often, they are beaten with batons. Most of the minors I encountered in the streets were scarred and injured. For them, this is a war zone."

This vulnerability extends beyond unaccompanied minors. Some parents who have arrived in Ceuta with their children have also found themselves without stable shelter.

A man named Anouar crossed with his nine-year-old son, Wael, leaving his wife and three other children behind in Morocco. Since arriving, he and his son have moved between the streets and the homes of people who occasionally offer them a place to sleep, charge their phones or take a shower.

Anouar, left, came to Ceuta with his nine-year-old son, Wael. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

Meanwhile, tensions on the streets of Ceuta have escalated in recent weeks.

"There has been a rise in demonstrations by fascists calling for attacks against migrants," Toufik said. Last week , dozens of residents blocked Red Cross workers from distributing food and water to migrants. Later, fires were set at migrant encampments on a beach.

The unrest came after the arrest of 12 migrants accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, smashing its windows and injuring four people inside.

'The soldier hit me with a stick'

A 17-year-old named Abdo told CBC News that about three weeks ago, some 30 Spanish soldiers used violence to force him and other migrants out of an abandoned hospital where they had been sleeping.

"The soldier hit me with a stick. He broke my phone and my power bank," Abdo said in a video call with CBC News. He held up his hand, which was in a cast.

Medical volunteers with No Name Kitchen (NNK), a humanitarian organization established in Ceuta, treated Abdo's injured hand.

Ric Fernández, co-ordinator of NNK, says the group has collected more than 150 testimonies from migrants reporting violence by "uniformed agents, from the National Police, the military or civilians in disguise."

Seventeen-year-old Abdo, who did not want his face to be shown in this photo, told CBC News that about three weeks ago, Spanish soldiers used violence to force him and other migrants out of an abandoned hospital where they had been sleeping. His arm is now in a cast. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

Abdo has been in Ceuta for more than a month. It was his ninth attempt to reach Europe.

In the previous two years, he had tried crossing the Mediterranean by boat, by hiding inside a truck on a ferry bound for Spain and by trying to enter through Melilla, Spain's other North African exclave.

"In Morocco, there aren't opportunities to work," he said. Youth unemployment in Morocco is around 36 per cent, according to the pan-African research institution Afrobarometer.

Abdo's father, a taxi driver, died in a car accident 10 years ago. His mother, who has five children and suffers from a uterine condition, is unable to work. His sister has a master's degree in law but has also been unable to find employment.

This year, Abdo completed Morocco's baccalaureate, a national qualification students can get at the end of high school, and says he was among the three top students at his school. He dreams of becoming a writer or journalist.

In the meantime, his main preoccupation is finding a safe place to sleep.

Abdo's friend l'Fassi looks out from a bridge in Ceuta at lights back in Morocco. Ceuta is one of two autonomous Spanish territories, along with Melilla, that has a land border between Africa and the EU. (Marouane Beslem/CBC)

For the past three days, Toufik, who helps minors wherever she can, has arranged temporary accommodation for Abdo and another migrant in a hotel room. But with hotel prices rising, they will soon have to leave.

As for Ikram, she has become friends with an 18-year-old named Hasna, also from Morocco.

Members of NNK informed Ikram and Hasna they had received notice that a local organization had set up a safe camp for girls. The two told CBC News they walked together through the night looking for the camp but eventually decided it was safer to wait in a park.

"Honestly, we are scared, but it's night. We'll go in early in the morning."

The next day, Ikram was accepted into the camp. Hasna, who is not a minor, was not — and is still living on the streets of Ceuta.

World.title: As Canada-U.S. relations sour, border towns of upstate New York fear damage will be permanent
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At his marina in Sackets Harbor, N.Y., on a cloudy Wednesday afternoon, Mayor Alex Morgia looks toward the water and paints a vivid picture of the beauty he often sees, even on an overcast day.

"Sometimes those are the best sunsets because the sun will peek through underneath and then you get all of the cascading colours on the underside of the clouds," Morgia says, looking out over what has recently become North America's most controversial lake.

"We get sunsets over the lake year-round," Morgia says, before clarifying: "Over Lake Ontario, not to be vague."

Sackets Harbor, located on the lake's eastern shore around a 40-minute drive from the Canadian border, finds itself caught up in a war of words and wares, as the United States and Canada feud over tariffs and U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America."

The harbour, Morgia points out, was even mentioned in Trump's executive order.

It's not the first time the quaint village has been at the front lines of a fight between these two nations: Sackets Harbor was the site of two major battles during the War of 1812, Morgia says.

"People find cannonballs in their yard all the time," he said. "People use them as doorstops."

Alex Morgia, mayor of Sackets Harbor, N.Y., says there was a brief period when U.S. President Donald Trump was distracted with other issues, and he hoped it would take his attention off Canada so the two countries could be friends again. (Benjamin Lopez Steven/CBC)

While Morgia downplayed how much support Trump has for renaming the lake, he — along with other U.S. residents and officials living near the border in upstate New York — is concerned this heightened fight could spell the end of close Canadian ties, to the detriment of their communities.

"We had a brief period of time where I thought he was distracted with other problems and was going to leave the Canadians alone and we could be friends again. Obviously, that ship has sailed," Morgia said.

'It hits in the heart'

About a half-hour drive north of Sackets Harbor, on the U.S. side of the Thousand Islands Bridge over the St. Lawrence River, Corey Fram is fretting that the already difficult situation he faces is about to get much worse.

As director of the Thousand Islands Regional Tourism Development Corporation, Fram is responsible for marketing on both sides of the border. But after Trump got elected for a second time, there was a substantial decline in Canadian spending and border crossing, he said.

"It hurts to lose that economic impact of Canadian visitors on the New York side. But in a border community, it hits in the heart," Fram added.

WATCH | Decline in Canadian cross-border travel continues: Decline in Canadian cross-border travel continues | Duration 1:56 The last long weekend of the summer is here. CBC’s Troy Charles looks at cross-border travel and, perhaps unsurprisingly, Canadians continue to avoid the United States.

While he understands there may be a strategy Washington and Ottawa are each pursuing that buoys their countries' economic standpoints, those efforts have the opposite effect on border communities, he said.

"There's almost a sense that those of us along the border are having to pay the price for what is a supposed economic benefit for the greater good of each of the respective countries," Fram said.

Anthony Adamczyk is facing the same issue in Ogdensburg, N.Y., about 45-minute drive northeast. He's the executive director of the Ogdensburg Bridge and Port Authority, which owns and manages the local bridge spanning the St. Lawrence.

Despite a slight uptick in border crossings from Canada in January 2025 compared to the previous year, they declined the following month and have never recovered, Adamczyk said.

Anthony Adamczyk, executive director of the Ogdensburg Bridge and Port Authority, says the volume of traffic from Canada at the border crossing decreased 23 per cent in 2025 compared to 2024. (Benjamin Lopez Steven/CBC)

Overall, traffic volume decreased 23 per cent in 2025 compared to 2024, equating to about 136,000 vehicles. The bridge's toll revenue went down 35 per cent, representing about $536,000 in lost revenue.

Fram's longer-term concern is that the number of Canadian tourists will permanently remain lower. He told CBC's The House that each time a major crisis affects border crossings — like the COVID-19 pandemic or the 9/11 terrorist attacks — the numbers fall and never return.

"My concern is this is yet another step, a big jump down that we're not going to get back to where we were in 2024 anytime soon, and maybe not ever."

Residents divided over Trump's tactics

The ongoing fight over tariffs and Lake Ontario's name puts residents of Ogdensburg and Sackets Harbor in a complicated position. The two areas fall within St. Lawrence County and Jefferson County, respectively — both of which Trump has won by more than 10 points in previous presidential elections.

Outside a Walmart in Ogdensburg, Greg Barr told The House he visits Canada all the time and has never had any issues with Canadians. But when asked about the trade war, he said he thinks the U.S. has been "way too generous."

"Not [just] to Canada but to other countries," Barr said. "[Trump's] getting things more even, to me. Maybe he has a different way of doing it, but he does get results."

Jim Rupert, who runs a taxi service that takes clients back and forth from Canada all the time, echoed Barr's view that Trump's tactics are a means of equalizing the playing field.

Taxi operator Jim Rupert says Trump's tariffs are a way of equalizing the economic playing field, and Canada can do more to improve its standing by developing more of its natural resources. (Benjamin Lopez Steven/CBC News)

"I hate to listen to [Trump] half the time because he rambles, he rants, he does this and that, but the policies are solid."

But Carol and Gary Davis, who say they've noticed how much more their groceries cost nowadays, say they can't make sense of Trump's actions.

"When he got elected, gas was going to be cheap, food was going to be cheap," Gary said. "It's just the opposite."

Carol, who voted for Trump in the last election, said she's disappointed with the president — though she felt there weren't better options when she cast her ballot.

"So, yeah, I guess I do have regrets now."

Carol and Gary Davis say Trump promised to make gas and food more affordable — but the opposite has happened. (Benjamin Lopez Steven/CBC)

Local Republican lawmaker weighs in

Scott Gray, a Republican assemblyman who represents Ogdensburg and Sackets Harbor, is aware of residents' concerns. He told The House he's not opposed to tariffs, but doesn't want them to harm either his residents or Canadians.

"We have enjoyed a long-time exchange in our economy and our trade, and I think we should try to maintain that," Gray said.

He said he hopes some key irritants, like U.S. access to the Canadian dairy market, can be corrected through trade negotiations. But tariffs, he added, can be disruptive — as are counter-tariffs.

Gray pushed back on behaviour from the White House, including Trump repeatedly calling Canada the 51st state and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth belittling two female Canadian cadets.

WATCH | Democratic senator calls Hegseth's comments 'deeply disrespectful': Hegseth's comments on Canadian military 'stupid,' says U.S. Democratic senator | Duration 1:37 Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego says recent comments regarding Canada's military by U.S. cabinet secretaries are 'deeply disrespectful to the men and women of Canada that have died fighting with [the U.S.].'

But he also placed some blame at Canada's feet, like when Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Trump could "kiss my ass" in response to tariff threats.

"We need to make sure there's a fair trade deal, and we need to do it without creating animosity and friction, which is largely caused by whatever antics that you want to describe out there," Gray said.

Back at the marina in Sackets Harbor, Morgia questions whether the U.S. government will stop antagonizing its northern neighbour. He's sympathetic to Canadians' calls for Americans to step up and pressure their leaders to back off on punishing their country.

"I guess not until [midterm elections in] November. People are trying, but right now the Republicans control most of the government. And until that changes, I don't think he's going to be held to account."

World.title: Putin orders 72-hour pause in strikes on Kyiv as U.S. envoys visit Russia and Ukraine
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered a 72-hour pause in strikes on Kyiv, the Kremlin said Saturday, as U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow to try to revive a stalled push to end Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today," presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russia's Tass news agency. He said the decision was tied to preparations for Witkoff and Kushner's planned visit to the Ukrainian capital, which Kyiv has said will take place on Sunday.

The envoys' trip comes as both sides escalate aerial attacks, some four and a half years after the Kremlin's invasion of its neighbour. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that Ukraine would halt airstrikes during the envoys' visit and urged Moscow to do the same.

Washington’s push to end the fighting, now in its fifth year, has lost momentum as U.S. attention has been focused for the last six months on its war with Iran.

The last known visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, was in January, when they met Putin in the Kremlin. They have never previously visited Kyiv.

The Americans were met at the airport by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, Tass reported. Dmitriev shared photos of him meeting the U.S. delegation as they disembarked, alongside the caption, "Welcome to Moscow Peacemakers."

With peace efforts stalled, Russia has intensified its attacks on Kyiv and other cities with relentless bombardments recently stretching into daylight hours, taking advantage of Ukraine's shortage of air defensive systems.

On Friday, a Russian drone hit one of the most important government buildings in Kyiv — the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, known as the SBU, which is one of the agencies involved in carrying out deep-strike operations inside Russia.

The long-range strikes by Ukraine have hit Russian military facilities, oil refineries and e-commerce hubs, seeking to undermine the Kremlin's war effort and economy, as well as make ordinary citizens feel the consequences of the war.

WATCH | Concerns about Russian escalation in Ukraine: Intelligence warns Putin is preparing escalation in Ukraine | Duration 2:07 As Western intelligence warns about a planned escalation in Ukraine, Russian airstrikes have killed at least 12 people in Kyiv over six days. Meanwhile, Germany formally accused Russia of sabotage on a Ukrainian plane at the Leipzig airport.

Zelenskyy links Russian strikes to envoys' visit

The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometre front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.

In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia had carried out overnight strikes on the Kyiv and Boryspil international airports, and he linked the attack to the planned U.S. visit.

"Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine," he said.

"We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side."

Strikes kill 5 at Ukrainian industrial site

Russian attacks killed five people and wounded five more at an industrial facility in Ukraine's southern Dnipropetrovsk region, local military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha said. He described those killed as employees at the site.

"A locksmith, an electrician, a plumber and a machinist. People of peaceful professions. They were simply working their shift. They were doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives," he said.

A 62-year-old man was wounded and several homes and an apartment building were damaged in a separate attack on the region's Nikopol district, Hanzha said.

WATCH | Destruction in Kyiv: See the aftermath of Russian strikes on warehouses around Kyiv | Duration 0:34 One woman described the stress of repeated attacks on Ukraine's capital as living in a state of 'constant fear,' saying there's no sleep for people in the area around Kyiv. Russia's latest wave of strikes killed at least 17 people and damaged warehouses and logistics centres, Ukrainian officials say.

In a statement on Saturday, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants in the region, describing them as "major suppliers of metal products for Ukraine's military production."

A further two people were wounded in an overnight Russian attack on Ukraine’s Kyiv region, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration. In the Boryspil district, a fire sparked by a strike partially destroyed a nine-storey residential building.

Russian forces also repeatedly struck a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging retail premises and sparking fires, Ukraine's state emergency services said. A 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl were hurt.

Emergency crews responding to the incident were repeatedly forced to withdraw to safety because of the threat of further strikes, returning whenever conditions allowed, the emergency services said.

Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones overnight, Ukraine's air force said. The drones included Shahed-type aircraft — about half of them jet-powered — as well as Geran and decoy drones. Ukrainian air defences shot down or suppressed 128 drones, according to the air force.

Elsewhere, Ukrainian attacks wounded three people, including a 14-year-old girl, in Russia's border region of Belgorod, local officials said. In a statement, Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.

World.title: Conrad Black: Mark Carney puts it all on the line
World.content:
Article content

If the prime minister is not successfully contradicted, as I wrote here last week, it will be a challenging time but a great opportunity to strengthen the Canadian nationality. If we really have been provoked into a commercial war, it will be time for Canada to shed the somewhat hackneyed image of the upright, red-coated Mountie portrayed by Nelson Eddy in the famous 1954 film Rosemarie, (where someone purporting to be Québec Premier Maurice Duplessis makes a cameo appearance), and resort to further unsportsmanlike measures. We should make cooperative arrangements with some of the Commonwealth Caribbean countries and actively entice winter migrants from Florida and other temperate U.S. states. More piquant and an undoubted public service to the United States would be to provide heavy funding for authentic American legal aid charities and clog American courts and reduce the obscene 98 per cent conviction rates in American criminal courts, 95 per cent of those without a trial. The United States today has four percent of the world’s population and about 25 per cent of its incarcerated people; many Americans would thank us for helping to relieve “the sweet land of liberty” of this shame and hypocrisy. These are areas where it would be hard for the United States to retaliate-both sides can keep raising tariffs if they want but it is unlikely to achieve very much, although we could eventually manufacture much more for ourselves and take over the U.S. part of our automobile industry.
