World.title: Langdon Appears in Prague! Netflix Presents New Series Based on Dan Brown
World.content:
Netflix has begun filming its new series based on Dan Brown’s The Secret of Secrets, bringing Harvard symbologist Robert Langdon back to Prague.

The production officially started in the Czech capital this week, with Netflix releasing a first look at Morgan Spector as Langdon and Rebecca Hall as scientist Katherine Solomon. The series is currently untitled and does not yet have a release date.



Netflix has now added five more actors to the production. Mamoudou Athie will appear as Michael Harris, Ben Levi Ross as Alex Conan, Anamaria Marinca as Dr. Gessner, Richard Sammel as Karl Muller and Elena Saurel as Susan Housemore.

The series is being developed by Carlton Cuse, who co-created Lost and later worked on Jack Ryan, Locke & Key, Bates Motel and Five Days at Memorial. Cuse serves as co-creator, showrunner, writer and executive producer. Emma Forman is also an executive producer for Genre Arts, alongside Cuse and Brown.

Brown is involved in the project as a co-writer and executive producer.

The novel takes Langdon through several recognizable parts of Prague, including Charles Bridge and the Klementinum, as he searches for answers following Solomon’s disappearance. Netflix says the television adaptation will combine scientific ideas, historical mysteries and mystical elements.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dan Brown (@authordanbrown)

The Secret of Secrets was published in September 2025 and became the latest installment in Brown’s Robert Langdon series. The book was released simultaneously in multiple countries, including the Czech Republic, and Prague is closely tied to its plot.

The Czech Republic is expected to play a significant role in the new television production. Prague has previously served as a filming location for a wide range of international productions, making the city a familiar setting for foreign film and television crews.

The arrival of the Netflix series could also have an impact beyond the production industry. Czech travel companies and Argo, the publisher of Brown’s books in Czech, have previously pointed to the potential for two waves of tourism connected with the project: first from readers discovering the novel and later from viewers of the television adaptation.

World.title: Prague Planetarium to Become a Concert Venue Under the Stars
World.content:
The Prague Planetarium in Stromovka will host a new series of chamber concerts combining live music with projections of the universe from September 2026.

Called Niche Nites, the series will feature 10 concerts between September 2026 and June 2027. Each performance will be accompanied by visuals projected across the planetarium’s 22-metre-wide dome, with the imagery responding to the music in real time.



The programme will take place on the final weekend of each month. Rather than staging repeated performances, each musician or group will appear at the planetarium only once, giving every concert its own programme and visual design.

The series will open on September 25 with cellist Terezie Kovalová, whose work combines classical music with pop, alternative and electronic influences.

Other performers confirmed for the programme include guitarist and composer Michal Pavlíček, who will appear with singer Bára Basiková, pianist and composer Beata Hlavenková, and singer-songwriter Lenka Dusilová. Further names will be announced by the organisers in the coming months.

Producer and dramaturg Michala Komrsková said the project is intended to present established Czech musicians in a more intimate setting than the large concert halls where they usually perform.

The planetarium’s technology will play a central role. Its dome is fitted with an LED system containing millions of diodes, allowing large-scale visual sequences to accompany the performances. The imagery will be prepared specifically for each concert rather than using a single projection throughout the series.

More recently, the planetarium was used during this year’s Spectaculare festival, which combined music by composer Rafael Anton Irisarri with visual work by Czech artists Dalibor Cée and Alex J. Jindrák.

World.title: Gipsy Kings by André Reyes to Perform in Prague This November
World.content:
The legendary Gipsy Kings by André Reyes will perform in Prague this November, bringing their distinctive mix of flamenco guitar, rumba and Latin rhythms to Lucerna Great Hall on November 29, 2026.

Led by founding member André Reyes, the group will perform some of the songs that made the Gipsy Kings famous around the world, including “Bamboleo,” “Djobi Djoba” and “Volare,” alongside newer material.



The concert is being presented by Gotobeat and will begin at 7 p.m. Tickets are online here.

From southern France to the world

The Gipsy Kings’ story began with the Reyes family and their musical roots in the south of France. André Reyes was one of the founding members of the group, which went on to combine traditional flamenco with rumba, Latin rhythms and pop influences.

Their energetic guitar playing and Spanish-language songs helped turn rumba flamenca into an international sound. Tracks such as “Bamboleo” and “Djobi Djoba” became global hits, while their version of “Volare” introduced the group to an even wider audience.

Music associated with the Gipsy Kings has sold more than 60 million records worldwide, making the group one of the most successful international acts to emerge from the flamenco-rumba tradition.

Their music has also appeared in popular culture, including their version of “Hotel California,” which featured in The Big Lebowski.

A new generation of the Reyes family

André Reyes continues the tradition today with Gipsy Kings by André Reyes, performing alongside younger members of the Reyes family.

The current show combines the group’s best-known classics with newer music, including material connected to Nací Gitano, the band’s latest project. The group is also touring internationally in 2026 as part of its Viva el Arte Tour.

For audiences, the concert offers a mix of familiar songs and new material, with the performance centred on the fast-paced guitar playing, percussion and vocals that have defined the Gipsy Kings sound for decades.

Date: Sunday, November 29, 2026

Time: 7 p.m.

Venue: Lucerna Great Hall, Štěpánská 61, Prague 1

Promoter: Gotobeat

World.title: No Tickets Needed: Six Free Events in Prague This September
World.content:
Prague is offering a packed lineup of free events this September, from an air show and science festivals to a rare public viewing of the Czech Crown Jewels and a celebration marking a local brewery’s 15th anniversary.

Here are some of the best events taking place across the Czech capital this month.



Free Sightseeing at Historic Sites

The National Heritage Institute will open selected state-owned castles, chateaux, monasteries and other historic sites to visitors for free on Sunday, September 27.

Most of the properties managed by the institute will take part, although the tours and routes available will vary by location. Free admission will cover standard tours and selected additional routes. Capacity is limited, so visitors must book a free ticket online in advance for a specific time.

The Prague 10 Science Festival returns to Gutovka on Saturday, September 12.

From 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., 25 stations will offer visitors the chance to take part in chemistry experiments, explore LEGO robotics, play math games and learn more about nature, technology and the human body.

The program will also include workshops, a competition, a toy and plant swap, and a science show by Michael Londesborough. DJ SÂN will perform from 6 p.m., with the festival continuing until 8 p.m.

Dokola Festival

The Dokola Festival will take place on September 10 and 11, focusing on creative ways to reuse items rather than throw them away.

Visitors can repair broken electronics, make furniture from leftover wood, upcycle old clothes or try making kimchi. The program will also feature talks, a clothes swap, an upcycled fashion show and stand-up comedy. Most of the program is free, although some workshops charge a nominal fee.

Břevnov Brewery Celebrates 15 Years

Břevnov Brewery will mark its 15th anniversary on Saturday, September 12, with a day of beer, live music and family activities.

From 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., the meadow beside Břevnov Monastery will feature beer from the local brewery, along with special brews from other monastic breweries from across the Czech Republic.

Live performances by HUGO, Funk Corporation and JAKSI TAKSI will accompany guided brewery tours, barrel-throwing and timed barrel-rolling competitions, as well as activities for children.

There will also be a workshop for visitors interested in learning how to brew beer at home.

Czech Crown Jewels on Display

One of Prague’s most prestigious treasures will go on public display this month, when the Czech Crown Jewels are exhibited in Vladislav Hall at Prague Castle from September 19 to 28. Admission is free.

The exhibition marks 500 years since Ferdinand I of Habsburg became King of Bohemia. Alongside the famous St. Wenceslas Crown, the display will feature the royal sceptre and orb, a coronation robe dating from 1653 and historic keys once used by guardians of the Crown Archive.

Visitors will enter through the South Gardens and Bull Staircase from Hradčanské Square. Everyone must pass through a security check, and organizers advise against bringing prams.

Letňany Airport Day

After a two-year break, Letňany Airport will once again open its doors to the public on Saturday, September 5.

This year’s event will focus on legendary training aircraft and pilot training during World War II and the postwar years.

The program will feature historic aircraft from the Czech Republic and abroad, demonstrations by the Czech Army and police, model aircraft and a chance to see the airport’s current operations.

Events will take place in half-hour blocks between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m.

World.title: Fire During C-Section at Bulovka Hospital Leaves Woman Seriously Burned
World.content:
A woman suffered serious burns during an emergency cesarean section at Prague’s Bulovka Hospital on Aug. 25, hospital spokeswoman Eva Stolejda Libigerová said.

The cesarean was performed because of an acute obstetric complication. The woman’s condition is now stable and she does not require intensive care, the hospital said. She is recovering in a standard ward with her newborn.



The hospital is investigating the incident as part of its internal procedures for reviewing patient safety and the quality of medical care. It said it would take appropriate measures once the investigation is complete.

Fire broke out during surgery

According to information obtained about the incident, medical staff were attempting to control bleeding toward the end of the operation when a fire broke out involving a surgical device.

The device was reportedly being used shortly after the patient’s skin had been treated with a disinfectant.

The woman suffered second- and third-degree burns to her inner thighs, sides, lower abdomen and genital area, according to the available information.

Two days after the operation, she was transferred to the Burns Medicine Clinic at University Hospital Královské Vinohrady for treatment. She was later returned to Bulovka Hospital’s postpartum ward.

The circumstances surrounding the fire, including how it started and whether established safety procedures were followed, are being examined by the hospital.

Previous incident at Bulovka maternity clinic

The hospital’s gynecology and obstetrics clinic was also the site of a serious medical error in March 2024.

In that case, staff mistakenly identified two patients of Asian origin. A pregnant woman who had arrived for a routine examination was incorrectly subjected to a curettage procedure, resulting in the loss of her pregnancy.

An internal investigation concluded that two employees had violated established procedures and internal rules. The hospital subsequently ended its cooperation with one of them.

Police also investigated the case on suspicion of negligent bodily harm but ultimately brought no charges.

The woman later reached a settlement with the hospital worth 2.3 million Czech crowns. One of the employees involved lost her job.

World.title: Ambiente to Open Its 35th Prague Establishment This September
World.content:
Restaurant group Ambiente is preparing to open its 35th establishment, with a second location of its Pult beer concept set to launch in Prague’s Holešovice district in mid-September.

The new venue will be located on Tusarova Street and will follow the concept of Pult in Prague 1, which opened in the Celnice building in 2021.



While both locations will focus on Czech lager, the new Holešovice branch will introduce a different food concept and its own selection of beers.

The original venue serves beers from six breweries, with an emphasis on precise storage, serving and temperature control.

A different approach to food

Food will be one of the main differences between the two Pult locations.

The original Pult in Celnice focuses largely on smaller dishes and snacks. The Holešovice restaurant will instead offer a more substantial menu designed specifically to accompany beer.

The menu is expected to focus heavily on Czech beef, including several versions of steak tartare and steaks. Unlike many restaurants where the kitchen closes earlier than the bar, the new Pult plans to serve food until closing at 1 a.m.

The restaurant will have space for around 130 guests.

Another new destination for Holešovice

The opening comes as Holešovice continues to attract new restaurants, cafés and cultural venues. The area has become home to places including Vnitroblock, Mexická, Slice Slice Baby, Eatery, Ema, Typika, Osada and Polepšovna.

Ambiente itself has expanded its presence in Holešovice this year. At the Holešovice Market, the group has opened a second location of its Myšák confectionery and Naše maso butcher shop, as well as Skô, a Slovak-focused restaurant concept.

World.title: 7 Autumn Bike Trips to Take Around Czechia
World.content:
With cooler temperatures and autumn colours arriving, September and October are among the best months for cycling in Czechia.

The country’s extensive network of marked trails makes it easy to plan anything from a relaxed day trip to a multi-day adventure.

Here are seven routes worth considering this autumn.



1. Prague–Mělník–Litoměřice

One of the easiest options for Prague residents is to head north along the Elbe. The route passes through Mělník, known for its vineyards and historic centre, before continuing towards Litoměřice.

Along the way, cyclists can see Roudnice Chateau, Mount Říp and the historic fortress town of Terezín. Mělník is particularly appealing in September, when its wine season is in full swing.

2. Znojmo Wine Route

For a combination of cycling and wine, South Moravia is hard to beat in autumn. The 63-kilometre Znojmo Wine Route connects vineyards and villages around Znojmo and is suitable for cyclists of different abilities.

September and October are also the region’s main wine-harvest season, with numerous wine and burčák events taking place.

3. Mikulov and Pálava

The Mikulov Wine Trail offers another relaxed way to explore South Moravia. The route takes cyclists through vineyards and the countryside around Mikulov, with the Pálava hills providing one of the region’s most distinctive landscapes.

It is particularly attractive in September, when the annual Pálava Wine Festival takes place.

4. Singltrek pod Smrkem

If road cycling isn’t your thing, head towards Liberec. Singltrek pod Smrkem has more than 60 kilometres of purpose-built mountain-bike trails, ranging from easier sections for beginners to more challenging routes.

The surrounding Jizera Mountains also make it a good destination for a weekend trip.

5. Bečva Cycling Trail

The almost 160-kilometre Bečva Cycling Trail follows the Bečva River across Moravia. The route can be completed over several days and is largely downhill when ridden from the river’s source towards its confluence with the Morava.

Highlights along the way include Helfštýn Castle, the Zbrašovské Aragonite Caves and the open-air museum in Rožnov pod Radhoštěm.

6. Ploučnice Cycle Path

The nearly 100-kilometre Ploučnice Cycle Path runs from the river’s source near Ještěd to Děčín. It passes through Česká Lípa, the Ralsko area and the Kokořínsko-Máchův kraj landscape before reaching the Elbe.

7. Prague–Vienna Greenway

For a more ambitious trip, the Prague–Vienna Greenway stretches 368 kilometres between the two capitals. The route passes through historic towns, castles and monasteries, including Tábor, Znojmo and Mikulov.

It takes roughly a week to complete with stops, making it better suited to a longer autumn holiday than a weekend ride.

World.title: How to Buy TikTok Followers Without Risking Your Account
World.content:
Building a TikTok audience from zero can be frustrating. Even well-produced videos may struggle to attract attention when an account has only a handful of followers.

This slow beginning encourages some creators and businesses to purchase followers in the hope of making their profiles appear more established. Follower count can influence first impressions. When visitors discover a profile with an existing audience, they may be more willing to watch its videos, explore older content, or follow the account themselves. However, purchased followers cannot replace engaging videos or genuine interaction. Low-quality services may also deliver inactive accounts that disappear quickly or create an unnatural gap between follower numbers and actual engagement. Anyone considering this approach should understand how follower services operate, what they can realistically provide, and which warning signs suggest that a seller should be avoided.

Why Creators Purchase TikTok Followers

New accounts frequently face a credibility problem. Viewers have little information to judge whether the creator is worth following, so the visible follower count becomes one of several signals they use to make that decision. A larger audience can make a profile appear more established. This is particularly relevant for businesses, influencers, musicians, and other new TikTok creators trying to build authority in a competitive category. Some creators also purchase TikTok followers to reach eligibility thresholds for particular TikTok features. TikTok commonly applies age, location, and follower requirements to features such as LIVE, although the exact conditions may differ between markets and can change over time. The important distinction is that purchased followers mainly affect appearance. They may strengthen the profile’s initial social proof, but they do not guarantee greater reach, more sales, or stronger engagement.

What Purchased Followers Can and Cannot Do

Follower count is visible to anyone who visits a TikTok profile, which means it can shape the visitor’s first impression. A profile with several thousand followers may look more credible than an otherwise similar account with fewer than 100. TikTok’s recommendation system, however, evaluates much more than audience size. Signals such as watch time, completion rate, rewatches, shares, comments, saves, and viewer satisfaction are generally more important when determining whether a video should reach a wider audience. This creates a potential problem. If an account displays 30,000 followers but its videos consistently receive only a few dozen views, the imbalance may look unnatural to both TikTok and real visitors. Brands evaluating the creator for a partnership may notice the same discrepancy. Purchased followers should therefore be understood as a limited form of social proof. They cannot:

Make weak videos more entertaining

Guarantee placement on the For You feed

Produce meaningful comments or conversations

Create loyal customers

Replace a consistent publishing strategy

Automatically generate revenue

The greatest risk comes from purchasing followers that are obviously automated, inactive, or created only to inflate account statistics. These profiles add little value and may be removed during platform cleanups.

How to Evaluate a TikTok Follower Provider

The market contains everything from established social media marketing platforms to temporary websites selling automated accounts. A professional design alone does not prove that a service is dependable, so each provider should be evaluated carefully. Platforms such as SocialWick offer clearly defined TikTok packages and a conventional ordering process. Regardless of which company is being considered, several basic checks should be completed before placing an order.

Check the Website’s Security

A provider should use HTTPS encryption to protect information submitted through its website. This can usually be confirmed by checking for the padlock symbol beside the address in the browser. Secure payment methods are equally important. Credit cards and reputable payment processors normally offer better consumer protection than cryptocurrency transfers, gift cards, or other payment methods that are difficult to reverse.

Never Provide a TikTok Password

A follower delivery service generally needs only the public username or a link to the TikTok profile. It should not require the account password, email login, recovery code, or two-factor authentication details. Requests for private credentials are a serious warning sign. Sharing this information could allow an unknown company to access the account, change its settings, publish content, or lock out the owner.

Review the Delivery Time

Instant delivery may sound convenient, but an enormous follower increase within minutes can look unnatural. A newer account is unlikely to gain tens of thousands of followers suddenly without a viral video or another clear reason. More credible providers commonly offer gradual delivery. This spreads the order across several hours or days and makes it easier to monitor the quality of the accounts being added.

Understand the Package Quality

Follower packages are often divided into labels such as standard, high quality, active, real, or premium. These terms are not standardized, so they can mean different things on different websites. A higher-priced package may include accounts with profile photos, usernames, existing posts, or more complete activity histories. Cheaper options frequently consist of empty or inactive profiles. Before paying extra for a so-called premium tier, buyers should read the description carefully and determine what the seller is actually promising. Independent comparisons of TikTok follower providers and package quality may provide additional context, but customer reviews and seller claims should still be treated cautiously.

Look for Accessible Customer Support

A legitimate business should provide a clear way to request assistance. Live chat, email support, or a functioning contact form gives customers somewhere to report missing followers, delayed orders, or payment problems. Support availability does not automatically prove that a provider is trustworthy. However, a website with no contact information, unanswered messages, and no stated resolution process presents a much greater risk.

Warning Signs That Should Not Be Ignored

Very low pricing is one of the most common signs of poor-quality delivery. Maintaining accounts that look authentic requires more resources than operating a large collection of disposable bots. Consequently, offers promising thousands of “real and active” followers for a few cents are unlikely to match their description. Other warning signs include:

Requests for passwords or security codes

Guaranteed viral results

Promises of automatic monetization

No terms of service or privacy policy

Prices far below comparable providers

Only irreversible payment methods

Broken pages or copied website content

No delivery estimate

No refund or replacement policy

Large numbers of identical customer reviews

Claims of guaranteed engagement also deserve scrutiny. No external provider can honestly promise that purchased followers will watch every video or become paying customers.

Why a Refill Policy Matters

Follower losses can occur after an order is completed. TikTok may remove suspicious accounts, users may deactivate their profiles, or low-quality followers may simply disappear. A refill policy allows customers to request replacements when the follower count drops within a specified period. Depending on the provider, this protection may last for several days or a month. The conditions should be reviewed before checkout. Some companies refill only when the loss exceeds a minimum amount, while others exclude certain packages. Buyers should also check whether the replacement is automatic or must be requested manually. A refill guarantee cannot eliminate every risk, but it shows that the provider has at least acknowledged the possibility of follower loss and established a process for addressing it.

Avoid Unnatural Growth Patterns

Sudden, unexplained growth can draw unwanted attention. An account that gains 10,000 followers overnight without publishing anything new may appear suspicious, particularly if its views and interactions remain unchanged. Gradual delivery is generally less disruptive than receiving an entire order immediately. However, spreading out a purchase should not be treated as a method for bypassing TikTok’s enforcement systems. Buying followers may still conflict with platform rules, and no delivery method can guarantee that an account will avoid restrictions or removals.

Creators who choose to purchase followers should keep the order proportionate to the profile’s existing size. Adding a modest number to an active account is less conspicuous than transforming a nearly empty profile into a large one overnight. Content should also continue to be published consistently. A larger number beneath the profile image will have little effect if visitors arrive and find outdated, irrelevant, or poorly produced videos.

Keep Engagement and Follower Numbers Balanced

Follower count is only one part of a TikTok profile. Views, likes, comments, shares, and posting frequency provide a broader picture of its actual performance. If follower growth significantly outpaces every other metric, the account may lose credibility. A profile with 20,000 followers and almost no interaction may look less trustworthy than one with 2,000 followers and an active community. Maintaining a reasonable balance requires genuine content work. Creators should continue to:

Publish videos on a consistent schedule

Capture attention within the opening seconds

Respond to real comments

Participate in relevant trends

Use searchable captions and keywords

Test different formats and video lengths

Review analytics to identify strong topics

Collaborate with creators in the same niche

These activities provide TikTok with behavioral signals that purchased followers cannot produce.

Turning Social Proof Into Organic Growth

The most practical reason to purchase followers is to improve the profile’s initial presentation. If that stronger appearance encourages more people to explore the content, it may indirectly support organic growth. This effect depends entirely on what visitors find after opening the profile. A clear bio, recognizable niche, strong video covers, and a useful collection of content can convert curiosity into a genuine follow. An inflated number without quality content is unlikely to accomplish the same result. Creators should prepare their profiles before purchasing anything. A complete profile should include:

A memorable username

A clear profile image

A concise description of the account

Several high-quality published videos

Pinned content that represents the creator’s best work

A consistent subject or visual identity

An appropriate call to action

Purchased followers may bring the profile closer to the starting line, but the content determines whether real viewers remain interested.

Final Considerations Before Buying TikTok Followers

Buying TikTok followers can improve the visible size of an account, but it should never be confused with building a real community. The number may influence first impressions, yet it cannot reproduce the value of genuine viewers who regularly interact with the content. Anyone considering a purchase should choose a provider carefully, avoid sharing login information, use protected payment methods, read the refill conditions, and remain skeptical of unrealistic guarantees. It is also important to recognize that follower purchases may violate TikTok’s rules and could lead to removals or other account consequences. The strongest TikTok profiles combine credibility with content that earns attention. Purchased followers may change how a profile looks, but sustainable growth still depends on originality, consistency, audience understanding, and videos that people genuinely want to watch.

World.title: Hungary weather: Cold front this weekend, then heat, heavy rain and sharp cooling next week
World.content:
Hungary’s weather is about to change several times within just over a week. A cold front crossing the country on Saturday will bring a temporary drop in temperatures for Sunday, before summer heat quickly returns. From the middle of next week, however, a much more significant change could arrive, bringing substantial rainfall and eventually genuinely autumnal temperatures.

A cold front is moving across Hungary from the north and north-west on Saturday, 5 September. Despite increasing cloud cover, significant widespread rainfall is not expected, although scattered showers and thunderstorms may develop.

HungaroMet has warned of possible thunderstorms in several counties, particularly in the north-east and south, with storms also possible in the south-west later in the day. Wind gusts of 60–70 km/h, locally exceeding 70 km/h, may accompany stronger storms, and isolated hail cannot be ruled out. Temperatures will nevertheless remain summery, with afternoon highs between 25 and 34°C.

Sunday: Cooler, sunny and mostly dry

The cold front will be more noticeable on Sunday, 6 September, when temperatures fall by several degrees.

Mostly clear or lightly cloudy weather is expected across Hungary, with no significant precipitation. More cumulus clouds may develop in the north-east, while north-westerly and northerly winds could occasionally strengthen.

Morning temperatures will generally range between 10 and 18°C, although sheltered areas could fall slightly below 10°C. Afternoon highs are forecast between 24 and 29°C.

The cooler weather will not last long, however. Temperatures will begin rising again almost immediately as Hungary heads into another short spell of late-summer heat.

Hungary weather next week: Day-by-day forecast

Monday, 7 September: Summer returns

Temperatures will begin climbing again on Monday, with mostly dry and warm conditions expected. Forecasts currently indicate afternoon highs of roughly 27–32°C, meaning the weekend’s brief cooling will already be fading.

Tuesday, 8 September: Temperatures above 30°C again

Tuesday could be one of the warmest days of the week. Maximum temperatures are expected to reach around 28–33°C, bringing summer-like heat back to much of Hungary.

For anyone hoping that Saturday’s cold front marked the beginning of autumn, the answer will therefore be a clear no – at least temporarily.

If you missed it: another popular Hungarian lake dries out, Bölömbika lookout shows critical conditions

Wednesday, 9 September: A major change begins

The first wave of a more substantial weather change is currently forecast to arrive from Wednesday, when another cold front reaches Hungary.

One of its most striking effects could be a large temperature difference between different parts of the country. Western Hungary may already experience much cooler conditions while the east remains hot, potentially creating a 10–15°C difference between the two sides of the country.

Unlike Saturday’s front, this system is also expected to bring more significant rainfall.

Thursday, 10 September: Cold front spreads across Hungary

The effects of the front are expected to become much more widespread by Thursday.

Temperatures should fall across larger parts of the country, while rain could affect numerous regions. Current forecasts suggest this will be the point when the first major cooling phase becomes established.

The exact location and amount of precipitation remain uncertain several days in advance, so the forecast may still change considerably.

Friday, 11 September: Sharp cooling possible in western Hungary

By Friday, some western parts of Hungary could experience a dramatic change compared with the heat seen earlier in the week.

Current projections suggest temperatures in some western areas may reach only around 15°C – potentially almost 20 degrees below Tuesday’s highest values.

Eastern parts of the country may remain somewhat warmer, but the overall trend will be firmly towards cooler weather.

Catch up on the week’s biggest stories from Hungary — politics, economy, business and diplomacy, all in one place. Subscribe here: Substack

Saturday, 12 September: Autumn weather and heavier rain

A second phase of the weather change could begin around Saturday.

Forecasts currently indicate that a Mediterranean cyclone may start influencing Hungary, bringing widespread and potentially substantial rainfall. From this point, autumnal temperatures are expected across the country rather than only in western regions.

Sunday, 13 September: Widespread rain could continue

Sunday could remain cool and wet as the Mediterranean system affects Hungary.

Between 12 and 15 September, current projections suggest that repeated rainfall could bring approximately 30–70 millimetres of precipitation across the country, with larger amounts possible in western Hungary.

Such rainfall would be particularly notable after the prolonged dry conditions of recent months.

Summer first, then a real taste of autumn

The coming days could therefore bring an unusually sharp weather contrast to Hungary: temperatures above 30°C on Tuesday, the arrival of a cold front from Wednesday, highs potentially around 15°C in parts of the west by Friday, followed by widespread autumnal weather and significant rainfall over the weekend.

Meteorologists stress that forecasts for the second half of next week still carry considerable uncertainty, particularly regarding the timing and strength of the expected Mediterranean cyclone and the amount of rainfall it may bring. Nevertheless, current models increasingly point towards a much more substantial change than the brief cold front crossing Hungary this Saturday.

World.title: Water-law permit in Hungary: 3 hidden traps only insiders discover
World.content:
My previous article examined how a water-law permit can affect property value: how a source with valid permits differs from one without them, and why official recognition as natural mineral water is an important condition for market access. This article adopts a different register. It is not about principles, but about reality. I have been involved in the permitting processes for two very different water-related property projects: a mineral-water well in the Börzsöny hills and a thermal well on the Great Hungarian Plain. Both lead to the same conclusion. The regulatory maze is not only slow and costly; it is also difficult to predict. The most serious obstacles often emerge not at the beginning, but years into the process.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

Parallel jurisdictions: when several bodies are involved

A water-related property development in Hungary will usually bring the investor into contact with several authorities and specialist bodies. Regional water-management and water-protection authority functions are exercised by the county government offices designated in Government Decree 223/2014 (IX. 4.). The National Directorate General for Water Management (OVF) and the regional water directorates are water-administration bodies. A regional directorate may, among other things, issue asset-management consent and a water-infrastructure identification statement during the procedure, but it is not the permitting authority.

The mining authority acts in relation to the exploration, extraction and use of geothermal energy in the cases specified by the Mining Act; the exceptions applicable to certain forms of thermal-water extraction must be examined separately. Where a Natura 2000 site is affected, nature-conservation rules and authorities may become relevant; agricultural-land-protection, building and land-registry rules and bodies may also play a role. The municipality defines the framework for land use through its local building regulations (HÉSZ) and other local decrees.

This fragmentation is not accidental. The regulatory framework has accumulated from legislation enacted at different times for different purposes. In a single project, the relevant procedures may proceed in parallel, but at independent speeds. A decision in one procedure does not automatically create a right in another. The investor is therefore not walking down one corridor, but navigating several intersecting systems at the same time.

The Natura 2000 collision: consequences that are not apparent at the outset

In the Great Plain thermal-well case, the Natura 2000 designation, specifically the HUBN10004 Heves Plain Special Protection Area, was not a late surprise. According to the case files available to me, the Natura 2000 legal designation was already recorded in the land register when the well was drilled in 2007. What became clear only during the permitting process was how far its consequences could extend.

Under Section 10 of Government Decree 275/2004 (X. 8.), the first question is whether a plan or development may affect the Natura 2000 site; a detailed impact assessment is required if the possibility of a significant effect cannot be ruled out. In this case, the assessment focused primarily on the potential effects on the species for which the site was designated, including the red-backed shrike. The authority imposed mitigation conditions, including the retention of woodland buffers and existing shrub belts and the exclusion of certain lower-lying areas from development. The process took years, while the well remained unused.

If you missed it – Looking beyond price per square metre: how Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest’s new-build home markets differ

The seven hectares discovered only years later

The most striking experience, however, was unrelated to Natura 2000 and arose through a separate regulatory channel. The local building regulations in force designate part of the Great Plain project’s development site, nearly seven hectares, as green space, specifically a public park. The owner did not learn this through the service of an authority decision. It emerged during a review of documents in an ongoing procedure, years after the property had been acquired: under the HÉSZ, that part of the site could not be built on or developed for the intended purpose because the municipal decree classified it as a public park.

This situation, which is not unique, illustrates a systemic feature of Hungary’s rural property market. The effect of a water-law permit on property value does not depend solely on the water-law procedure. Land-use classification, local building regulations, zoning and the land register are partly independent systems.

A property’s title sheet does not necessarily disclose every restriction contained in the HÉSZ. The municipal decree that determines what may be built on a plot is not automatically reproduced in the land register. A buyer who reviews only the title sheet, without separately checking the current local building regulations, may acquire property whose development potential is fundamentally constrained by a municipal decree of which the buyer was unaware.

What this means for the long-term viability of a water-law permit

The operating water-law permit for the Great Plain well expired in 2018. The proposed use, which required a larger water allocation, called for updated water-use plans and a fresh examination of the permitting conditions; the absence of the necessary asset-management consent delayed the procedure.

While the permit reserving 320,000 cubic metres per year remained in force, the absence of actual abstraction did not automatically eliminate liability for the water resource charge (vízkészletjárulék). Under Section 15/B(3) of the Water Management Act, where actual use is lower, the general calculation base is 80 per cent of the authorised quantity, which in this case would be 256,000 cubic metres.

The amount payable cannot, however, be determined from that volume alone. The formula under KHVM Decree 43/1999 (XII. 26.) also takes account of the type of water, the purpose of use, metering, the status of the water body and any applicable exemptions. Under certain combinations of parameters, the annual amount may exceed HUF 10 million. Any liability arising after the permit expired must be assessed separately by reference to the relevant period and the actual legal position.

The Börzsöny lesson: the value of patience and preparation

The Börzsöny mineral-water project followed a different course. There, the process from hydrodynamic modelling to official recognition as natural mineral water advanced with careful preparation. The interdependence of the procedures was planned in advance, and where one decision was a prerequisite for the next, the project waited for that decision to become final. Questions concerning the water-law regime, the HÉSZ, zoning and neighbouring properties were addressed before development began. This may extend the preparation phase, but it substantially reduces the risk of surprises later. Whether procedures should run in parallel or sequentially must be decided separately for each project on the basis of a tailored timetable.

Also interesting – From the offer to the land registry extract: how a safe property purchase works in Hungary

What every investor needs to understand

Together, the two cases offer three lessons.

Map the parallel constraints before purchase. The value created by a water-law permit can be realised only if Natura 2000 implications, HÉSZ zoning, agricultural-land-protection obligations and any green-space or public-park designation are known in advance. A permit is not perpetual. Its validity period, conditions and scope for amendment must be examined separately. A buyer acquiring property associated with an existing permit should have an expert verify whether the permit remains valid, who holds it, the conditions for changing the permit holder or owner, whether it can be amended, and whether its validity can be extended. The HÉSZ and the title sheet are separate sources. They must be checked independently of one another.

In closing

Hungary’s water resources, from mineral-water wells in the Börzsöny hills and thermal sources on the Great Plain to the use of geothermal energy, embody genuine and still underexploited value. That value does not realise itself. Regulatory procedures, interlocking specialist rules and long lead times stand between the resource and the investor. The outcome, a legally final permit, a recognised source and a properly protected water base, may constitute an asset that the market can rarely replicate. That is its cost, and that is its value.

Legislation cited

Emese Széll, an expert in Hungary’s premium property market. premiumingatlanok.com

This article provides general market and legal information only and does not constitute individual legal, water-law, mining, nature-conservation or investment advice. The project-specific data and authority history described above should be verified against the original permits, decisions, registers and expert documentation. The English titles of Hungarian legislation are descriptive translations; the Hungarian-language legal text is authoritative. Legislation checked as at 3 September 2026.

World.title: Where centuries-old Hungarian folk traditions are still alive – PHOTOS
World.content:
Hungarian folk traditions are still very much part of community life in the small village of Kiscsősz, in western Hungary. A new Anadolu photo series captures residents in traditional dress as they perform folk dances, play music and preserve customs that have been passed down through generations.

The photographs were taken in Kiscsősz, Veszprém County, on 13 August. They show villagers wearing authentic traditional costumes and taking part in folk dances accompanied by traditional music.

According to Anadolu, the local community actively preserves centuries-old Hungarian rural traditions, folklore and cultural heritage. The images also highlight indigenous musical instruments and community gatherings designed to ensure that these customs are passed on to younger generations.

Hungarian folk traditions remain part of village life

What makes Kiscsősz particularly striking is that these traditions are presented not simply as historical exhibits, but as part of a living community.

Folk dance and traditional music have long played an important role in Hungarian cultural identity, with regional variations in costumes, choreography and musical styles reflecting the country’s diverse rural heritage.

In Kiscsősz, that heritage remains visible through community events and performances where different generations take part together. Anadolu’s photographs show both the elaborate detail of traditional clothing and the social side of folk culture, with musicians, dancers and residents gathering in an intimate village setting.

The emphasis on transmitting traditions to younger people is particularly important, as many rural customs across Europe face the challenge of surviving demographic change and increasingly urban lifestyles.

A different side of Hungary

For international visitors, Kiscsősz offers a glimpse of Hungary far removed from Budapest’s grand architecture, ruin bars and thermal baths.

Small communities such as this one preserve another layer of the country’s identity: one shaped by village life, traditional music, colourful costumes and customs that have survived for generations.

The Anadolu gallery captures that atmosphere particularly well. Rather than presenting Hungarian folk traditions as something frozen in the past, the photographs show a culture that continues to be practised, shared and celebrated today.

World.title: Cost of living in Hungary: Inflation has fallen – so why do people still feel poorer?
World.content:
The cost of living in Hungary remains a major source of anxiety even as inflation has fallen sharply and real wages are rising again. A new PwC Hungary survey suggests that many households still feel financially stretched, with a sizeable share struggling to build savings, cover unexpected setbacks or even make their salary last until the next payday.

The findings highlight a gap between Hungary’s improving headline economic indicators and the way many people perceive their own financial situation.

According to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH), consumer prices were just 1.2 percent higher in July 2026 than a year earlier, while prices actually fell by 0.1 percent compared with June. Food prices were down 1.1 percent year on year, although services were still 4.7 percent more expensive.

Wages have also been gaining purchasing power. Real earnings rose by 7.6 percent year on year in June, according to the latest KSH figures.

Yet the latest survey from PwC Hungary shows that the improvement in the macroeconomic picture has not necessarily translated into a feeling of financial security.

Cost of living in Hungary continues to squeeze households

According to PwC Hungary’s Financial Wellness survey, 42 percent of respondents said their salary was generally failing to keep pace with rising living costs, while only 4 percent believed their pay was fully keeping up.

The survey also suggests that a substantial proportion of households have little room for a serious financial shock.

Thirty percent of respondents said their household would not be able to cover basic expenses if its main earner were unable to work for six months. Another 20 percent were unsure how long their existing reserves would last.

Day-to-day finances are also proving difficult for some. Fourteen percent said they often or always run out of money between paydays, while another one in five said this happens from time to time.

PwC found that 45 percent of respondents experienced at least a moderate level of stress when managing their finances, while 16 percent described themselves as particularly stressed. For 35 percent, financial anxiety had increased during the previous year.

The numbers are particularly notable because falling inflation does not mean that prices have returned to where they were several years ago. It simply means they are now increasing much more slowly. Households may therefore still be adjusting to the cumulative price rises of previous years even as current inflation becomes less severe.

If you missed it – Cost of living in Hungary in 2026: rent, groceries, transport and monthly budgets

Long-term savings are another weak point

Financial pressure is also affecting preparations for the future.

Among respondents who had not yet retired, 36 percent said they were not saving anything specifically for retirement. A further 13 percent said they intended to start but had not yet done so.

Concerns about the future extend beyond retirement savings. Around 32 percent of those surveyed said they believed their generation was financially worse off than previous generations had been at the same age. A similar proportion expected the next generation’s financial prospects to be no better.

This suggests that the debate around the cost of living in Hungary is increasingly about more than immediate inflation. Financial resilience, housing plans, retirement and the ability to build wealth are becoming part of the same conversation.

Photo: Daily News Hungary

Financial pressure is spilling into the workplace

PwC’s research also found signs that money worries are affecting working life.

Some 42 percent of employees surveyed were at least somewhat concerned about the future security of their jobs. Meanwhile, 45 percent felt that their employer did little or nothing to support their financial wellbeing.

The consequences can extend beyond personal budgeting. Respondents reported that financial stress can affect sleep, health, self-esteem, relationships and performance at work.

Why the figures matter despite falling inflation

For foreign observers, the survey offers an important qualification to Hungary’s improving inflation and wage statistics.

Lower inflation and rising real wages are positive developments, but they do not immediately undo several years of higher prices or rebuild household savings. The PwC findings suggest that many Hungarians remain focused on financial security rather than feeling the full benefit of the improving headline numbers.

The Hungarian survey was carried out in July 2026 in two waves among more than 3,200 adult Hungarian internet users who shop online, using a nationally representative sample for that group. The results should therefore be interpreted within that methodological scope rather than as a survey of every Hungarian household.

For now, the picture is mixed: inflation has eased substantially and purchasing power is recovering, but for a significant share of those surveyed, financial confidence appears to be recovering much more slowly.

World.title: Could Hungary back EU countries’ Rwanda plan?
World.content:
A plan to send migrants with no legal right to remain in the European Union to “return hubs” outside the bloc is rapidly moving from theory towards policy. Rwanda is emerging as a possible destination, raising a particularly interesting question for Hungary: would Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s new government support such a solution to Europe’s migration crisis? Budapest has not yet endorsed the Rwanda proposal, but its recent statements suggest it could be receptive to the idea.

Rwanda returns move to the centre of Europe’s migration crisis

Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands have been working together on the creation of return hubs outside the European Union. Representatives of the five countries recently travelled to Rwanda, where negotiations are under way over the possibility of hosting people ordered to leave EU territory.

According to Euractiv, one location being discussed is the Gashora Transit Centre, around 60 kilometres from Kigali. The facility has previously housed migrants evacuated from Libya while longer-term solutions were arranged. Rwanda has confirmed that preliminary negotiations with European governments are taking place.

The initiative has progressed quickly. The five governments have now set a target of establishing their first return-hub system by 2027, while Rwanda and Uganda are among the potential partner countries being considered. Denmark has said it hopes transfers could begin by the end of next year.

The proposal has become possible because EU migration policy itself is changing. The European Parliament approved new return rules in June allowing member states to conclude agreements with non-EU countries and transfer people who have received a return decision to facilities there. Unaccompanied minors are excluded, while partner states would have to respect international human rights standards and the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits sending people somewhere they face persecution or serious harm.

Importantly, this is not identical to the controversial British Rwanda scheme abandoned in 2024. The emerging EU model is primarily aimed at people who have already been found to have no legal right to remain in the EU, rather than simply moving asylum processing abroad.

Even so, considerable legal and humanitarian questions remain. The UN Refugee Agency has argued that return hubs should be used only where a person has undergone a full and fair asylum procedure and direct return to their country of origin is not possible within a reasonable period. The Council of Europe has also called for strict independent monitoring and legally enforceable human-rights guarantees.

If you missed it yeasterday: Hungary extends ‘mass migration crisis’ until end of 2026, PM Magyar vows no easing of border rules

Britain already tried Rwanda – and it failed. But Europe’s new plan is different

The obvious question is whether Europe is now repeating an experiment that has already failed.

Britain agreed its controversial Rwanda scheme in 2022, planning to relocate certain people who had arrived irregularly in the UK to Rwanda, where their asylum claims would be processed. In practice, however, the policy never became operational on the scale intended.

In November 2023, the UK Supreme Court ruled that the scheme was unlawful in its existing form because of the risk that asylum seekers sent to Rwanda could ultimately be returned to countries where they faced persecution or inhumane treatment. The Conservative government subsequently negotiated a new treaty with Kigali and passed legislation declaring Rwanda a safe country, but the planned deportation flights still did not take place before the government changed.

According to the British Home Office, during more than two years of the programme only four people travelled to Rwanda voluntarily, while no asylum seekers were forcibly relocated under the scheme. The Labour government discontinued the policy after taking office in July 2024.

The emerging European proposal, however, is different in one crucial respect. The British scheme was designed largely for people whose asylum applications would not be considered in the UK and would instead be processed in Rwanda. The EU return-hub concept is primarily intended for people who have already received a return decision and therefore no longer have a legal right to remain in the European Union.

That distinction could make the European model easier to defend politically and legally. Rather than outsourcing the asylum procedure itself, return hubs would be intended as destinations for people whom EU governments have already decided must leave – particularly in cases where returning them directly to their country of origin proves difficult.

The British experience nevertheless provides a warning. Any European system involving Rwanda or another third country is likely to face intense scrutiny over human rights safeguards, legal responsibility and the risk of unlawful onward deportations.

Péter Magyar’s government has kept Hungary’s tough migration policy

The question for Hungary is particularly significant because the change of government in May did not bring the major reversal in migration policy that some foreign observers might have expected.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar said this week that, while individual measures introduced by Viktor Orbán’s previous government could be debated, Hungary had been fundamentally right in its assessment of migration. He specifically backed both the southern border fence and the country’s strict migration rules.

Magyar also said there could be no relaxation of Hungarian asylum regulations and that his government wanted to ensure that not “one more” irregular migrant entered the country. At the same time, he is seeking an agreement with Brussels rather than another prolonged confrontation over EU migration rules.

That stance is important for understanding how Budapest might approach the latest migration crisis proposal.

Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai has repeatedly said since the new government took office that Hungary’s position on irregular migration remains unchanged. In July, his ministry also revealed that Hungary was closely monitoring the practical experience of Italy’s controversial agreement with Albania – another attempt to handle aspects of migration outside normal EU territory.

Then, following renewed migration pressure at the EU’s external border in August, the Hungarian government explicitly called for “innovative policy tools” going beyond existing solutions, while stressing stronger external border protection and action against abuses of the asylum system.

Hungary has also discussed the support of returns directly with Austria, one of the five countries now pushing the return-hub initiative.

Migrant crisis in the EU. Photo: depositphotos.com

What’s next: Hungary joins 21 EU leaders in criticism of Spain’s migration response after mass arrivals

Could Hungary support the Rwanda return hubs?

Taken together, those positions provide a credible basis for believing that the Magyar government could support return hubs in principle.

Such a policy fits several elements of Budapest’s current approach: preventing irregular entry, maintaining strict asylum rules, strengthening the EU’s external borders and making it easier to remove people who have no right to stay.

It could also be politically easier for Magyar to support than parts of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact involving solidarity between member states. Sending people with final return decisions outside the EU is fundamentally different from requiring Hungary to receive asylum seekers transferred from another member state – something Budapest has strongly resisted.

However, there is an important distinction between saying the Hungarian government would probably find the concept attractive and saying it supports Rwanda specifically. Hungary is not currently part of the five-country initiative, and neither Magyar nor Pósfai has publicly committed Budapest to the Rwanda negotiations.

What happens next?

The next few months should provide a clearer answer. The five participating governments are expected to continue negotiations with potential host countries, with another meeting planned in Munich in September and concrete agreements targeted before the end of 2026.

For Hungary, much will depend on the final legal and financial structure. If return hubs remain voluntary, comply with EU and international law and do not require Hungary to accept migrants from other member states, the proposal would sit comfortably with much of the migration policy the Magyar government has outlined so far.

That makes Hungarian support a plausible scenario – but not yet a government position. The Rwanda debate may therefore become one of the first major tests of how much Hungary’s approach to Europe’s migration crisis has really changed under Péter Magyar: less confrontational towards Brussels, perhaps, but not necessarily more permissive on migration.

World.title: Ryanair and Wizz Air sound the alarm – what could happen to air fares?
World.content:
Air fares could become significantly more expensive if oil and jet fuel prices remain elevated, with both Ryanair and Wizz Air warning that sustained cost pressure could eventually be passed on to passengers. The warnings come as airlines around the world grapple with higher fuel bills, capacity cuts and increasingly difficult decisions over ticket prices.

The pressure is already visible well beyond Europe. Southeast Asian budget airlines including AirAsia, Scoot and Cebu Pacific have struggled to recover soaring fuel costs through higher fares, with several reporting losses. AirAsia has even considered cutting seat capacity by as much as 25 percent as part of efforts to contain costs.

China’s three largest state-owned airlines – Air China, China Eastern and China Southern – meanwhile reported combined net losses of USD 1.22 billion for the first half of 2026, after fuel expenses jumped by roughly 35–38 percent.

Passengers in the United States are also already paying considerably more. US airline fares were 25.5 percent higher in July than a year earlier, while United Airlines chief executive Scott Kirby said he expects prices to continue rising gradually in the first half of 2027.

The situation highlights one of aviation’s biggest vulnerabilities: fuel is among an airline’s largest operating expenses, and sharp increases cannot be absorbed indefinitely. Many carriers use fuel hedging – contracts that lock in prices in advance – to soften short-term shocks, but those protections eventually expire.

Ryanair warns European air fares could rise materially

Ryanair has issued one of the clearest warnings yet about what prolonged high oil prices could mean for European passengers.

According to The Guardian, Europe’s largest low-cost airline has reduced its passenger target for the financial year ending 31 March 2027 from 216 million to 214 million, partly to reduce its exposure to expensive unhedged fuel during the typically loss-making winter season.

The carrier expects winter passenger numbers between November and March to remain broadly unchanged from a year earlier.

Ryanair said that if high oil prices continue into summer 2027, short-haul air fares in Europe could increase “materially”. The airline also warned that some competitors with less extensive fuel hedging could struggle to maintain their current capacity – and in extreme cases might not survive the winter.

Jet fuel was trading at around USD 140 a barrel when Ryanair issued its warning. The airline itself is relatively well protected, having hedged around 80 percent of its fuel requirements through March 2027 at approximately USD 67 a barrel.

Cutting winter capacity is expected to reduce Ryanair’s seasonal losses by between EUR 70 million and EUR 100 million.

If you missed it – Budget flights are getting expensive: How Ryanair and Wizz Air make money from hidden extras

Wizz Air: capacity cuts may come before higher ticket prices

Hungary-linked low-cost carrier Wizz Air has now also acknowledged that persistently high fuel prices could ultimately result in more expensive tickets.

In a statement provided to 24.hu, Wizz Air said sustained high oil and jet fuel prices would inevitably put pressure on the European aviation sector, particularly as airlines’ existing fuel hedges gradually expire.

However, the company stressed that it was still too early to quantify the possible impact on air fares in 2027.

Wizz Air expects airlines to respond first by reducing capacity. Pricing measures could follow later, depending on how supply and demand develop.

The airline said a sustained Brent crude price of USD 90–100 a barrel or above would create additional pressure on the industry. Over time, that could push market fares higher if airlines cut capacity or attempt to pass part of their additional costs on to passengers.

For Wizz Air itself, the immediate impact is partly cushioned by its hedging portfolio and relatively fuel-efficient fleet. Even so, the company acknowledged that persistently high prices would eventually affect the unhedged portion of its fuel costs and therefore profitability.

The airline did not rule out ticket increases, saying that prolonged higher costs would ultimately also be reflected in fares.

Why it matters

For passengers, the most important point is that higher oil prices do not automatically translate into more expensive tickets overnight. Fuel hedging can delay the impact, while fierce competition may prevent airlines from immediately passing costs on to customers.

But the Ryanair and Wizz Air statements point to another mechanism that could ultimately prove just as important: capacity.

If airlines respond to high fuel costs by operating fewer flights, withdrawing aircraft or abandoning less profitable routes, the number of available seats falls. If passenger demand remains strong at the same time, fares can rise even without airlines directly adding a fuel surcharge.

That means travellers in Hungary and across Europe could eventually face a combination of fewer flight options and higher air fares if the current fuel-price environment persists into 2027.

For now, both Ryanair and Wizz Air retain significant protection through hedging. The real test will come as those contracts expire – and airlines are forced to buy a larger share of their fuel at prevailing market prices.

World.title: Putin adviser claims Ukraine could lose Transcarpathia, calls Western Ukraine a ‘den of evil’
World.content:
A senior adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin has made an interesting claim about the future of Ukraine’s western territories, including Zakarpattia, saying Ukraine will eventually lose regions that once belonged to Hungary, Poland and Romania.

Anton Kobyakov, Putin’s adviser and executive secretary of the organising committee of the Eastern Economic Forum, made the comments while speaking to journalists about the results of the forum.

His remarks echo increasingly frequent statements from senior Russian officials about the possible future of Ukraine’s western regions — including territory that was historically part of the Kingdom of Hungary. According to Kobyakov, these areas are now a “den of evil” where Ukrainian nationalism is being fostered.

‘Ukraine will eventually lose its western territories’

Kobyakov referred to comments previously made by Putin, who has argued that Ukraine will sooner or later lose its western territories.

“Ukraine will sooner or later lose its western lands that belonged to Poland, Romania and Hungary before the Second World War,” Kobyakov said, referring to the Russian president’s position.

He described these territories as the place where Ukrainian nationalism is allegedly being cultivated. Kobyakov went on to draw a highly controversial parallel between modern Ukraine and fascism, claiming that Russia and Ukraine had once fought together against Nazi Germany.

“We fought against the fascists together. How did it happen that they are now at the head of the ‘Ukrainian Reich’?” he said. He further claimed that Ukraine had become “the vanguard of European fascism”.

If you missed it: Ukraine makes major gesture towards Hungary, officially condemning Soviet atrocities against Transcarpathian Hungarians

Putin has previously mentioned Hungary and Zakarpattia

Kobyakov is not the first senior Russian figure to raise the possibility of Ukraine losing its western territories. Putin himself spoke about the issue at a meeting with Russian naval personnel in St Petersburg earlier this year. He said he believed Ukraine would eventually lose territories that had previously belonged to Poland, Hungary and Romania.

Putin suggested that such a development could occur years or even decades from now, saying that “historically, everything will fall into place”. He also claimed that Russia had been the only guarantor of Ukraine’s territorial integrity, a statement made against the backdrop of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev has likewise repeatedly referred to the possible partition of Ukraine. On one occasion, he published a fictional map depicting a divided Ukraine in which neighbouring countries, including Hungary, would receive parts of the country’s western territories.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Kobyakov also made a claim about Kyiv

Kobyakov concluded his latest remarks with another statement reflecting the Kremlin’s historical narrative, saying that Kyiv “was and will remain the mother of Russian cities”.

The comments come as Russia continues its full-scale war against Ukraine, while questions surrounding the future of territories occupied or claimed by Russia remain at the centre of international negotiations and diplomatic efforts.

World.title: Toxic solvent found in soil at Hungarian battery plant – local wells ordered to be tested
World.content:
A potentially hazardous solvent has been detected in soil at the SK On battery plant in Iváncsa, raising concerns about possible contamination of groundwater in the area.

The company informed the local council that its own monitoring tests had detected NMP (N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone) in a monitoring well located inside the factory site. NMP is a solvent used in industrial processes and is classified as hazardous to human health, including because of its potential to harm unborn children.

The contamination was reportedly discovered on 28 August, according to the company. Authorities were notified immediately, and investigations have since begun. SK On told the municipality that the source of the contamination had been eliminated and that processes capable of causing further pollution had been suspended.

Local authorities order independent water testing

According to Hungarian News Agency (MTI), Iváncsa Mayor Tibor Molnár ordered the immediate testing of water from one drilled or dug well on every street in the village. The samples will be collected and analysed by an independent, accredited laboratory, with the full cost covered by the municipality.

Gabriella Sáfár, the municipality’s clerk, said the tests would be repeated within a month regardless of the results of the initial sampling. “The speed of action and the health of local residents are more important than money,” she said.

The municipality has also requested information from the environmental authorities about the ongoing investigation. Importantly, officials stressed that the village’s main drinking water supply is not affected by the incident. Iváncsa’s piped drinking water is supplied from Ercsi through a pipeline.

If you missed it: New battery industry plant could be coming to Debrecen despite earlier government denial

Authorities investigating whether contamination has spread

Tisza Party MP Ervin Nagy, who represents the area, said he had consulted the relevant authorities following the discovery. According to Nagy, an immediate investigation was launched and the operator stopped wastewater discharges linked to the affected technological processes. A second-degree water management emergency was also declared on 2 September following a recommendation from the water authority.

Accredited water samples have already been taken, although the results are not yet available. Nagy said the authorities were also preparing a more extensive investigation, including exploratory drilling and further groundwater testing, while a remediation procedure was being initiated.

For now, it therefore remains unclear whether the contamination has spread beyond the factory’s internal monitoring area or affected groundwater outside the site.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

SK On says it has suspended the relevant equipment

SK On Hungary confirmed the contamination in a statement sent to MTI. The company said it had immediately taken the necessary precautionary measures in accordance with its internal procedures, including suspending the operation of the relevant equipment.

It added that it was fully cooperating with the authorities’ investigation and any further measures that may be required.

“We sincerely regret if this matter has caused concern among local residents and the community, as well as the relevant authorities and our employees,” the company said. SK On stressed that safety and environmental protection remain its top priorities.

Iváncsa plant previously fined HUF 100 million

The latest incident comes only weeks after the Iváncsa battery plant was fined HUF 100 million following an investigation into workplace safety.

According to previously reported findings, authorities concluded that the health and physical safety of 65 workers had been seriously and directly endangered. Among the concerns was the inadequate provision of protective equipment when handling hazardous mixtures.

Workers reportedly needed P3-level respiratory protection and gloves suitable for protection against chemical exposure, but were instead instructed to use FFP2 masks and latex gloves. The authorities also found shortcomings in the separation of contaminated work clothing from clean street clothes.

World.title: Netopia Payments expands license to include money remittance services after Romania’s Central Bank approval
World.content:
Romanian payments and technology platform Netopia Payments is entering a new stage of development after it received the authorization of the National Bank of Romania (BNR) to expand its payment institution license to include money remittance services, the company said.

The company, which processes more than RON 10 billion annually, is preparing new embedded finance solutions and developing an integrated financial platform for merchants, it said.

The company aims to expand its portfolio of services for merchants beyond traditional online payment processing and toward a comprehensive financial ecosystem.

At the same time, it is preparing to diversify the payment methods it accepts, including through the integration of account-to-account (A2A) solutions such as RoPay, and to expand financing options offered through partners, including merchant cash advance products.

Netopia’s priorities for the coming period include operationalizing its newly licensed activities, developing new financial products, and expanding its technology and operational infrastructure.

“Obtaining the license from the National Bank of Romania validates our security and compliance standards, but more importantly, it provides the foundation on which we are building Netopia’s future. Our vision is to become a comprehensive growth partner for entrepreneurs in Romania,” Raluca Micu, CEO of Netopia, said.

In the medium term, the company aims to build a one-stop shop model for merchants, a unified platform integrating multiple payment methods, rapid funds collection, automated transaction reconciliation, and complementary financial services.

Netopia Payments is a Romanian payments and technology platform for merchants, providing digital payment infrastructure and financial solutions to thousands of companies. Since 2023, private equity fund Innova Capital holds a majority stake in the company.

(Photo: the company)
