A further 19% said their decision would depend on their financial situation.

For Kajal Singh, an HR professional working at a consultancy firm in Delhi, the workplace she wants comes down to âflexible work options, better work-life balance & a supportive environment.â

Harshita, a working professional from Bhopal, takes the idea of flexibility further. In her ideal workplace, she wants âflexibility and respect for the opinions of Gen Zs,â along with room for employees to decide how they execute their work.

The pattern is not confined to India. A separate Deloitte 2026 survey of Gen Zs and millennials found that 55% of Gen Zs and 52% of millennials are delaying major life decisions because of financial pressures. Only 25% of Gen Zs and 21% of millennials prefer rapid career progression through frequent promotions, while just 6% in both groups identify leadership as their primary career goal.

At the same time, 74% of both Gen Zs and millennials use AI to some extent in their day-to-day work, with many viewing it as an opportunity to improve productivity and open new career paths â even as they feel they are adapting faster than their organisations.

Taken together, the findings point to a generation caught between two competing demands: the need for financial security and the refusal to define success solely by the traditional career ladder.

The stereotype problem

The generation also appears to be tired of having that negotiation interpreted as a lack of ambition.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

More than half of respondents said older generations completely misunderstand Gen Zâs attitude towards work, while another 42.9% said they misunderstand it somewhat.

The most irritating stereotype was the idea that âGen Z doesn't want to workâ, selected by 81% of respondents. âGen Z quits too easilyâ followed at 76.2%. Other commonly selected stereotypes included being lazy, expecting too much and having no loyalty.

What does the survey indicate?

For employers, that makes the Gen Z workplace conversation less about choosing between stability and balance and more about whether the two can exist together. For young workers, the bigger challenge is figuring out which compromises build a career and which ones slowly consume the life that career was supposed to support.

World.title: Former wrestler ends life with her two children, dowry charges filed against in-laws
World.content:
Former national-level wrestler Ashwini Pol (30) and her two children died at Naldurg fort in Maharashtra’s Dharashiv district, while her third child has been seriously injured.

Dharashvi police have registered a case of abetment to suicide and dowry harassment against Ashwini’s spouse and her in-laws after a complaint was made by her father, Tanaji Shivaji Mohite (54). Mr. Mohite is a resident of Whantal in Umarga and a teacher by profession.

The incident was reported on Thursday (September 3, 2026), when her body was recovered from a 100-foot-deep gorge from the Upli bastion at the Naldurg Fort in Tuljapur tehsil.

“The prima facie investigation shows that Ashwini was harassed over dowry and mentally tortured for giving birth to twin daughters,” said Ravindra Gaikwad, investigating officer in the case.

Police registered the case under the under sections 80 (dowry death), 108 (abetment of suicide) and 85 (cruelty by a husband or his relatives against a woman) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).

Ashwini had won five gold and six silver medals in State- and national-level competitions of wrestling.

On the day of the incident, the wrestler, along with her six-year-old son, Ajinkya, and two-and-a-half-year-old twin daughters, Kranti and Veera, visited the fort. Ashwini and her son died on the spot, while one of the daughters, Kranti, succumbed to injuries during treatment at the hospital and Veera was put on ventilator, as per the police.

Before death, Ashwini and her children were living at her maternal home in Whantal in Umarga Tehsil.

[Assistance for overcoming suicidal thoughts is available on the State’s health helpline 104, Tele-MANAS 14416 and SNEHA’s suicide prevention helpline - 044 24640050 or from any of the numbers in this link]

World.title: University faculty recruitment to be completed by April 2027: Nara Lokesh
World.content:
Minister for Human Resource Development (HRD) Nara Lokesh on Saturday said the government would complete the recruitment of university faculty, including Professors, Associate Professors and Assistant Professors, by April next year.

Speaking at the State-level Best Teacher Awards ceremony in Vijayawada, Mr. Lokesh said the government would conduct the next three District Selection Committee (DSC) teacher recruitment examinations with the same transparency as the first one.

He highlighted the record of Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu, saying that 14 DSC examinations conducted during his tenure had resulted in the recruitment of nearly two lakh teachers. After becoming Chief Minister for the fourth time, Mr. Naidu’s first signature was on the DSC file, he said.

Describing teaching as a sacred responsibility, Mr. Lokesh said children spent more time with teachers than at home and learnt values, education and discipline from them. He cited A.P.J. Abdul Kalam’s teacher Sivasubramania Iyer as an example of how practical teaching could inspire extraordinary achievements.

The Minister said the government had expanded the “One Class-One Teacher” model to 10,000 primary schools, cancelled GO 117, filled 16,000 teacher vacancies through Mega DSC, introduced a Teacher Transfer Act and seniority lists, revised the curriculum and launched the LEAP app to address teachers’ service-related matters.

He said 1.10 lakh students had shifted from private schools to government schools this year, attributing the trend largely to the efforts of teachers. The government was also developing LEAP Model Schools and planned to establish such schools in every constituency, he said.

Mr. Lokesh said school education reforms had largely been completed and that the government was now focusing on higher education and universities. A unified university law was planned, while universities would be integrated with emerging sectors such as space, drones, aquaculture, pharmaceuticals and data centres, besides other industrial clusters, he said.

The government was making universities more research-oriented, with politically neutral appointments of Vice-Chancellors and stronger academic calendars, he said.

Mr. Lokesh said the government’s goal was to make Andhra Pradesh the No. 1 State in the National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF) rankings. He also urged teachers to pay close attention to students’ mental well-being, saying every child’s emotional state should be taken seriously. Failure, he said, should be viewed as a learning opportunity rather than the end of a student’s future.

Referring to “No Admission” boards displayed at some government schools, he said they showed that the reforms were beginning to produce results. The government would continue reviewing university courses, removing outdated programmes and introducing courses aligned with modern technologies and industry needs, he said.

World.title: B-to-A Khata conversion rebate window ends with 80,412 applications; only 12% of total beneficiaries
World.content:
Despite a 60% rebate on B-to-A Khata conversion charges, a meagre 12% of the estimated beneficiaries have applied for the conversion.

By the time the rebate window ended on August 23, the corporations under the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) had received 80,412 applications, while the revised estimate of the total number of properties stood at over 7 lakh.

According to GBA data, the applications received have generated a total of ₹525.7 crore in revenue for the corporations. One of the corporation commissioners told The Hindu that many applications are still under review and that the revenue would go up.

Bengaluru North City Corporation received the highest number of applications at 23,354, generating ₹144.9 crore in revenue. It was followed by the west corporation with 22,479 applications and a revenue of ₹131.1 crore and the south corporation with 17,262 applications, which generated ₹124.3 crore.

According to the GBA officials, the north and west corporations also have a larger number of B-Khata properties, which is why they have received more applications.

Rebate spurs takers

When the rebate was announced, the conversion charge was set at 5% of the guidance value in the area, which meant property owners had to spend lakhs of rupees, making it unattractive.

Fewer than 14,000 applications were received in the first few months. The government subsequently announced a discount by reducing the conversion charge to 2% of the guidance value.

A corporation commissioner said that even with the rebate, the scheme did not attract much interest initially, but gained substantial momentum in the last nine days of the discount window. Until August 14, about 48,000 applications had been received. In the next nine days, however, 32,000 applications flooded the corporations.

When asked whether the rebate scheme would be extended considering the last-minute surge, the officials said there were currently no discussions about it.

“The properties for which we have received most applications are also in places where the guidance value is relatively less, which means many are still contemplating the scheme. We also have cases where owners have applied for conversion and checked the charges, eventually retreating and not paying the charges,” the official added.

One of the major setbacks to the scheme is that the conversion would regularise the property or site, but would not automatically regularise buildings constructed on it.

Corporations not on board with another rebate

According to the GBA sources, the corporations are not interested in announcing rebates again, citing the drop in revenue. For instance, the north corporation’s 2026-27 budget outlay was over ₹4,300 crore, of which ₹680 crore was estimated to come from the B-to-A conversions. Similarly, other corporations had also made substantial revenue estimates, which have now taken a hit.

World.title: A.P. NGOs welcome U.N. decision to name Nov. 27 as day against child marriage
World.content:
Various Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) and child rights activists in Andhra Pradesh have welcomed the United Nations decision to declare November 27 as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage.

According to the National Family Health Survey (NFHS, 2019-21), 23.3% of women aged 20-24 were married before 18 years was 20.1% in the 2023-24 NFHS, said Child Rights Advocacy Foundation (CRAF) State Programme Director P. Francis Thambi.

The Centre has set a target to reduce child marriages by 10% in 2026, said JRC founder and international child rights activist Bhuwan Ribhu.

Advocate P. Rajya Lakshmi, who was fighting against child and forced marriages, urged the government to take measures for strict observance of the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriages on November 27. “An action plan should be prepared to create awareness among students in schools and colleges on the health and legal consequences of child marriages,” Ms. Lakshmi said on Saturday.

World.title: Artist Mohammed Ayazuddin Patel to attend cultural exchange, workshop in Italy
World.content:
Kalaburagi-based internationally acclaimed artist and photographer Mohammed Ayazuddin Patel has been invited to participate in the ‘International Collaborative Art Performance & Sculpture Workshop’ in Venice, Italy, from September 17 to 20.

Titled ‘Art Beyond Borders: A Creative Dialogue Between India and Italy’, the three-day artistic exchange is jointly organised by the S.M.D. Foundation and H.U. Venezia, and will bring together 11 distinguished Indian artists representing Karnataka, Assam, Kolkata, Mumbai, Delhi, Madhya Pradesh and Baroda, alongside leading European artists.

The workshop seeks to transform art into a bridge between cultures through collaborative performances, sculpture, dialogue and creative exchange, fostering friendship and deeper connections between Indian and European artistic communities.

The Venice programme forms part of a 15-day European study tour from September 9 to 23, covering France, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland and Italy, as well as Florence, Rome and Vatican City. The participating artists will visit celebrated museums, galleries and monuments, encountering masterpieces associated with Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Vincent Van Gogh, Rembrandt, and Picasso.

For Mr. Patel, the journey will include visits to the Louvre Museum, the Van Gogh Museum, the Sistine Chapel, the Accademia Gallery, and the Colosseum, offering an inspiring encounter with the artistic heritage of Europe.

A noted resource person on the art, architecture, and history of the Deccan dynasties, Mr. Patel is a recipient of the National Lalit Kala Award (2014), the CCRT National Fellowship, Ministry of Culture (2016-17), and the Karnataka Lalit Kala Academy Senior Fellowship (2018), among several other honours. He has also established his own art gallery, museum and research centre.

Having travelled extensively across the United States, United Kingdom, Russia, Turkey, China, Egypt, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Bhutan and several other countries, Mr. Patel continues to expand his artistic journey across borders.

From the Deccan to Venice, the journey carries more than an artist; it carries a dialogue between cultures and histories.

World.title: NSAB member calls for reverse migration to villages
World.content:
National Security Advisory Board (NSAB) member G. Satheesh Reddy on Saturday called for reverse migration to villages, stressing the need to improve farm incomes and revive the rural economy.

According to a press release, Mr. Reddy was speaking after launching the Atria Foundation’s Project Chittoor at the Agro Wellness Centre in Thirumalarajapuram of Palasamudram mandal. He said that India, which once exported agricultural produce, was now importing pulses and other basic crops, underlining the neglect of farmers and villages.

He called for greater adoption of natural and organic farming to increase farm output while making rural areas healthier and more attractive for people to reside.

Project Chittoor founder C.S. Sunder Raju said that a 600-acre integrated farm had already been developed. The initiative plans to expand to 6,000 acres by June 2027 and ultimately cover 60,000 acres within 24 months. “The project integrates sustainable agriculture, renewable energy, rural education, and agro-wellness tourism to create sustainable rural incomes,” he said.

World.title: Andhra Pradesh aims to achieve 100% literacy by 2027, says CM Naidu
World.content:
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu on Saturday called for sweeping reforms in the education system to keep pace with rapidly evolving technology, adding that the government aims to achieve 100% literacy in Andhra Pradesh by 2027.

Courses from the school level to higher education must be restructured to meet future requirements, and teachers have a crucial responsibility in preparing students for emerging challenges, he said while speaking at the Teachers’ Day celebrations.

The Chief Minister greeted teachers on the occasion and urged them to create awareness among students about emerging fields such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), quantum technology, robotics and data analytics.

‘Technology can’t replace teachers’

Mr. Naidu said that despite the growing use of AI and other technologies, teachers can never be replaced. Along with technological knowledge, students must be equipped with values, culture, patriotism and love for the nature.

He stressed that education should not remain confined to theory and called for greater opportunities for students to learn through practical experience outside the classroom.

The Chief Minister asked teachers to develop their schools into distinctive brands and ensure that every school-age child pursues education.

Teachers should encourage students to develop a love for learning while nurturing innovation, creativity, problem-solving and leadership qualities, he said, suggesting that students should begin developing proficiency in AI from Class VII itself.

Mr. Naidu stressed the importance of sports, nature, yoga and meditation in the overall development of students. He suggested using Saturdays, observed as ‘No Bag Day’, for activities such as tree plantation and other experiential learning programmes.

He said that technologies such as Clicker and AI Tutor were being used to transform teaching methods. He said the education system should also be aligned with industrial requirements.

Referring to the government’s broader vision, Mr. Naidu said the foundation for India to become a global leader by 2047 and Andhra Pradesh to emerge as the No. 1 State must be laid in schools, with teachers playing the central role. He called upon teachers to shape students into future leaders and said India could regain its position as Vishwaguru only through the efforts of teachers.

The Chief Minister recalled that the coalition government’s first signature was on the file related to the recruitment of teachers through Mega DSC exam. Despite attempts to obstruct the recruitment process through more than 350 petitions, the government overcame the hurdles and provided jobs, he said.

175 teachers felicitated

Later, the Chief Minister and HRD Minister Nara Lokesh felicitated 175 teachers selected as the State’s best teachers.

World.title: Nandyal school alumni honour teachers with unique chariot celebration
World.content:
Nearly 750 alumni from various batches of Sri Ramakrishna Vidyalayam, Nandyal, gathered on the occasion of the Teachers Day celebrations to honour teachers on Saturday. The teachers were seated on a chariot as students and well-wishers pulled it through the streets using ropes. “This was done to convey the message that teachers are the charioteers who guide students through the journey of life,” the organisers said.

By pulling the chariot, we express our gratitude and acknowledge the invaluable role of our teachers in shaping our lives, character and future, said M.V. Sivakumar Reddy, an alumni of the school and founder of Mana Ooru-Mana Gudi- Mana Bhadyatha (Our Village, Our Temple, Our Responsibility) organisation.

Mr. Sivakumar Reddy and his teammates cleaned the school two days before the event.

World.title: Naqvi says new administrative units to be formed only with people's consent
World.content:
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Saturday said that any new administrative units in the country would only be formed if the people voiced their support for such a move.

Addressing the National Policy Dialogue in Lahore, he said, “Reset does not mean breaking the system. Under no circumstances does it mean breaking the system. It means that whatever is wrong should be changed.”

Naqvi stressed that the changes should be brought through “political consensus” and “according to the will of our people”. He added that if the nation did not want the new administrative units, they would not be created.

He emphasised that such a change could not be brought about only based on the will of an individual, a political party or a government.

“And this would only happen if the people want it and consent to it,” he maintained.

The interior minister called for a dialogue that would consider the positive and negative aspects of new units. “Draft a thing and present it to the people, asking them whether they accept it or not.”

On the question of how many new administrative units should be created with what territorial limits, Naqvi emphasised the need to review their “benefits, methods and financial consequences”.

“Most importantly, our parliament, experts and those people responsible for it should debate on it, and finally, we must seek our public’s opinion.”

The minister clarified that his comments from last month were not about any particular political party, but rather about the “system” that has been in place since the country’s independence.

Naqvi called for undertaking the proposed administrative reforms as per the Constitution. “It has to be done through democratic means.”

“Under no circumstances are we ready to accept that we have become so incapable that we cannot reset this system,” he said, calling for political parties to hold deliberations on the matter.

The interior minister asserted he would not abandon the idea, adding that many “emotional” speeches were being made about the administrative units.

He urged politicians not to get emotional about the topic, adding that the change was not one that would happen overnight.

The minister contended that the country’s administrative system had lost its effectiveness and its “impact is not reaching the public at all”.

Acknowledging administrative issues, Naqvi said, “Even today, four out of every 10 children are not receiving the education they need. Today, only 55 per cent of the population has access to clean drinking water, and there are still two million cases pending in our courts.”

These were the issues that the government was trying to rectify, he contended.

Describing himself as the “biggest supporter of Islamabad province”, Naqvi called for the federal capital to receive its share of the National Finance Commission (NFC) Award.

“Islamabad is the only city that does not get a single rupee from the budget of Pakistan,” he insisted, adding that declaring Islamabad a province would give its citizens their rights.

The minister also highlighted the population factor in the disbursement of the NFC award, saying it remained an “incentive” for provinces. “That incentive is present till today, so are we waiting for that bomb to explode? […] Does this not need to be reset?”

Naqvi further said, “Governments keep changing; policies keep changing; budgets come and go; and we keep making plans. But the biggest issue is how much we are able to deliver in the end.”

He added that if, despite all the potential that Pakistan has, “we are still not getting the results, it is necessary to reset it (the system)”.

Citing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an example, Naqvi said the politicians who came to power as mayors knew their citizens and their problems the best.

The minister stressed that the proposed reforms would aim to empower the people. He said a Sindhi would remain Sindhi and a Punjabi would remain Punjabi. “No one will be asked to surrender their identity,” he assured the public.

He added that the discussion on the proposed reforms was not supposed to be based on generational, tribal or regional divides. “Its aim is improved governance, a competent system and bringing people closer to the government.”

Concluding his address, Naqvi reiterated: “In no circumstances should we stray from the will of the people. All political parties will have to deliberate on this. It cannot be one person’s issue or one province’s decision.”

He added, “If this is what the public wants, then it will happen no matter what.”

In July, Naqvi had proposed a dialogue among all political parties to bring about reforms to the current governance system, while also calling for new provinces and urgent administrative reforms.

His comments had ignited an animated debate across the country, with the PPP referring the question to its top decision-making forum, the Sindh chief minister flatly rejecting it, Lahore’s lawyers terming it unconstitutional and Sindhi nationalist groups demanding the minister’s resignation.

World.title: Punjab faces greater threat from other provinces than 'neighbouring countries': CM Maryam
World.content:
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz on Saturday said the province faced a greater security threat from “neighbouring provinces than from neighbouring countries”, stressing that terrorism entered Punjab through its provincial borders.

Speaking at an AI technology event in Lahore, the chief minister said, “The unfortunate thing is that the threat [Punjab] faces comes less from my neighbouring countries and more from my neighbouring provinces.”

“Terrorism enters Punjab from there. Everyone has their eyes on Punjab, but, thank God, Punjab remains safe. The kind of threats we face come from all our provincial borders,” she said.

The chief minister asserted that there had been a significant improvement in the law and order situation since her government came to power in 2024.

She identified organised crime and religious intolerance as some of the main challenges that Punjab faced.

In an apparent reference to the now-banned Tehreek-i-Labbaik Pakistan (TLP), CM Maryam said some groups “spread hatred under the cover of religion” and were “political parties in reality”.

She went on to state that religious events were now held peacefully, compared to the situation of “religious polarisation” a couple of years ago.

Maryam said Punjab was now the country’s “most AI-enabled province” and had invested billions of rupees in technology and security to protect and strengthen it.

She said that when she assumed office, she discovered that terrorists possessed more advanced technology than the government, including night-vision cameras, and were carrying out attacks with carefully devised plans.

“Thank God, we now have a complete system in place,” she said, adding that cameras had been made bulletproof because terrorists used to target them. Thermal cameras and drones had also been deployed at checkpoints and joint checkpoints to strengthen security and protect people.

The Punjab CM recalled that attacks on checkpoints had previously resulted in the deaths of five people and, at times, as many as 10. “Attacks still happen, but the loss of life has been significantly reduced,” she said, attributing the improvement to investment in fortification and technology.

Referring to the katcha areas, Maryam said they had previously been a hub of terrorism and crime, including kidnappings for ransom and honey traps.

“With the support we have received from the military and the Punjab government, and with the cooperation of the Sindh government, the situation has now changed. The area has become largely crime-free, and the writ of the state has been established,” she declared.

The chief minister also said she had decided “a few days ago” to take action against elements involved in corruption.

“I am not talking about government ranks or referring to police ranks … I am talking about us as a nation. We have become so accustomed to corruption that it has become part of our daily routine,” she said.

Maryam noted her government had also established a system to ensure immediate action against corrupt elements. “If people do not trust their state, that country can never move forward,” she remarked.

World.title: JI warns of nationwide wheel-jam strike unless govt provides economic relief
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Saturday warned that the party would launch a nationwide wheel-jam strike if the government delayed approving public demands for economic relief.

The development came two days after a countrywide protest, during which six party workers were arrested for allegedly burning motorcycles and tyres in Karachi. The JI has distanced itself from these elements.

On the same day, Rehman, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal and Prime Minister’s Adviser Rana Sanaullah announced that the JI and federal government would form committees to recommend measures for reducing the petroleum levy and providing relief to the public.

Addressing a news conference in the federal capital alongside JI Deputy Chief Mian Muhammad Aslam and Islamabad Amir Nasrullah Randhawa, Rehman said formal negotiations with the government would begin on Monday, while sit-in protests across the country would continue simultaneously.

He also criticised the current administration and bureaucracy, describing them as an unconstitutional “Form-47 arrangement” that was passing the burden of its inefficiency and extravagance on to the public through heavy taxation.

Highlighting that the JI had protested for 21 days, with sit-ins held at dozens of locations, including 20 sites in Balochistan and Swat, Rehman maintained that public pressure had forced electricity prices down by Rs10–12 per unit, saved the national exchequer Rs4,300 billion through negotiations with IPPs, and prevented petrol prices from rising further.

Addressing the national economic crisis, the JI chief said Pakistan’s total debt had reached Rs110,000bn, while annual interest payments stood at Rs8,000bn.

He argued that a three per cent cut in the central bank’s policy rate would eliminate the need for the petroleum levy altogether.

Criticising systemic corruption, he highlighted Rs1,300bn in annual losses due to “incompetence” at the Federal Board of Revenue and condemned continued payments to re-gasification plants even when liquefied natural gas was not being supplied.

The JI chief also drew attention to governance failures in the social sector, citing a devastating fire at the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences and a 50pc failure rate in Punjab’s ninth-grade examinations.

Rehman criticised Sindh’s key political parties, describing them as “opportunistic” and accusing them of leaving Karachi’s issues unaddressed. He said the grievances had driven residents to demand a separate province.

Announcing the party’s future plans, Rehman said the JI would launch a signature campaign targeting 50 million citizens to push for structural relief, local government reforms and a reduction in bread prices to Rs10.

World.title: US ambassador says Israel not planning forced displacement from Gaza
World.content:
The US ambassador to Israel said on Saturday there was no plan underway to force Palestinians out of Gaza, after Israeli ministers laid out ideas on how to expel the war-battered territory’s two million people.

“I can tell you categorically there is no plan of the Israelis to displace people out of Gaza against their will,” Ambassador Mike Huckabee told reporters as he visited Palestinian-Americans in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

Israeli far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir laid out a plan on Thursday that aims to see the departure of 250,000 Palestinians from Gaza in the first year, followed by the rest of the roughly two million residents over the following six years.

His remarks came a day after Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel was ready to remove Palestinians from Gaza by sea and land but was waiting for the United States, which he said was discussing where the population would go. Katz, without citing his source, claimed 80 per cent of people in Gaza wanted to leave but that Hamas was preventing them.

Huckabee said that President Donald Trump’s administration — which has made hostility to international migration a central priority — wanted to give Palestinians the option to leave by choice.

“There is an open-mindedness if people wish to leave, that they should have the right to leave,” Huckabee said, calling it a “disgrace” to “incarcerate” Palestinians inside Gaza.

“Nobody is suggesting there would be forced displacement — the Israelis are not, the Americans are not. I know of no one who supports that,” he said.

Forced displacement of a civilian population from occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva Conventions.

Virtually the entire population of Gaza has already been displaced internally by Israel’s military offensive following the Hamas-led Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel.

Since the war, some far-right Israeli politicians have spoken of bringing settlers back to the Gaza Strip, where Israel dismantled settlements in 2005 as part of a unilateral plan to disengage from the densely populated region.

The remarks on displacement come in the run-up to the October 27 elections, in which polls show a tight race for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has brought once-shunned far-right figures into his cabinet.

US President Donald Trump stunned the world early in his second term by proposing to displace all Palestinians at least temporarily from Gaza and turn the rubble-strewn Mediterranean territory into a luxury resort.

He backtracked after pushback from countries including Egypt, the only country other than Israel to border Gaza.

Israel has ‘responsibility’ to ensure safety of West Bank Palestinians

The US ambassador to Israel also said that the Israeli government bore responsibility for West Bank Palestinians’ safety and should impose “severe consequences” over violence, as he visited families after a surge in settler attacks.

Mike Huckabee, long known as a staunch supporter of Israel and settlers, visited a Palestinian-American’s home in the West Bank that has been repeatedly targeted by settlers and said he wanted to hear the community’s “legitimate grievances”.

As the ambassador met families inside a finely manicured old house in the town of Turmus Ayya, where around 80pc of the 4,000 residents hold US citizenship, a settler from a nearby illegal outpost approached in a quad bike.

“One of the messages that we have been sending and we will continue to send is that people in these communities have a right to live with a level of security and safety, and that the government has a responsibility to make sure that that happens,” Huckabee said.

Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967 and violence by Israeli settlers towards Palestinian residents has persisted for years, often with little or no legal consequence, but recent months have seen a surge in attacks ahead of October 27 elections.

Huckabee stopped short of criticising Israel by name but said: “Our clear message is that crime is crime, terror is terror.

“When people do it they should have an expectation that they will have severe consequences,” Huckabee said.

He said that taking action was in the “best interest” of Israel, which already faces growing criticism around the world, including in key ally the United States, over the devastating offensive in Gaza in response to the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack.

“Their reputation does not do well when it appears that this tiny little group of marauders are somehow representative of the larger population. I don’t believe that it is,” Huckabee said.

“There may be a few hundred who are responsible, but that’s a few hundred too many,” Huckabee said.

‘US has the ability’

“We have many issues that we will address,” Nawwaf Zaghoul, the town’s mayor, told reporters ahead of the meeting, describing what he said were constant attacks by settlers.

He said that the town’s residents would be asking the ambassador to help secure their safety and security. About 80 per cent of the town’s roughly 3,000 residents were Palestinian Americans, he said.

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee is greeted by members of the local municipality as he arrives to visit the home of an American-Palestinian resident who has previously been twice attacked and faces ongoing harassment from Israeli settlers, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank town of Turmus Ayya, about 23 kilometers northeast of Ramallah, where a large proportion of the town’s residents hold dual nationality on Sept 5, 2026. — AFP

Huckabee spent about two hours meeting Palestinian-Americans inside the home of Samir Hazmeh before joining the community in a lunch of maqluba, a dish of rice and meat served after flipping the pot upside down.

Hazmeh said the house in which he welcomed Huckabee had its windows smashed twice by settlers, who have also tried to open the gates and burn it down. He has put up both barbed wire and an American flag in hopes of protection.

Yasser Alqam, who met the ambassador, owns land just 100 metres away but said he cannot return after several attacks by settlers.

“The United States already has the ability to put pressure on Israel to at least arrest those settlers who are known to the authorities,” he said, voicing shock that US President Donald Trump lifted sanctions on settler extremists imposed by predecessor Joe Biden.

Alqam’s wife Jinan, wearing a traditional Palestinian dress, said she voiced hope to Huckabee that he “can do something for us and provide us with protection from the settlers so that we can reach our land and pick the olives” in the coming season.

Huckabee also visited Taybeh, one of the only Christian villages remaining in the West Bank, in June 2025 after a church there was vandalised. Huckabee said at the time that the desecration of a place of worship was an act of terror and a crime.

‘Thou shalt not steal’

Ahead of elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has been ramping up approval of new settlements, which are illegal under international law. More than 500,000 Israelis live in the West Bank amid three million Palestinians.

Despite Huckabee’s dismissal of violent settlers as a small minority, Netanyahu has brought into his government far-right ministers who have openly mused about expelling the Palestinian population.

Huckabee, an evangelical Christian pastor and former governor of Arkansas, has long cited his faith to back Israel and earlier would not even use the term Palestinian.

Speaking of violence by settlers, Huckabee said, “I think the Scripture is pretty clear — Thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not kill, and thou shalt not even covet.”

Huckabee earlier intervened when settler extremists camped out and blocked basic supplies from reaching another Palestinian-American in the town of Qusra last month, leading to rare condemnation by Netanyahu of settlers.

Huckabee refers to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, a term used by the Israeli government but not adopted by the US government. He has visited Shiloh, a settlement near Turmus Ayya, at least twice since 2025.

In February, Huckabee drew widespread condemnation from at least 14 countries, including Pakistan, after he suggested that he would not be opposed to Tel Aviv taking over large swathes of the Middle East.

World.title: Karachi police arrest two over alleged abduction of young man in DHA
World.content:
KARACHI: Police on Saturday said they had arrested two suspects in connection with the alleged assault of a young man in DHA Phase 8.

South Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Syed Asad Raza told Dawn that two of the suspects, Ibrahim Fahad and Waqar, had been arrested in connection with the case.

He said a third suspect, Ibrahim Malik, had fled to Lahore, while a fourth, Irtiza, was still absconding.

According to the DIG, the incident reportedly stemmed from a dispute involving a girl.

The first information report (FIR), a copy of which is available with Dawn, was registered at Sahil police station in the early hours of Saturday on the complaint of Syed Ali Jafri. According to the FIR, the incident took place on the night of Aug 29.

The FIR invoked sections 34 (acts done by several persons), 337-A(i) (punishment of shajjah), 337-V(arsh for hair), 365 (kidnapping or abducting with intent secretly and wrongfully to confine person) and 506-B (criminal intimidation if threat be to cause death or grievous hurt) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC).

Jafri also spoke to the media on Saturday, recalling details of the incident and explaining that the “delay” in getting the FIR registered was because he had been threatened by the suspects against doing so.

In his complaint, Jafri said he “remained silent” after the incident as he was scared, but approached the police after the suspects shared his video on social media.

Jafri stated that he and his friend had gone to an e-gaming facility in Bukhari Commercial, where his friend’s acquaintance also joined them.

He said he had never met the acquaintance before. The three later went to a nearby cafe and, upon leaving, were approached by a vehicle that stopped in front of them. A man, whom Jafri identified as another acquaintance of his friend, then stepped out of the vehicle.

The man struck Jafri on the neck with a baseball bat, after which the friend’s acquaintance and “three unknown persons” accompanying him allegedly shoved the complainant into the vehicle and took him to an empty plot at Sahil Avenue in Phase 8, the FIR alleged.

He further alleged that he was beaten on his legs with the baseball bat and that his hair was pulled, causing some of it to come out. He was then asked to “eat them”, the FIR said.

Jafri said one of the unknown individuals was carrying a gun and that the attackers recorded a video of the assault. According to the FIR, he was shown pictures of his family members and threatened with similar action against them if he complained about the incident.

Jafri said he was taken back to Bukhari Commercial in the same vehicle. The complainant also alleged that the suspects demanded Rs30,000 from him. By the time he reached home, he said, one of the individuals involved had already informed his family about the incident.

The complainant nominated the three as suspects in the FIR.

Last month, a scuffle took place in DHA’s Phase 6 between residents of two apartments, with an inquiry revealing that police officials were involved in the incident and recommending action against them.

World.title: GB CM constitutes committee to review trekking rules after deadly Broad Peak avalanche
World.content:
GILGIT: Gilgit-Baltistan Chief Minister Amjad Hussain has constituted a three-member committee to review the 1999 Trekking Rules and Regulations, according to a statement issued by the CM House on Saturday, a few weeks after 10 mountaineers lost their lives when an avalanche struck on Broad Peak.

The 10 members were part of an expedition led by world-renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja. They were struck by the avalanche on July 30. Purja’s company later announced that there were no survivors.

CM Hussain expressed deep concern over multiple accidents during mountaineering activities this year, which claimed the lives of 13 foreign climbers including two Pakistanis.

In another recent accident, Pakistani clim­ber Asma Mushtaq, 34, died on GB’s Spantik Peak on Aug 20 while desc­ending from the mountain after suffering from high-altitude sickness. A ground team recovered her body on Monday, almost 10 days after her death on the 7,027-metre-tall mountain.

The GB chief minister has directed the committee to review the relevant procedures, terms and conditions, and standard operating procedures (SOPs) for dealing with mountaineering incidents. It has also been tasked with determining responsibility for any negligence or administrative lapses in the delayed rescue operations following recent accidents.

The committee will be headed by Forest, Wildlife and Parks Secretary Subtain Ahmed, with Information Technology Secretary Zameer Abbas and Baltistan Division Commissioner Kamal Khan serving as members.

The CM has further directed the committee to determine responsibility for any shortcomings in the Broad Peak incident, conduct a clause-by-clause review of the existing trekking regulations, and identify outdated, ineffective or incomplete provisions.

He also directed the relevant institutions to ensure the safety and security of mountaineers, trekking groups, guides and porters.

A source told Dawn that complaints had been submitted to CM Hussain regarding negligence and delay in rescue operations.

CM Hussain said it was essential to update regulations concerning permits and registration, briefing and debriefing, the responsibilities of liaison officers and mountain guides, safety equipment, porters’ wages and welfare, insurance, medical facilities and evacuation, communication systems, and emergency response procedures.

He specifically directed a review of the existing insurance coverage for liaison officers, mountain guides and porters, adding that realistic and effective insurance coverage should be proposed in view of current risks and costs.

He further directed the committee to review arrangements for search and rescue, helicopter evacuation, weather forecasting and early warning systems, communications, and emergency assistance in remote and restricted areas.

CM Hussain tasked the committee with developing mandatory safety protocols to minimise the risk of loss of life in the future.

The chief minister said that, given the growing popularity of trekking and mountaineering in Gilgit-Baltistan, the existing classification of open and restricted zones, as well as various trekking routes and mountain passes, should also be updated in accordance with ground realities.

He said a digital permit and registration system, effective coordination among relevant institutions, and periodic reviews of laws governing the trekking and mountaineering sector were now essential.

CM Hussain also reiterated that the GB government would promote mountaineering and tourism in the region without compromising the safety and security of tourists, mountaineers, guides and porters.

The committee has been directed to submit a comprehensive report, recommendations and a draft of the proposed amendments to the laws and SOPs to the relevant authority within 15 days.

The committee has not yet submitted its report.

A government official familiar with the region’s tourism industry told Dawn that the committee had found some tour operators responsible for violating mountaineering rules during the expedition.

According to the official, some tour operators had failed to arrange insurance for climbers or helicopters in case of a rescue operation.

“Under the rules, if a ground rescue team or helicopter is needed, the tour operator is responsible for arranging a rescue team and paying for helicopter insurance,” the source said.

Some operators had also failed to conduct the briefing and debriefing sessions required under the 1999 Trekking Rules, according to the official.

In a recent statement, the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) said that search-and-rescue operations relied on government resources, adding that Pakistan lacks a dedicated and properly established high-altitude rescue system.

The ACP said that it was working with relevant authorities to develop an effective rescue framework and support improvements to the country’s mountaineering infrastructure.

More than 2,200 foreign climbers and trekkers visited GB during the summer season from April to August this year, a senior official of the GB Tourism Department said.

Sajid Hussain, deputy director of the GB Tourism Department, told Dawn that foreign adventurers visited the region to scale some of the world’s highest peaks and trek in restricted areas, including K2 (8,611 metres), Nanga Parbat (8,126m), Broad Peak (8,047m), Gasherbrum-I (8,080m) and Gasherbrum-II (8,035m).

The official added that a large number of foreign and domestic tourists were currently visiting popular destinations across GB. Foreign tourists visiting open-zone areas do not require permits.

Officials further said foreign tourists visiting GB’s tourist destinations and open-zone areas from multiple countries during the spring, summer and autumn seasons were expected to surpass 10,000 this year.

GB Tourism Department’s Hussain said the number of foreign adventurers visiting GB this summer was higher than last year.

As of June 30, the GB government had earned Rs350 million from expedition and trekking pe­­rmits for this summer.

World.title: Eight Pakistan Bar Council members reject proposed changes to council rules
World.content:
Eight members of the Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) have rejected proposed amendments seeking to make the council’s proceedings and deliberations confidential, saying the regulatory body of the legal fraternity should instead operate with transparency.

In a letter to the PBC secretary, the eight members — Abid Shahid Zuberi, Muhammad Maqsood Buttar, M Shafqat Mehmood-Chauhan, Munir Ahmed Kakar, Abdul Sattar Khan, Salman Akram Raja, Salahuddin Ahmed and Qazi Muhammad Arshad — said all proceedings of the council should be open, since it was an elected body representing the entire legal fraternity.

“We are not a private club or some secretive government agency,” the two-page letter said. A copy of the letter was also sent to Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Usman Awan, who is the ex-official chairman of the PBC.

The letter emphasised that, as a general rule, all proceedings, deliberations and business of the council should be open and transparent and available for scrutiny by the more than 100,000 lawyers it represented, as well as the public at large.

The PBC intends to amend Rule 97 of the Pakistan Legal Practitioners and Bar Councils Rules, 1976, by introducing a new Rule 97-A to provide for the confidentiality and classification of proceedings of the council and its committees.

Under the proposed rule, all acts, proceedings, deliberations and business of the PBC, its committees, tribunals, sub-committees and other bodies constituted under its authority would be treated as confidential and classified. Such information could not be disclosed, communicated, circulated, published or otherwise made available to any person without the express authorisation of the council or the relevant committee.

The proposed amendment also states that no PBC officer, employee, consultant, adviser or any other person with access to the council’s confidential proceedings or records by virtue of their office or functions may disclose, reproduce, transmit, circulate or publish such information, except as otherwise provided under the rules.

The confidentiality under this rule will extend to electronic records, emails, electronic communications, audio or video recordings, digital files, photographs, copies and reproductions of any document or proceedings of the council or its committees, the amendment suggested.

The members recalled that it was also stated in the Sept 4 letter to the members, which was circulated through WhatsApp, that the rules committee had decided that, since the meeting was not being convened shortly, the amendments should be circulated among the members of the PBC under Rule 91 of the Pakistan Legal Practitioners & Bar Councils Rules, 1976, for their views or approval.

The eight members, in their letter, had also drawn the council’s attention to the fact that they had taken strong exception, at the outset, to the manner in which the 1976 rules were sought to be amended, i.e. by way of circular resolution.

Firstly, Rule 91 of the 1976 Rules provides that, “in case of emergency”, the PBC may pass a resolution by way of circulation.

However, neither the secretary nor the rules committee has explained the “emergency” that requires the overnight amendment of the statutory rules, the letter emphasised, adding that circular resolutions were not a substitute for a proper meeting of the PBC, where the merits and demerits of a proposal could be fully discussed and members would have an opportunity to debate and convince each other.

“Unfortunately, there appears to be a trend now in the PBC to pass hugely important and consequential amendments to statutory rules through circular resolutions and bypass the requirement of convening a meeting, even when, clearly, there is no ‘emergency’,” the letter regretted.

Besides, under Rule 91, the rules committee has the power, in case of an emergency, to pass a circular resolution instead of convening a meeting of the rules committee itself. However, it has no power to do so in respect of meetings of the council.

The rules committee is not the convening authority for the full PBC house, nor can it determine when a full PBC meeting is likely to be held, or decide whether any “emergency” exists, the letter highlighted.

The contents of the proposed amendment, however, are even more shocking, the letter stated, as it provides that all acts, proceedings, deliberations and business of the PBC (and any of its committees or other bodies) shall be confidential and classified and shall not be disclosed, circulated or communicated by any PBC member or employee without express permission.

The eight members urged all other members to remember that the council was an elected body and its members were statutory representatives of the entire legal fraternity, rather than a “private club or some secretive government agency”.

“Therefore, all its proceedings, deliberations and business, as a matter of general rule, must be open, transparent and available for the scrutiny of the more than one lakh lawyers we represent, as well as the public at large.”

There may possibly be some limited exceptions to this general rule (for example, in sensitive disciplinary cases involving the privacy of individuals), but the general rule for the PBC must be transparency, the letter emphasised.

“Neither we, personally, nor the PBC, collectively, have anything to hide. Unfortunately, this proposed amendment seeks secrecy as the general rule and disclosure and transparency as the exception,” the letter stated.

The proposed amendment violates the freedom of speech guaranteed under Article 19 of the Constitution and also violates the right to information guaranteed under Article 19-A of the Constitution, the letter highlighted, rejecting the proposed amendments.

World.title: Fresh Yemen clashes kill more than 60: military, medical sources
World.content:
Fighting between Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and the country’s Houthi rebels killed more than 60 people on Saturday, including civilians, medical and military sources told AFP.

The renewed clashes in Yemen’s southwest over control of a gateway to the Red Sea came after Friday saw some of the deadliest fighting in years, following the collapse in July of a 2022 ceasefire.

According to three Yemeni military sources, 26 government troops were killed during several hours of fighting in the country’s southwest, while medical and military sources from the Houthis said 31 rebel fighters were killed.

One medical source in the government-held city of Taiz said a missile strike also killed six civilians travelling by bus and wounded seven others.

A government official blamed the strike on the bus, travelling between Taiz and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in Aden, on the Houthis.

In Taiz, a military officer said the “coming hours will be decisive” after the Houthis seized positions near the city a day earlier.

The officer added that reinforcements had been arriving from Aden in response to the Houthi offensive, which aims to cut off the government-held port city of Mokha, under fire for weeks, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

On Friday, the fighting killed 129 people, according to an AFP tally compiled from several sources.

With Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ships, the Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint has gained importance as a transit route for oil from Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest exporter of crude.

A military official told AFP on Saturday that three airstrikes by Saudi Arabia, a key backer of the government in Aden, had targeted positions recently captured by the Houthis in Taiz.

In July, a fragile truce between the Houthis and Yemen’s government fell apart after the rebels welcomed an Iranian plane to the capital Sanaa, setting off a spate of attacks.

The fighting between the Houthis and government troops supported by US ally Saudi Arabia signals the emergence of a new front in the wider Middle East war, which broke out in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

The Houthis have also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and have begun targeting its ships and territory.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.
